abunai.meaning_mnemonic: The rope bridge on the mountain trail is missing every third plank, and the river roars a long way down through each gap. Standing where one bad step drops you into that is <vocabulary>dangerous</vocabulary>.
abunai.reading_mnemonic: A marmot on the mountain trail whistles something like <reading>'a boo, nigh'</reading> whenever a hiker drifts toward the cliff edge. Hikers learned that the shrill <reading>あぶない</reading> whistle means the next step is <vocabulary>dangerous</vocabulary>.

achira.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane never turns to point at the shrine gate. She just tips her chin toward <vocabulary>over there (polite)</vocabulary> and lets the cats show the way.

aeru-potential.meaning_mnemonic: There is nothing extra to learn here, since the <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> point at exactly the same idea.
aeru-potential.reading_mnemonic: You already say 「あ」 this way in 会う, so <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> is nothing more than <reading>あえる</reading>.

agaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>up</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to go up</vocabulary> verb point the same way. The trailing kana just turn it into a verb where the thing rises on its own, with nobody lifting it.
agaru.reading_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, <reading>a guru</reading> watches the tortoise's crack climb from the ground line on its own and whispers 「<reading>あがる</reading>」: no hand lifts it, yet it starts <vocabulary form="上がる">to rise</vocabulary>.

ageru.meaning_mnemonic: A kangaroo has taken over the konbini till and keeps reaching into its pouch to <vocabulary>give out</vocabulary> a free onigiri to everyone in line. A <reading>kangaroo</reading> handing its whole pouch away, one item at a time, is <reading>あげる</reading>.

ageru-raise.meaning_mnemonic: Get both hands under a crate and shove it <kanji>up</kanji> until it rests higher than it began. Doing that on purpose to some object is to <vocabulary>raise</vocabulary> it.
ageru-raise.reading_mnemonic: You already know 上 is read 「あ」 from 上がる, so <vocabulary>to raise</vocabulary> is simply <reading>あげる</reading>.

aida.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>between</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>between</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning, so there is nothing new to learn here.
aida.reading_mnemonic: Kids at the open gate dare each other, '<reading>I dare</reading> you,' to step into the sliver of low sun caught <vocabulary form="間">between</vocabulary> the two doors: 「<reading>あいだ</reading>」.

aisukuriimu.meaning_mnemonic: One touch of the cold scoop on a filled tooth and you let out an <reading>I scream</reading>. The frozen sweet that caused it is <vocabulary form="アイスクリーム">ice cream</vocabulary>, <reading>アイスクリーム</reading>.

aite.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hand</kanji> that reaches back to meet yours from the <kanji>mutual</kanji> side of a deal or a match is <vocabulary>the other party</vocabulary>.

aka-color.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>red</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, so the meaning simply carries over.
aka-color.reading_mnemonic: You already met this reading in 赤ちゃん, so the word for <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> is just <reading>あか</reading> again.

akachan.meaning_mnemonic: New babies are born with tightly scrunched, <kanji>red</kanji> faces, so a <vocabulary>baby</vocabulary> is the reddest person in any room.
akachan.reading_mnemonic: Out in the hospital lot a <reading>car</reading> alarm blares, and the brand-new 「<reading>あかちゃん</reading>」 scrunches its face even redder, easily the reddest <vocabulary form="赤ちゃん">baby</vocabulary> in the room.

akai.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>red</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so nothing about the meaning shifts. The trailing い is the piece that makes it an adjective, ready to sit before a noun.
akai.reading_mnemonic: You already know 赤 is read 「あか」 from 赤ちゃん earlier in the course, so <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> is just that sound carried on into <reading>あかい</reading>.

akarui.meaning_mnemonic: You flick one switch in the windowless storeroom and ten strip lights blaze on at once, and suddenly you are squinting. A room that hard on the eyes is <vocabulary>bright</vocabulary>, and because it ends in い it works as an adjective.
akarui.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>kangaroo</reading> bounds across the school sports field at dusk and trips the motion sensor, and every floodlight bangs on at once. The whole pitch floods <reading>あかるい</reading>, <vocabulary>bright</vocabulary> as high noon.

akeru.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning at Grandma Kane's shrine someone unbars the big wooden doors and folds the shutters right back so the cats can stream through. Doing that to a shut door is <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary> it.
akeru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>A crow</reading> at Grandma Kane's shrine has learned to wedge its beak under the offering-box lid and lever it up. The cats now leave every latched thing on the grounds for the bird <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary> <reading>あける</reading>.

aki.meaning_mnemonic: The leaves let their green drain out, go the colour of dry straw, and drop. Crops come in, the evenings turn sharp, and that long wind-down is <vocabulary>autumn</vocabulary>.
aki.reading_mnemonic: A caretaker at the school rakes a mat of fallen leaves off the running track, every one the same dull <reading>khaki</reading>, and grunts 「<reading>あき</reading>」. The season that strips the trees and browns the field is <vocabulary>autumn</vocabulary>.

amai.meaning_mnemonic: You bite what you take for a plain savoury cracker and it is rolled in sugar, so sticky it glues your back teeth together. Anything that ambushes your mouth like that is <vocabulary>sweet</vocabulary>, and the closing い is what makes it an adjective.
amai.reading_mnemonic: You wash down that sugar-rolled cracker with <reading>a Mai Tai</reading> thick with syrup, and now your back teeth are glued twice over. You groan <reading>あまい</reading>, because it is all far too <vocabulary form="甘い">sweet</vocabulary>.

amami.meaning_mnemonic: The flavour children chase and dentists warn against, the one that makes you shut your eyes at the first bite of warm cake, is <vocabulary form="甘み">sweetness</vocabulary>.
amami.reading_mnemonic: You already know 甘 is 「あま」 from 甘い, so the noun for that flavour, <vocabulary form="甘み">sweetness</vocabulary>, is just <reading>あまみ</reading>.

amari.meaning_mnemonic: The castle <reading>armory</reading> — say it slowly, <reading>あまり</reading> — has been raided so often there is <vocabulary>(not) much</vocabulary> left on the racks but three bent spears and a cracked shield.

ame-v.meaning_mnemonic: You have met this shape already: the <kanji>rain</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>rain</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning does not shift at all.
ame-v.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Amy</reading> presses her nose to the window under the flat roof and counts the four dashes falling down each side of the glass, calling every one 「<reading>あめ</reading>」, the <vocabulary form="雨">rain</vocabulary>.

anata.meaning_mnemonic: Point your finger straight at one otter in a crowd and there's no doubt left: the otter you're pointing at is <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>.
anata.description: Rarely used to address someone directly; a name or title is normally used instead.

ane.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, one loud kid bosses even the coaches around and nobody dares stop her. That commanding energy is exactly an <vocabulary>(my) older sister</vocabulary>.
ane.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's sports day, a coach asks to change the relay order, and your bossy <vocabulary form="姉">older sister</vocabulary> answers 「<reading>あね</reading>」, a flat '<reading>ah, nah</reading>', and nobody dares argue.

ani.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the biggest kid in the yard always carries three backpacks at once. That's simply what an <vocabulary>(my) older brother</vocabulary> is for.
ani.reading_mnemonic: In Sei's school yard, three backpacks press down on your <vocabulary form="兄">older brother</vocabulary> until his legs buckle and he yelps '<reading>ah, knee</reading>!', the exact sound of <reading>あに</reading>.
ani.description: 兄 is what you call your own older brother when speaking about him to an outsider. Addressing him directly calls for a warmer, more polite word instead.

anna.meaning_mnemonic: Anna and you spot a scarecrow in a top hat on the far bank of the river, and you both call it <vocabulary>that kind of (far)</vocabulary> nonsense.

annai.meaning_mnemonic: Someone who holds the whole <kanji form="案">plan</kanji> of a place in their head can lead you <kanji form="内">inside</kanji> it without a wrong turn, and that service is <vocabulary form="案内">guidance / information</vocabulary>.

annai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You walk ahead of the visitor with the floor <kanji form="案">plan</kanji> clear in your mind and name each room <kanji form="内">inside</kanji> as you open its door. Doing that for someone is <vocabulary form="案内する">to guide / show around</vocabulary>.

ano.meaning_mnemonic: You stand on the mountain trail and ignore everything close by. Your arm swings straight past every near rock and points at <vocabulary>that vending machine over there</vocabulary>.

anzen.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji form="安">Peaceful</kanji> across the <kanji form="全">whole</kanji> of a place, with no corner left unguarded, is what makes it <vocabulary form="安全">safe</vocabulary>. As a な adjective, it wants な before the noun it describes.

ao-color.meaning_mnemonic: Standing on its own, the <kanji>blue</kanji> kanji is the whole <vocabulary>blue</vocabulary> word, and the sense does not shift.
ao-color.reading_mnemonic: Holding a fresh sprout up against the moon, a gardener pricks his thumb and yelps <reading>ow</reading>, <reading>あお</reading>, as the leaves turn the eerie shade of the moonlit sky: <vocabulary form="青">blue</vocabulary>.

aoi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>blue</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>blue</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning. Adding い on the end is what turns it into an adjective you can put in front of a noun.
aoi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 青 is read 「あお」 from the word 青, so stretching it out to <reading>あおい</reading> just hands you <vocabulary>blue</vocabulary> as a describing word.

apuri.meaning_mnemonic: You press one bright square on the glass and it does exactly one job — counts your steps, nothing else. A small program you <reading>apply</reading> to a single task is an <vocabulary form="アプリ">app</vocabulary>, and every square on that screen is one <reading>アプリ</reading>.

arashi.meaning_mnemonic: Sometimes the wind, the rain, the black cloud and the noise all arrive together and stay for a whole day. A whole sky misbehaving at once is a <vocabulary form="嵐">storm</vocabulary>.
arashi.reading_mnemonic: Wind, rain, black cloud and thunder all arrive in <reading>a rush</reading>, and the dock hand shouts <reading>あらし</reading> as the whole sky misbehaves at once: a <vocabulary form="嵐">storm</vocabulary> that will last all day.

arau.meaning_mnemonic: You hold a filthy boot under the tap and work every seam with your thumbs until the water finally runs clear. Driving grime off a thing with water is what it means to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary>.
arau.reading_mnemonic: Sei's team tracks the whole muddy field into the hallway and kicks up <reading>a row</reading> over whose boots stink worst. Sei lines every boot at the tap, because someone has to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary> the lot, and mutters 「<reading>あらう</reading>」.

are.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the very top of the mountain trail is still just a dot on the ridge, too distant to name — you can only point and call it <vocabulary>that over there</vocabulary>.
are.description: Marks something distant from both you and the listener, not just from you — or a shared thing you both already know about, even out of sight.

arigatou.meaning_mnemonic: Hand an <reading>alligator</reading> a warm towel and even it will grunt out a grudging <reading>ありがとう</reading>. Stripped of the manners it is simply <vocabulary>thank you</vocabulary>, favour noted.

aru.meaning_mnemonic: Strip an apartment down to bare walls and bare floor, and haul out every last piece of furniture. Nothing is left, yet <reading>a room</reading> is still there around you, a thing that simply <vocabulary>exists</vocabulary> — <reading>ある</reading>.

aruku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>walk</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to walk</vocabulary> word are exactly the same. The kana tacked on the end just makes it a verb.
aruku.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>rook</reading> on the shrine steps has decided that flying is beneath it. It now chooses to <vocabulary>walk</vocabulary> down every mossy step on foot, croaking <reading>あるく</reading> with each footfall.

asa.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>morning</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>morning</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
asa.reading_mnemonic: A butler opens the window on the striped sunrise light, the moon still hanging there, and says <reading>ah, sir</reading>, <reading>あさ</reading>: it is <vocabulary form="朝">morning</vocabulary>.

asagohan.meaning_mnemonic: Sit down to a <kanji>meal</kanji> while the <kanji>morning</kanji> moon still hangs in the window, and that meal is <vocabulary>breakfast</vocabulary>.

asai.meaning_mnemonic: You wade into the lake ready to swim, and fifty steps out the water still only reaches your knees. Water that never gets deep enough to swim in is <vocabulary form="浅い">shallow</vocabulary>.
asai.reading_mnemonic: Fifty steps out into the lake the water still only reaches your knees, so you let out <reading>a sigh</reading>, <reading>あさい</reading>, because nobody can swim in water this <vocabulary form="浅い">shallow</vocabulary>.

asatte.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>day</kanji> that falls <kanji>behind</kanji> the very next one is <vocabulary>the day after tomorrow</vocabulary>.
asatte.reading_mnemonic: Days stand in line; a cook <reading>sautés</reading> for the very next one, and the day falling behind it must wait for <reading>あさって</reading>, <vocabulary form="明後日">the day after tomorrow</vocabulary>.

ashi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>foot / leg</kanji> kanji is exactly the <vocabulary>foot / leg</vocabulary> word, one character doing both jobs, so the meaning never changes.
ashi-v.reading_mnemonic: The legs skid to such a hard stop that the <vocabulary form="足">foot</vocabulary> at the end comes up grey and <reading>ashy</reading> with dust, and the mouth on top yelps 「<reading>あし</reading>」.

ashita.meaning_mnemonic: The next <kanji>day</kanji> that hasn't arrived yet is always the one everyone calls <vocabulary>tomorrow</vocabulary>.
ashita.reading_mnemonic: The next day has not arrived yet, so it waits covered by <reading>a sheet</reading>, and the tag on it says <reading>あした</reading>: it gets unveiled <vocabulary form="明日">tomorrow</vocabulary>.

asobu.meaning_mnemonic: Turn a knot of kids loose in a park and they run in looping circles for no reason and to no end. That aimless motion, done for its own sake, is what it means to <vocabulary>play</vocabulary>.
asobu.reading_mnemonic: Toss <reading>a soap</reading> bubble into the park and the knot of kids runs looping circles after it, for no reason and to no end, <reading>あそぶ</reading>: that is to <vocabulary form="遊ぶ">play</vocabulary>.

asoko.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, your guide points past every switchback you can see to a speck lost in the mist — too far from either of you to be anything but <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

atama.meaning_mnemonic: The single body part that holds every thought you have, sits highest of all, and takes the worst sunburn every summer is your <vocabulary>head</vocabulary>.
atama.reading_mnemonic: Basking upright on a sunny rock all summer, an <reading>otter mama</reading> burns only her 「<reading>あたま</reading>」, the highest spot on her body, her peeling <vocabulary form="頭">head</vocabulary>.

atarashii-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>new</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>new</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character with the same meaning. The kana on the end finish in い, and that い is what marks it an adjective, as every い adjective does.
atarashii-adj.reading_mnemonic: A woodcutter swings his axe into the standing tree and gasps at the pale wood laid bare, so <reading>utterly shiny</reading>, <reading>あたらしい</reading>, that it looks brand <vocabulary form="新しい">new</vocabulary>.

atatakai.meaning_mnemonic: Think of the first real afternoon of spring, when the sun has finally taken the edge off the air and you carry your coat instead of wearing it. That easy, sink-into-it heat is <vocabulary>warm</vocabulary>.
atatakai.reading_mnemonic: On that first spring afternoon, a teacher with his coat over one arm loosens <reading>a taut tie</reading> as well and sighs <reading>あたたかい</reading>, because the sun has made the air easy and <vocabulary form="暖かい">warm</vocabulary>.

atsui-hot.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing い makes this word an adjective. Aim it at a day, a room, or a long grey August, and it says the air itself has turned <vocabulary>hot (weather)</vocabulary>.
atsui-hot.reading_mnemonic: Through a long grey August the air in every room thickens like <reading>a stew</reading>, and everyone sweating in it sighs <reading>あつい</reading>: the day itself has gone <vocabulary form="暑い">hot</vocabulary>.

atsui-obj.meaning_mnemonic: Here the <kanji>heat</kanji> is trapped inside one solid thing, like a mug, a pan handle, or a feverish forehead. The closing い makes it an adjective for that object being <vocabulary>hot (object)</vocabulary>.
atsui-obj.reading_mnemonic: Grab the iron kettle on Grandma Kane's stove and your hand jerks back with a sharp <reading>ah-tsoo-ee</reading>. That burnt-finger yelp is 「<reading>あつい</reading>」, the word for a thing that is <vocabulary>hot (object)</vocabulary> to the touch.

au.meaning_mnemonic: Two friends round the same blind corner from opposite sides at a full run and <vocabulary>meet</vocabulary> forehead to forehead.
au.reading_mnemonic: The twins sprint round the corner and crack heads, and both yelp <reading>ow</reading>. That yelp is exactly how <reading>あう</reading> sounds on the day they finally <vocabulary>meet</vocabulary>.

ayamaru.meaning_mnemonic: You back your bike into a parked car, wince at the fresh scratch, and go knock on the owner's door to say sorry and offer to pay. Owning that you did wrong and saying so to the person is what it means <vocabulary form="謝る">to apologize</vocabulary>.
ayamaru.reading_mnemonic: You knock on the door to confess the scratch your bike left on the parked car, and <reading>a llama</reading> answers, so you bow, offer to pay and <vocabulary form="謝る">apologize</vocabulary> anyway: <reading>あやまる</reading>.

baai.meaning_mnemonic: Take one <kanji form="場">place</kanji> and one particular way the details inside it <kanji form="合">fit</kanji> together. That exact arrangement is the <vocabulary form="場合">case / situation</vocabulary> you are talking about.

baggu.meaning_mnemonic: Load a leather shoulder <reading>bag</reading> with your purse, phone and keys until its sides go round and firm. Carried as part of an outfit, that piece is a <reading>バッグ</reading>, a <vocabulary form="バッグ">bag</vocabulary>.

ban.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell only once, right as <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary> settles over the mossy steps.

ban-order.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>turn</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>number</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they carry the same meaning.

bangohan.meaning_mnemonic: Nobody is allowed near the <kanji>meal</kanji> until <kanji>nightfall</kanji>, and the spread they finally fall on is <vocabulary>dinner</vocabulary>.

bangou.meaning_mnemonic: Take your <kanji>place in the series</kanji> and write it down as a digit, and that digit is your <vocabulary>number</vocabulary>.

basho.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail has exactly one flat ledge wide enough to stand on. Hikers guard that <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> because there is nowhere else to plant your feet.

basu.meaning_mnemonic: A city <vocabulary>bus</vocabulary> pulls in so heavy that the <reading>bass</reading> of its engine rattles the shelter glass. You feel that <reading>バス</reading> in your teeth before it even rounds the corner.

basukettobooru.meaning_mnemonic: A street <reading>busker</reading> gives up on coins. He nails his hat to a lamppost, lobs a rubber ball through it again and again, and that hooped, hand-thrown game is <vocabulary form="バスケットボール">basketball</vocabulary>, <reading>バスケットボール</reading>.

beddo.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker stuffs a sack with straw and drops it flat on the mountain trail. He sprawls across that lumpy <reading>bed</reading> and sleeps like a log, and 「<reading>ベッド</reading>」 is what he mutters for his <vocabulary>bed</vocabulary>.

bengoshi.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="士">scholar</kanji> you hire to <kanji form="護">protect</kanji> you works the case like a <kanji form="弁">valve</kanji>, opening and shutting what the court is allowed to hear. Someone who guards you by controlling that flow is a <vocabulary form="弁護士">lawyer</vocabulary>.

benkyou.meaning_mnemonic: Pour in enough <kanji>exertion</kanji> to build a <kanji>strong</kanji> hold on a subject, sweatband wrung dry, and that grind is <vocabulary>study</vocabulary>.

benkyou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>study</vocabulary> is <kanji>exertion</kanji> made <kanji>strong</kanji> and held for hours on end. You keep wringing the same sweatband out over one textbook until the pages go limp.

benri.meaning_mnemonic: A gadget that hands you real <kanji>convenience</kanji> and a clear <kanji>advantage</kanji> at the same time is exactly what <vocabulary>convenient</vocabulary> means. Handle it as a な adjective, so な comes before the noun it describes.

bentou.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a lunch box split into <kanji>petal</kanji>-shaped compartments, each one holding exactly the <kanji>right</kanji> amount for a single meal. That neatly portioned box is a <vocabulary>boxed lunch</vocabulary>.

betsu.meaning_mnemonic: Twins show up in the exact same coat. The teacher makes them hang the coats on <vocabulary>separate</vocabulary> hooks so nobody mixes them up.

betsuni.meaning_mnemonic: Something you can keep <kanji form="別">separate</kanji> from what matters is not worth bringing up, so when nothing is really on your mind you answer <vocabulary form="別に">not particularly</vocabulary>.

biiru.meaning_mnemonic: A swarm of bees has taken over the beach bar, and their one <reading>bee rule</reading> is that the taps pour for them first. They only ever order <reading>ビール</reading>, so the whole place reeks of spilled <vocabulary>beer</vocabulary>.

bijutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Take raw <kanji>beauty</kanji>, the kind that just happens in a sunset, and make a person sit down and build it on purpose; that deliberate version is <vocabulary>art</vocabulary>.

bikkuri-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You lift the lid off a plain little lunch and a <reading>big curry</reading> the size of a car tyre is steaming there instead. You jump back hard, and that is what it is <vocabulary>to be surprised</vocabulary>, 「<reading>びっくりする</reading>」.

boku.meaning_mnemonic: In the thicket, the one figure still visible always answers as <kanji>me</kanji>, and when a man says it, that answer is exactly <vocabulary>I (male)</vocabulary>.
boku.description: Used mainly by men and boys speaking casually or semi-formally; women rarely use it for themselves.

booru-pen.meaning_mnemonic: Clip a <reading>ball pen</reading> to your notebook. A tiny ball rolls the ink across the page, and that rolling ball is the whole idea behind <reading>ボールペン</reading>, an ordinary <vocabulary>ballpoint pen</vocabulary>.

boueki.meaning_mnemonic: Once two countries make it <kanji>easy</kanji> to swap whatever each of them has stacked up in surplus, that steady back-and-forth swapping is <vocabulary>trade (commerce)</vocabulary>.

boushi.meaning_mnemonic: Take a piece of full-size <kanji>headgear</kanji> and shrink it down to <kanji>child</kanji> size. What perches on one head now, light and small, is a <vocabulary>hat</vocabulary>.

buchou.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="長">leader</kanji> whose reach stops at the edge of one <kanji form="部">section</kanji>, with someone above them running everything else, is a <vocabulary form="部長">department head</vocabulary>.

bungaku.meaning_mnemonic: A child under that cover who spends every year on how <kanji>sentence</kanji>s are built, and on style, is doing the <kanji>learning</kanji> we call <vocabulary>literature</vocabulary>.

bunka.meaning_mnemonic: The slow <kanji>change</kanji> that a people's <kanji>style</kanji> of dress, food and speech goes through over centuries is their <vocabulary>culture</vocabulary>.

bunmei.meaning_mnemonic: When a people's <kanji form="文">literature</kanji> grows <kanji form="明">bright</kanji> enough to light the road for everyone who comes after, that shared glow is a <vocabulary form="文明">civilization</vocabulary>.

buta.meaning_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini the scraps bin lies tipped over, and a fat pink animal stands in the spill with its snout down, grunting as it eats. Nothing empties a bin like a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>.
buta.reading_mnemonic: The farmer fattens the animal every night on a bucket of <reading>butter</reading> and kitchen scraps until it can barely walk. That round, greasy thing is a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>, and he calls it 「<reading>ぶた</reading>」.

byou.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till beeps once for every item scanned, and that single beep marks exactly one <vocabulary>second</vocabulary>.

byouin.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body checks into the one <kanji>institution</kanji> built to house the sick until they mend, and that building is a <vocabulary>hospital</vocabulary>.

byouki.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body is one whose <kanji>spirit</kanji> got bumped down to third class. That drop is what an <vocabulary>illness</vocabulary> is.

chairo.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a cup of <kanji>tea</kanji> to stew until it is almost black, and the <kanji>color</kanji> it stains the rim, the tablecloth, and your fingers is <vocabulary>brown</vocabulary>.

chawan.meaning_mnemonic: Take that steaming <kanji>tea</kanji> cup and make it deep and wide enough to pack with a scoop of rice, and it turns into a <vocabulary>rice bowl</vocabulary>.

fukanou.meaning_mnemonic: Erase the <kanji form="能">ability</kanji> to do it, erase the fact that it <kanji form="可">can</kanji> be done, then stamp a <kanji form="不">negative</kanji> across what is left, and the thing is flatly <vocabulary form="不可能">impossible</vocabulary>. As a な adjective, it wants な before any noun it describes.

fukou.meaning_mnemonic: Draw one hard <kanji form="不">negative</kanji> stroke through that stalk of <kanji form="幸">happiness</kanji> standing in your own soil, and what is left is <vocabulary form="不幸">unfortunate / misfortune</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な comes before the noun it describes.

fuku.meaning_mnemonic: A coat is fabric that has agreed to <kanji>obey</kanji> your body. It bends when your elbow bends, never argues, and a closet full of that obedient cloth is your <vocabulary>clothes</vocabulary>.

fukusou.meaning_mnemonic: One piece of <kanji form="服">clothing</kanji> is just that one piece. The whole matching set you put on to be seen in public is your <vocabulary form="服装">attire</vocabulary>.

fukuzatsu.meaning_mnemonic: A plan built from <kanji form="複">doubled</kanji>, overlapping layers and stuffed with <kanji form="雑">miscellaneous</kanji> odd parts is a <vocabulary form="複雑">complicated</vocabulary> one. As a な adjective, it takes な before the noun it describes.

fun.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>minute</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>minute</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.

fun-counter.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>minute</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>minutes</vocabulary> counter are the very same character, so they mean the same thing.

fune.meaning_mnemonic: Something big enough to carry people and cargo can still ride on top of deep water instead of sinking into it. Anything that manages that is a <vocabulary>ship / boat</vocabulary>.
fune.reading_mnemonic: Loaded with people and cargo yet riding high on the deep water, the <vocabulary form="船">ship</vocabulary> puffs smoke from its one <reading>funnel</reading>, and dockhands shout 「<reading>ふね</reading>」 as it floats past.

furu-rain.meaning_mnemonic: The grey sky over the mountain trail lets down a steady curtain onto every leaf, with nobody pouring it. Water coming out of the clouds like that is what it means to <vocabulary>fall</vocabulary>.
furu-rain.reading_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail pulls up her <reading>fur</reading> hood as the grey sky lets a steady curtain down onto every leaf, 「<reading>ふる</reading>」, water starting to <vocabulary form="降る">fall</vocabulary>.

furui-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>old</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>old (thing)</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning. The closing い is the adjective marker, and it sits on every い adjective without exception.
furui-adj.reading_mnemonic: The mouth that has counted to ten every morning for centuries has grown a <reading>furry</reading> grey beard of dust, and it mumbles <reading>ふるい</reading> between numbers, as <vocabulary form="古い">old</vocabulary> as the counting itself.

futatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> kanji doesn't change to make <vocabulary>two things</vocabulary> — it already means exactly that on its own.
futatsu.reading_mnemonic: An owl lands beside the two chopsticks lying on the table, one above the other, and gives two <reading>hoots</reading>, <reading>ふたつ</reading>, one for each of the <vocabulary form="二つ">two things</vocabulary>.
futatsu.description: This belongs to the native Japanese counting series for objects, used as a general default counter when no specific counter word applies.

futoi-adj.meaning_mnemonic: You have already met the kanji <kanji form="太">thick</kanji>, so the word <vocabulary form="太い">thick / fat</vocabulary> is nothing new: it is the same character with the same meaning.
futoi-adj.reading_mnemonic: That one extra drop of fat lands on a <reading>foot</reading> already stretched as big as it can stand, and now no shoe fits. A foot gone that wide is <reading>ふとい</reading>, <vocabulary form="太い">fat</vocabulary>.

futsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> flat lines slide under the <kanji>day</kanji> mark without changing shape. That doubled mark means <vocabulary>two days</vocabulary> have passed.
futsuka.reading_mnemonic: Stuck in the mud, the hiker <reading>Foot Sucker</reading> slides two flat lines under the day mark in his diary and groans 「<reading>ふつか</reading>」, because that doubled mark means <vocabulary form="二日">two days</vocabulary> gone.

futsuu.meaning_mnemonic: A thing so <kanji form="普">universal</kanji> that it can <kanji form="通">pass through</kanji> any town and nobody looks up is simply <vocabulary form="普通">normal / usual</vocabulary>. As a な adjective it takes な before the noun it describes.

fuufu.meaning_mnemonic: Put a <kanji>husband</kanji> and a <kanji>wife</kanji> under one roof, rings on, and the pair of them together make a <vocabulary>married couple</vocabulary>.

fuyasu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="増">increase</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="増やす">to increase</vocabulary> word are the same word. This is the form with a worker in it, someone shovelling load after load of earth on to raise the mound.
fuyasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 増 is 「ふ」 from 増える, so for someone <vocabulary form="増やす">to increase</vocabulary> the pile on purpose is <reading>ふやす</reading>.

fuyu.meaning_mnemonic: Your breath shows indoors and the puddles wear a lid of ice by morning. The days shrink to a short grey window, and that hard still stretch is <vocabulary>winter</vocabulary>.
fuyu.reading_mnemonic: Leaving work, a commuter finds only a <reading>few</reading> minutes of grey light left in the sky and grumbles 「<reading>ふゆ</reading>」 at the dark. The season that keeps trimming every day down to nothing is <vocabulary>winter</vocabulary>.

gaikoku.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>country</kanji> is walls thrown up around the one jewel its people will not share. Any such enclosure <kanji>outside</kanji> your own is a <vocabulary>foreign country</vocabulary>.

gaikokujin.meaning_mnemonic: Step <kanji>outside</kanji> the walled <kanji>country</kanji> that guards its one jewel, and any <kanji>person</kanji> you meet there is a <vocabulary>foreigner</vocabulary>.

gakki.meaning_mnemonic: Take a hollow <kanji form="器">vessel</kanji>, a stretched drum or a boxed rack of strings, and build it so that striking it gives off <kanji form="楽">music</kanji>. Any container made for that is a <vocabulary form="楽器">musical instrument</vocabulary>.

gakkou-v.meaning_mnemonic: Fill the <kanji>school</kanji> grounds where the tree-lined paths cross with children who have nothing to do but <kanji>study</kanji>, and that place is a <vocabulary>school</vocabulary>.

gakusei.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>life</kanji> spent buried in books, with nothing to show for it yet but <kanji>study</kanji>, is exactly what we call a <vocabulary>student</vocabulary>.

gakusha.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> stacked so high with days of <kanji>study</kanji> that they grumble about it has turned into a <vocabulary>scholar</vocabulary>.

gamen.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="画面">screen (display)</vocabulary> is the flat <kanji form="面">face</kanji> of the device, and every <kanji form="画">picture</kanji> it shows is painted straight onto that face.

ganbaru.meaning_mnemonic: To be <kanji form="頑">stubborn</kanji> about how far you can <kanji form="張">stretch</kanji> yourself, and then hold that stretch when it burns, is to <vocabulary form="頑張る">try hard</vocabulary>.

ganbatte.meaning_mnemonic: Someone who is <kanji form="頑">stubborn</kanji> keeps <kanji form="張">stretch</kanji>ing toward a goal long after their arms ache. Telling a friend to be exactly that stubborn is what <vocabulary form="頑張って">good luck / do your best</vocabulary> means.

gatsu-month.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>month</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>month</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean the same thing.

geemu.meaning_mnemonic: Kids too broke for a real board split one stick of <reading>gum</reading> as the prize and make up rules for winning it on the spot. Any contest run like that is a <vocabulary form="ゲーム">game</vocabulary>, <reading>ゲーム</reading>.

genin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> thing that set an accident moving, traced back through every step, is its <vocabulary>cause</vocabulary>.

genki.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>spirit</kanji> still burning at its <kanji>beginning</kanji> strength is a <vocabulary>healthy / lively</vocabulary> one. It is a な adjective, so な slips in before the noun it describes.

genkin.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Money</kanji> you can slap on the counter this second, <kanji>right there</kanji> in paper and coin instead of a card or a promise, is <vocabulary>cash</vocabulary>.

genzai.meaning_mnemonic: The water that flowed past the bridge is gone, and the water upstream has not arrived. Only the stretch <kanji form="在">exist</kanji>ing right under you now is real, and that is <vocabulary form="現在">the present</vocabulary>.

getsuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> claims the earliest <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>, ahead of the sun, and that day is <vocabulary>Monday</vocabulary>.

gijutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Years of drills turn shaky hands into hands that can build or fix almost anything. That hard-won ability is your <vocabulary form="技術">technology / skill</vocabulary>.

gimu.meaning_mnemonic: When plain <kanji>morality</kanji>, not your boss, is what hands you a <kanji>task</kanji>, that unpaid assignment is a <vocabulary>duty / obligation</vocabulary>.

ginkou.meaning_mnemonic: When you run low on <kanji>silver</kanji>, you <kanji>go</kanji> to one particular crossroads in town. That corner building is the <vocabulary>bank</vocabulary>.

gitaa.meaning_mnemonic: The six strings stretched over the flat wooden box are so sticky they might as well be strung with <reading>gee, tar</reading>, yet you still strum them for a tune. That sticky-stringed box is a <vocabulary form="ギター">guitar</vocabulary>, <reading>ギター</reading>.

go-shujin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>main</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> running a household is what you call someone's <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>.

go-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>five</kanji> kanji never grew into anything else, so it and the <vocabulary>five</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing.

gochisousama.meaning_mnemonic: Too stuffed to move after dinner, you flop onto the <reading>Gucci sofa, Ma</reading> and let out a long groan. That groan, 「<reading>ごちそうさま</reading>」, is exactly how you say <vocabulary>thanks for the meal</vocabulary> once your plate is clean.

gogo.meaning_mnemonic: Once the clock falls <kanji>behind</kanji> <kanji>noon</kanji>, every hour left in the day counts as <vocabulary>afternoon</vocabulary>.

gohan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>meal</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>cooked rice</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.

gomennasai.meaning_mnemonic: Sei knocks Grandma Kane's teacup off the mossy step and blurts <reading>ごめんなさい</reading> before it even hits the ground, a rushed <reading>go-men-nah-sigh</reading>. It is the full, please-forgive-me <vocabulary>I'm sorry</vocabulary>.

gomi.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon works the alley bins like a <reading>gourmet</reading> picking a buffet, but every fish skeleton, mouldy rice ball, and coffee filter it drags out is just <vocabulary form="ごみ">trash / garbage</vocabulary>. The raccoon's five-star spread is <reading>ごみ</reading>.

gomibako.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="箱">box</kanji> whose only job is to hold the trash you throw out all day is a <vocabulary form="ごみ箱">trash can</vocabulary>.
gomibako.reading_mnemonic: By evening the box that holds everything you threw out all day has gone sticky, a <reading>gummy bucket</reading> of wrappers, <reading>ごみばこ</reading>, so you drag your <vocabulary form="ごみ箱">trash can</vocabulary> to the curb.

goran-ni-naru.meaning_mnemonic: You set the photo album on a stand and step back with folded hands, offering it up the way a gallery presents its finest piece. Letting an honored person <vocabulary form="ご覧になる">see something, honorifically</vocabulary>, means presenting it to them like that.

gorufu.meaning_mnemonic: A ball sails off the tee, clears a wide sandy <reading>gulf</reading> of a bunker, and drops beside a little flag. Walking eighteen of those crossings in an afternoon is <vocabulary form="ゴルフ">golf</vocabulary>, <reading>ゴルフ</reading>.

goukaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Either your score <kanji form="合">fits</kanji> the <kanji form="格">rank</kanji> the examiners drew or it falls short. The moment it fits, you have <vocabulary form="合格する">passed (an exam)</vocabulary>.

gozen.meaning_mnemonic: Every hour that still stands <kanji>front</kanji> of <kanji>noon</kanji> counts as <vocabulary>morning</vocabulary>, before lunch begins.

gozonji.meaning_mnemonic: A fact your honored guest is already <kanji form="存">aware of</kanji> was sitting in their head before you spoke. Something that already <kanji form="存">exists</kanji> in a superior's mind before it is said is the honored form of <vocabulary form="ご存じ">knowing</vocabulary> it.

guuzen.meaning_mnemonic: Two things line up by pure <kanji>accident</kanji>, with nothing behind it but being <kanji>that sort of thing</kanji>, and you call it a <vocabulary>coincidence</vocabulary>. It takes な before the noun it describes.

gyogyou.meaning_mnemonic: Scale that odd little tree-stump <kanji>business</kanji> up until a whole coast of boats is hauling nets of fish to market, and you have the <vocabulary>fishing industry</vocabulary>.

gyouji.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="事">matter</kanji> that the whole calendar has to <kanji form="行">go</kanji> ahead with on one fixed date is an <vocabulary form="行事">event / function</vocabulary>.

gyuunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>cow</kanji> makes far more of the white stuff than her one calf could ever drink, so the rest gets bottled and sold as <vocabulary>milk</vocabulary>.

ha-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini keeps a shelf of rock-hard rice crackers right by the till. Every year a customer bites down wrong and leaves a chipped <vocabulary>tooth</vocabulary> on the counter.
ha-tooth.reading_mnemonic: The konbini night clerk answers every joke with one flat <reading>ha</reading>. That bark is your <reading>は</reading>, and it always flashes the gold <vocabulary>tooth</vocabulary> at the side of his grin.

haburashi.meaning_mnemonic: Shrink a stiff scrubbing brush until it fits behind your back teeth, fix it to a long handle, and you are holding a <vocabulary>toothbrush</vocabulary>.
haburashi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 歯 is 「は」 from 歯, so a <vocabulary>toothbrush</vocabulary> is just <reading>はブラシ</reading>.

hachi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji is the <vocabulary>eight</vocabulary> word too — no separate story needed, they were always the same character.

hae.meaning_mnemonic: You set the bowl down for one minute and three of them already crowd the rim, rubbing their legs and testing the food. Nothing finds a meal faster than a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly (insect)</vocabulary>.
hae.reading_mnemonic: You set the bowl down on a bale of <reading>hay</reading>, and three of them climb out of the stalks onto its rim, rubbing their legs and buzzing <reading>はえ</reading>: each one a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly</vocabulary>.

haha.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji already means mother, and that is exactly what <vocabulary>(my) mother</vocabulary> means too.
haha.reading_mnemonic: Your <vocabulary form="母">mother</vocabulary> holds a small child tight under each arm, and when both wriggle at once she just laughs '<reading>ha-ha</reading>', the exact sound of <reading>はは</reading>.
haha.description: 母 is what you call your own mother when speaking about her to an outsider, never to her face — direct address uses a more polite word.

hai.meaning_mnemonic: Someone asks if you are coming and your hand is already <reading>high</reading> in the air before you make a sound. <reading>はい</reading> is that raised-hand reflex boiled down to one syllable, a flat clear <vocabulary>yes</vocabulary>.

hai-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Fill a cup to the brim, drink it dry, then set it back down, and that is one. Tally every time a bowl or glass gets emptied like that, and the total is your count of <vocabulary>cupfuls</vocabulary>.

haiken-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You bow so low over the offered document that your <kanji form="見">seeing</kanji> eye has to peer up at it from just above the floor. Looking at what someone shows you from that far down is how you <vocabulary form="拝見する">see it, humbly</vocabulary>.

hairu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>enter</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to enter</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. This is the intransitive one: you walk in under your own steam, nobody pushes you through the door.
hairu-v.reading_mnemonic: Leaning forward, one leg stepping ahead, you duck under the low doorway calling <reading>hi, Ruth</reading>, and on <reading>はいる</reading> you <vocabulary form="入る">enter</vocabulary> under your own steam.

hajimaru.meaning_mnemonic: A race that the gun sends tearing off the line with nobody there to start it has simply come <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> all by itself.
hajimaru.reading_mnemonic: On the school sports field the gun cracks and the kangaroo the kids call Jim is already gone. Shout <reading>Ha, Jim, a roo</reading> and you have <reading>はじまる</reading>, a race that came <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> on its own.

hajime.meaning_mnemonic: Open a fresh notebook and your hand hovers over that clean first line for a full minute before it dares to touch down. That paralysed first mark is the <vocabulary>beginning</vocabulary>.
hajime.reading_mnemonic: Your hand hovers over the fresh notebook's clean first line until your little brother grabs the pen, 「<reading>はじめ</reading>」, with a <reading>ha, gimme</reading>, and scrawls the <vocabulary form="初め">beginning</vocabulary> himself.

hajimemashite.meaning_mnemonic: You shake hands with a man called <reading>Jimmy</reading> who instantly <reading>mashes</reading> your knuckles flat, and out falls <reading>はじめまして</reading>. It is the fixed opening line for a first meeting, <vocabulary>nice to meet you</vocabulary>.

hajimeru.meaning_mnemonic: You open the book, set the pace, and drive the class forward yourself, and making something start by your own hand like that is <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.
hajimeru.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound in 始まる, so the one where you start something yourself is <reading>はじめる</reading>, <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.

hako.meaning_mnemonic: Anything with six stiff flat sides and a lid you must lift before you can see what is inside is a <vocabulary>box</vocabulary>.
hako.reading_mnemonic: A hawk stalks round all six stiff sides of a shut <vocabulary form="箱">box</vocabulary>, screeching <reading>hah-koh</reading>, 「<reading>はこ</reading>」, until someone lifts the lid to show it what is inside.

hakobu.meaning_mnemonic: A sack of rice on the ground is just furniture. Hoist it onto your shoulder and start walking, and now you <vocabulary>carry</vocabulary> it.
hakobu.reading_mnemonic: You hoist the rice sack onto one shoulder and <reading>half a coop</reading> of hens onto the other, <reading>はこぶ</reading>, and start walking: now you <vocabulary form="運ぶ">carry</vocabulary> it all.

han-time.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>half</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>half (past)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
han-time.description: This word means "half past" an hour, not half of a general quantity — it always attaches to a time, never a whole object.

hana-nose.meaning_mnemonic: The single vending machine at the top of the mountain trail sells nothing but tissues, because everyone who finishes that climb arrives with a streaming <vocabulary>nose</vocabulary>.
hana-nose.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker with a <reading>banana</reading>-sized <vocabulary form="鼻">nose</vocabulary> buys every tissue in the vending machine and honks 「<reading>はな</reading>」 into each one.

hana-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>flower</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>flower</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, so the bloom it draws is the bloom it means.
hana-v.reading_mnemonic: A hen named <reading>Hannah</reading> pecks through the green grass until one blade changes its top into bright colour, then clucks <reading>はな</reading> and guards that new <vocabulary form="花">flower</vocabulary>.

hanabi.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="火">fire</kanji> that bursts open in the sky as a huge <kanji form="花">flower</kanji> of coloured sparks is what <vocabulary form="花火">fireworks</vocabulary> are.

hanaseru.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the nonstop <kanji form="話">talker</kanji> with the wagging tongue an open microphone and the words just pour out, no gap anywhere. Being able to let language run like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="話せる">be able to speak</vocabulary>.
hanaseru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 話 is read 「はな」 from 話す, so <vocabulary form="話せる">can speak</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>はなせる</reading>.

hanashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>talk</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning.
hanashi.reading_mnemonic: A parrot on the riverbank has memorised exactly one rambling <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> and retells it to every heron that lands, squawking <reading>はなし</reading> like <reading>'her Nashi pear'</reading> at the same spot each time.

hanashiau.meaning_mnemonic: Each side <kanji form="話">talk</kanji>s, story after story, until the two accounts finally <kanji form="合">fit</kanji> together. Talk that both sides work at until it matches is <vocabulary form="話し合う">to discuss / talk over</vocabulary>.

hanasu-v.meaning_mnemonic: A mouth with a nonstop wagging tongue keeps pouring out one <kanji>story</kanji> after another. Doing that out loud, aimed at another person, is what it means to <vocabulary>speak</vocabulary>.
hanasu-v.reading_mnemonic: A parrot loose in the school hallways is dead sure it <reading>has news</reading>. It corners every passing student to <vocabulary>speak</vocabulary> at them and squawks 「<reading>はなす</reading>」.

hanbun.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>half</kanji> only counts as a real <vocabulary>half</vocabulary> once it is also a clean <kanji>part</kanji> you can lift away and hand to someone.

hanko.meaning_mnemonic: Picture your family name carved into a small red-inked <reading>hunk o'</reading> boxwood that you press onto every official form. That carved 「<reading>はんこ</reading>」 is your <vocabulary form="はんこ">personal seal (stamp)</vocabulary>, and it signs for you all over Japan.

hantai.meaning_mnemonic: Slap an <kanji>anti-</kanji> sticker across any poster and you have planted yourself firmly <vocabulary>opposite / against</vocabulary> whatever it sells. It is a な adjective, so な comes before the noun.

harau.meaning_mnemonic: You <vocabulary>pay</vocabulary> by peeling banknotes off a fat roll one at a time until the shopkeeper's outstretched hand finally curls shut.
harau.reading_mnemonic: Old Hara drags a rusty <reading>harrow</reading> across his field all autumn to earn his coins. He carries them to the tax office and mutters <reading>はらう</reading> as he counts them out to <vocabulary>pay</vocabulary>.

haru.meaning_mnemonic: You give up on a bare brown branch as dead wood. A week later it is covered in green buds, and that overnight comeback is <vocabulary>spring</vocabulary>.
haru.reading_mnemonic: Gardener <reading>Harold</reading> nearly saws off the bare brown branch as dead wood, then spots green buds on it a week later and gasps <reading>はる</reading>: the branch is back, and so is <vocabulary form="春">spring</vocabulary>.

haru-attach.meaning_mnemonic: You press a stamp onto the envelope's corner and smooth it until it will not lift. Fixing one flat thing onto another by hand is to <vocabulary>stick</vocabulary> it there.
haru-attach.reading_mnemonic: Koichi slaps a name sticker reading <reading>Harold</reading> onto every onigiri on the shelf and rubs each one down, 「<reading>はる</reading>」, and pressing a label flat onto a surface is to <vocabulary>paste</vocabulary> it on.

hashi-bridge.meaning_mnemonic: The left riverbank and the right riverbank are tired of shouting across the water, so a long plank gets laid from one to the other. You walk over on that plank, and it is a <vocabulary>bridge</vocabulary>.
hashi-bridge.reading_mnemonic: A ferryman on the riverbank keeps warning that the current is <reading>harsh</reading>, so the villagers stop listening and build <reading>はし</reading> to cross on dry feet. That word now means the <vocabulary>bridge</vocabulary> that ended his job.

hashi-chopsticks.meaning_mnemonic: Two slim tapered sticks you pinch in one hand to carry food up to your mouth are <vocabulary>chopsticks</vocabulary>.
hashi-chopsticks.reading_mnemonic: Koichi pinches two slim tapered sticks in one hand and lifts <reading>hash</reading> browns up to his mouth, 「<reading>はし</reading>」, bite by bite with his <vocabulary form="箸">chopsticks</vocabulary>.

hashireru.meaning_mnemonic: Same character, same meaning: the <kanji form="走">run</kanji> kanji you already know is all there is to <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary>.
hashireru.reading_mnemonic: The 「はし」 here is the same one from 走る, so <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary> reads as <reading>はしれる</reading>.

hashiru.meaning_mnemonic: Your legs pump so fast the fence posts smear into one green line and your breath tears in and out. That is what it means to <vocabulary>run</vocabulary>.
hashiru.reading_mnemonic: The coach has one <reading>harsh rule</reading>: keep going until the fence posts smear into one green line, so every kid has <vocabulary form="走る">to run</vocabulary>, gasping 「<reading>はしる</reading>」.

hataraku.meaning_mnemonic: You are on the go from the first bell to the last, with no real break, until your whole body aches. That endless grind is what it means to <vocabulary>work</vocabulary>.
hataraku.reading_mnemonic: From the first bell to the last, a waiter dashes between the tables and the <reading>hat rack</reading> with no break, groaning 「<reading>はたらく</reading>」 as his body aches. That is what it means <vocabulary form="働く">to work</vocabulary>.

hatsuka.meaning_mnemonic: Stack <kanji>two</kanji> blocks of <kanji>ten</kanji> <kanji>days</kanji> on the calendar and together they mark the <vocabulary>20th / twenty days</vocabulary>.
hatsuka.reading_mnemonic: The hat van <reading>Hats-Car</reading> waits while two blocks of ten days stack up on the calendar, then honks 「<reading>はつか</reading>」 the moment all <vocabulary form="二十日">twenty days</vocabulary> are crossed off.

hatsumei.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="明">bright</kanji> idea that <kanji form="発">departs</kanji> your head and turns into a working thing on the bench is an <vocabulary form="発明">invention</vocabulary>.

hayai-early.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>early</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>early</vocabulary> word are the very same character. The extra い on the end just makes it an adjective.
hayai-early.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sees the sun just ten finger-widths above the hills and is already calling <reading>hiya</reading> to the shrine cats. Being up that soon is <reading>はやい</reading>, which is <vocabulary form="早い">early</vocabulary>.

hayai-fast.meaning_mnemonic: You blink at the riverbank and the paper boat that was at your feet is already a speck under the far bridge. Nothing that beats your own eyelids is anything but <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary>.
hayai-fast.reading_mnemonic: A surfer paddles up the riverbank swearing she left <reading>Hawaii</reading> straight after breakfast this morning. Crossing an ocean before lunch is about as <reading>はやい</reading> as it gets, which is plain <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary>.

hayashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="林">grove</kanji> kanji you have already met and the <vocabulary form="林">woods / grove</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they carry the same meaning.
hayashi.reading_mnemonic: Ranger <reading>Hayashi</reading> plants a second tree so close to the first that their branches tangle, then nods <reading>はやし</reading>: two trees that close already make a <vocabulary form="林">grove</vocabulary>.

hazukashii.meaning_mnemonic: That single kanji carries the plain sense of <kanji>shame</kanji>, and adding the い ending turns it into the adjective <vocabulary>embarrassing</vocabulary>.
hazukashii.reading_mnemonic: A customer burns with shame at the till: the man <reading>has a cashier</reading> staring at him, and his whisper of 「<reading>はずかしい</reading>」 trails off into a long ee, because this is so <vocabulary form="恥ずかしい">embarrassing</vocabulary>.

hebi.meaning_mnemonic: The hose coiled on the riverbank path lifts one end, flicks a thin forked tongue, and pours itself smoothly off into the long grass. A rope that moves on its own is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>.
hebi.reading_mnemonic: A hiker nudges what looks like a <reading>heavy</reading> length of rope lying across the trail, and it coils back on itself and hisses. Rope that fights back is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>, 「<reading>へび</reading>」.

heiki.meaning_mnemonic: Let your <kanji form="気">spirit</kanji> lie as <kanji form="平">flat</kanji> and cool as a freshly mown field, and you stay <vocabulary form="平気">calm</vocabulary> no matter what happens. As a な adjective, it takes な before the noun it describes.

henpin-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You carry the <kanji form="品">goods</kanji> back to the counter that sold them and hand them over for a refund. Doing that is <vocabulary form="返品する">to return an item</vocabulary>.

herasu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="減">decrease</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="減らす">decrease</vocabulary> word are the same thing. The trailing kana make it transitive, so you are the one cutting an amount down, not the amount falling on its own.
herasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 減る, so the transitive twin, the one where you <vocabulary form="減らす">decrease</vocabulary> something else, is <reading>へらす</reading>.

heru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="減">decrease</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="減る">to decrease</vocabulary> word are the same word. This is the form that falls on its own, the water level dropping once the plug is gone with no one draining it.
heru-v.reading_mnemonic: Pull the bathhouse plug and a clump of <reading>hair</reading> spins at the drain as all the water races out. Watching the level <vocabulary form="減る">decrease</vocabulary> on its own, you murmur <reading>へる</reading>.

heta.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>hand</kanji> that sits a clear notch <kanji>below</kanji> every other hand at the table is <vocabulary>unskillful</vocabulary>. Like any な adjective, it drops な in front of the noun it describes.
heta.reading_mnemonic: At the card table, Heather's hand always lands a notch below every other hand, and the <reading>hater</reading>s jeer <reading>へた</reading>, because she is hopelessly <vocabulary form="下手">bad at</vocabulary> the game.

heya.meaning_mnemonic: Wall off one <kanji>section</kanji> of the <kanji>house</kanji>, hang a door on it, and that boxed-in piece is a <vocabulary>room</vocabulary>.
heya.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane throws open a door at the shrine and barks 「<reading>へや</reading>」 at the cats hiding inside, which is just <reading>hey, you</reading> aimed at whoever will not come out of that <vocabulary>room</vocabulary>.

heya-bangou.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>section</kanji> of a building under its own <kanji>roof</kanji>, plus that room's <kanji>number in a series</kanji>, gives you the <vocabulary>room number</vocabulary>.
heya-bangou.reading_mnemonic: In a building under one roof, a bingo caller reads each door's number in the series and yells <reading>hey-ya-bingo</reading> at yours, 「<reading>へやばんごう</reading>」, your <vocabulary form="部屋番号">room number</vocabulary>.

hi-sun-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun / day</kanji> kanji is the whole of the <vocabulary>sun / day</vocabulary> word, one character with no extra pieces bolted on, so its meaning never shifts.
hi-sun-v.reading_mnemonic: When dawn climbs behind the tall window with one bar, its first ray hits Hiro square in the eyes. He hisses <reading>hee</reading>, <reading>ひ</reading>, glaring at the <vocabulary form="日">sun</vocabulary> through the glass.

hidari-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>left</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>left</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning.
hidari-v.reading_mnemonic: A builder <reading>hid a ring</reading> in the glove of the hand that only braces the girder while the other one bolts, so 「<reading>ひだり</reading>」, his <vocabulary form="左">left</vocabulary>, never moves enough to lose it.

higashi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Written on its own, the <kanji>east</kanji> kanji is already the whole <vocabulary>east</vocabulary> word, and the meaning does not shift at all.
higashi-v.reading_mnemonic: At dawn the sun forces a <reading>big gash</reading> of light through the <vocabulary>east</vocabulary> horizon. Hear that tearing sound and you are saying <reading>ひがし</reading>.

hikaru.meaning_mnemonic: A deep-sea fish throws off its own cold <kanji>light</kanji> where the sun never reaches, with nothing switched on. A thing giving out light from itself is what it means to <vocabulary>shine</vocabulary>.
hikaru.reading_mnemonic: Deep where the sun never reaches, a diver switches nothing on: <reading>he calls Roo</reading>, the deep-sea fish, and with a cold 「<reading>ひかる</reading>」 it begins to <vocabulary form="光る">shine</vocabulary> by itself.

hiki.meaning_mnemonic: Farmers count cattle by the <kanji>head</kanji>, one nodding face after another. Shrink that same habit down to frogs, cats and beetles and you are counting <vocabulary>small animals (counter)</vocabulary>.
hiki.reading_mnemonic: A startled cat bolts past the riverbank washer and jolts a sharp <reading>hiccup</reading> out of her. By the third one she is tallying the <vocabulary>small animals (counter)</vocabulary> by hiccups alone, each a soft <reading>ひき</reading>.

hikidashi.meaning_mnemonic: Give the desk-front a <kanji>pull</kanji> and the whole tray slides forward until it almost <kanji>exits</kanji> the desk. That tray you haul out and push back is a <vocabulary>drawer</vocabulary>.

hikkoshi.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> the last box off the old floor and <kanji form="越">cross over</kanji> into an empty new flat, that whole change of address is <vocabulary form="引っ越し">moving (residence, noun)</vocabulary>.

hikkosu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> every box, every stick of furniture, and your whole life out of one apartment and cart it across town to the next. Dragging your entire household to a new address is what it is to <vocabulary form="引っ越す">move</vocabulary>.

hikouki.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>machine</kanji> built to <kanji>fly</kanji> carries you where your own feet never could. You board it to <kanji>go</kanji> clear across an ocean in an afternoon, and that machine is an <vocabulary>airplane</vocabulary>.

hikui.meaning_mnemonic: The limbo bar at school keeps dropping until it sits so <vocabulary>low</vocabulary> that even the cat cannot slink under it. The final い just marks it as an adjective, the badge every い adjective wears.
hikui.reading_mnemonic: At the school limbo contest the bar sinks so <vocabulary form="低い">low</vocabulary> that the cat gets stuck under it, and the kid bending back next lets out a nervous <reading>hiccup</reading>, <reading>ひくい</reading>.

hima.meaning_mnemonic: A block of <kanji>spare time</kanji> with nothing you have to do in it is <vocabulary>free time</vocabulary>.
hima.reading_mnemonic: With a whole block of spare time and nothing to fill it, Hana the crow tugs her mother's wing and whines <reading>hee, Ma</reading>, <reading>ひま</reading>, because all she has is <vocabulary form="暇">free time</vocabulary>.

hiragana.meaning_mnemonic: Rumor goes that <reading>Hera gonna</reading> teach the soft, looping letters first, before anything with a sharp edge, and that rounded beginner script is <vocabulary>hiragana</vocabulary>. Say the goddess and her plan in one breath and you land on <reading>ひらがな</reading>.

hiroi.meaning_mnemonic: A caped hero lands on the school field, throws his arms wide for a pose, and still has room to run a full lap. Only a truly <vocabulary>wide / spacious</vocabulary> field leaves that much room to spare.
hiroi.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>hero</reading> paces Grandma Kane's shrine, grumbling that the yard is not <reading>ひろい</reading> enough to land a single jump. He will only strike a pose somewhere properly <vocabulary>wide / spacious</vocabulary>.

hiru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>daytime</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>noon</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
hiru.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>hero</reading> holds the ruler up from the daybreak line, and when the sun climbs to its top mark he shouts <reading>ひる</reading>: it is <vocabulary form="昼">noon</vocabulary>.

hirugohan.meaning_mnemonic: The sun climbs until it hits <kanji>noon</kanji> and the whole working day halts for one <kanji>meal</kanji>. That break in the middle is <vocabulary>lunch</vocabulary>.

hito.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>person</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
hito.reading_mnemonic: One leg stays planted while the other steps out on tiptoe, so you whisper '<reading>he toes</reading>' as the lone walker passes: a single <reading>ひと</reading>, one <vocabulary form="人">person</vocabulary>.

hitori-de.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> stands in the room and not a soul is beside them. Doing the whole thing with nobody else there is <vocabulary>alone</vocabulary>.

hitotsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>one</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>one thing</vocabulary> word share the very same stroke: nothing was added, nothing was changed.
hitotsu.reading_mnemonic: A bowler tries to <reading>hit two</reading> pins, but only one falls and lies on the floor as a single flat line. The scorer calls <reading>ひとつ</reading>: <vocabulary form="一つ">one thing</vocabulary> down.
hitotsu.description: One of the native Japanese counting words for generic objects, used instead of the ordinary number words when there is no specialized counter for whatever is being counted.

hitsuji-anim.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="羊">sheep</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same animal.
hitsuji-anim.reading_mnemonic: The shepherd yells <reading>hit, Suzy</reading> to hurry her, but the animal with two short horns just stands calmly on stiff legs and chews: a <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary>, <reading>ひつじ</reading>.

hoka.meaning_mnemonic: You order the set meal with grilled fish. The kitchen has run out, so the waiter brings the same set built around some <vocabulary>other</vocabulary> main.
hoka.reading_mnemonic: The kitchen ran out of grilled fish, so the waiter calls out like a market <reading>hawker</reading>, 「<reading>ほか</reading>」, and sets down your set meal built around some <vocabulary form="他">other</vocabulary> main.

hoken.meaning_mnemonic: You pay a little now to <kanji form="保">keep a guarantee</kanji> that pays out later, when the road turns <kanji form="険">steep and dangerous</kanji>. That standing promise is <vocabulary form="保険">insurance</vocabulary>.

homerareru.meaning_mnemonic: Hand a drawing to the teacher and she holds it up to the whole class, naming every good line in it. Having your work lifted up for the whole room to see is what it means <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>.
homerareru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「ほ」 from 褒める, so the same thing coming back at you, <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>, is <reading>ほめられる</reading>.

homeru.meaning_mnemonic: Your kid brings home a drawing, and you pin it on the fridge, point to the careful shading, and tell her it is genuinely good. Saying plainly to someone that what they made is good is how you <vocabulary form="褒める">praise</vocabulary> them.
homeru.reading_mnemonic: You pin your daughter's drawing on the fridge, point at the careful shading and cheer as if she hit a <reading>home run</reading>: <reading>ほめる</reading>, which is how you <vocabulary form="褒める">praise</vocabulary> her.

hon.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>book</kanji> kanji you have already met and the <vocabulary>book</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.

hon-counter.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>book</kanji> is really a tree trunk pressed flat, and a trunk is the plainest long, straight thing there is. Stand pencils, bottles and roads next to it and you count each one as a <vocabulary>long objects (counter)</vocabulary>.

hon-yaku.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="翻訳">translation</vocabulary> is made by taking the foreign page, giving it one full <kanji form="翻">flip</kanji>, and <kanji form="訳">translating</kanji> the side now facing you into words you can read.

honoo.meaning_mnemonic: Strike a match and a small pointed shape of light stands up on the tip, orange at the edges and bluish at the base. That upright, leaning tongue of burning light is a <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary>.
honoo.reading_mnemonic: A knight strikes a match and swears on his <reading>honor</reading> to keep the small orange point on its tip alive, whispering <reading>ほのお</reading> as he cups his hands around the <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary>.

honto-desu-ka.meaning_mnemonic: What holds true to its <kanji form="本">origin</kanji> and lands exactly <kanji form="当">right</kanji> is the plain truth, so to ask whether something really is, you say <vocabulary form="本当ですか">really?</vocabulary>

hontou-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Trace any claim back to its <kanji>origin</kanji> and check whether it lands a clean <kanji>hit</kanji> there. When it strikes that root dead center, the claim is <vocabulary>really / truly</vocabulary> so.

hoshi.meaning_mnemonic: Every night the sky quietly sets out thousands of tiny lamps and never sends anyone the bill. Each cold pinprick of light hanging up there is a <vocabulary>star</vocabulary>.
hoshi.reading_mnemonic: Each night a lamplighter climbs up to light the sky's thousands of tiny lamps. Asked if the sky ever sends a bill, he chuckles <reading>ho, she</reading> never does, <reading>ほし</reading>, and lights one more <vocabulary form="星">star</vocabulary>.

hoshii.meaning_mnemonic: That itch of <kanji>longing</kanji> when a friend unwraps a present and you realise you want one too is exactly what it means to <vocabulary>want (to have)</vocabulary> something. The い on the end makes it an adjective.
hoshii.reading_mnemonic: When her friend unwraps a gleaming garden hoe, Mika sighs <reading>oh, she</reading> got one, <reading>ほしい</reading>, and that itch of longing means she <vocabulary form="欲しい">wants</vocabulary> one too.

hoshizora.meaning_mnemonic: Wait until a <kanji form="空">sky</kanji> that looked empty all day fills after dark with thousands of small points of light, and you are looking at a <vocabulary form="星空">starry sky</vocabulary>.

hosoi-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="細">thin</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="細い">thin / slender</vocabulary> word are the same character and carry the same sense. The い on the end is what lets it stand in front of a noun like any adjective.
hosoi-adj.reading_mnemonic: The farmer lays a <reading>hose</reading> along the mud path between the rice fields, and it only fits because each path is no wider than a thread. Anything that narrow is <reading>ほそい</reading>, <vocabulary form="細い">thin</vocabulary>.

hoteru.meaning_mnemonic: A bellhop wheels his cart past a hundred identical numbered doors. Say the English word <reading>hotel</reading> in three flat, clipped beats and it comes out as 「<reading>ホテル</reading>」, the place you rent a bed for one night, a <vocabulary>hotel</vocabulary>.

hotondo.meaning_mnemonic: Pull the bun from the steamer basket and it is <reading>hot on dough</reading> right around the outside, but the middle is still raw. Cooked that near to done is <reading>ほとんど</reading>, <vocabulary form="ほとんど">almost / mostly</vocabulary>.

hou.meaning_mnemonic: The wooden signpost at the riverbank has spun loose on its post. Now every one of its four arrows points the same <vocabulary>direction / way</vocabulary>, and travellers stand there bickering over which arrow to trust.

houhou.meaning_mnemonic: Which <kanji form="方">direction</kanji> you choose to come at a task from is your <vocabulary form="方法">method</vocabulary> for getting it done. Pick a different way in and you have a different method.

houkoku.meaning_mnemonic: When you stand up and formally <kanji form="告">tell</kanji> the room exactly what happened, start to finish, what you have given is a <vocabulary form="報告">report</vocabulary>.

houritsu.meaning_mnemonic: Every rule the whole country has agreed to write down and back with courts, police and prisons, instead of leaving it to a friendly handshake, is <vocabulary>law</vocabulary>.

housou.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="放">set free</kanji> a voice into the air and <kanji form="送">send</kanji> it out to every radio in the country at once. That single push to everyone is a <vocabulary form="放送">broadcast</vocabulary>.

hyaku-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hundred</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>hundred</vocabulary> word are the very same thing, nothing added and nothing changed.

ichi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>one</kanji> kanji is just that single flat line. Read on its own, it is simply the word <vocabulary>one</vocabulary>, so the kanji and the word are exactly the same.

ichiban.meaning_mnemonic: Pull the <kanji>one</kanji> slip from the <kanji>turn</kanji> dispenser and you are holding the top spot in the whole line. Served ahead of everyone else is <vocabulary>most / number one</vocabulary>.

ichiji.meaning_mnemonic: Pause the meeting for <kanji form="一">one</kanji> turn of the <kanji form="時">hour</kanji> hand, then start it again. Stopping for just that long means you stopped it <vocabulary form="一時">temporarily</vocabulary>.

ie.meaning_mnemonic: Every other door you have to be buzzed through or invited into. The one place you already own the key to is your <vocabulary>house / home</vocabulary>.
ie.reading_mnemonic: A courier works the whole lane, asking at every door whether anyone truly lives there. At the last one a tired voice finally says <reading>「いえ」</reading>, which is just <reading>yeah</reading>, this is my <vocabulary>house / home</vocabulary>.

igo.meaning_mnemonic: A phone calendar sorts every date <kanji form="以">by means of</kanji> the day you first opened the app. Each date that lands <kanji form="後">behind</kanji> that one is <vocabulary form="以後">from now on</vocabulary>.

ii.meaning_mnemonic: Sink your teeth into a perfectly ripe peach and the only sound you can make is a long, helpless <reading>eee</reading>. That squeal is 「<reading>いい</reading>」, and it means the peach is <vocabulary>good</vocabulary>.

iie.meaning_mnemonic: Offer Sei a spoonful of sticky fermented beans and she leans back with a long <reading>ee-eh</reading>, both vowels curling away from you. Stretched out like that, <reading>いいえ</reading> is a gentle <vocabulary>no</vocabulary>.

iin.meaning_mnemonic: A small <kanji>institution</kanji> run by a single <kanji>doctor</kanji> who pulls the arrow out of you and sends you straight home is a <vocabulary>clinic</vocabulary>.

ikaga.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi is so eager to please every customer that he never just asks outright; he bows first, and only then wonders aloud <vocabulary>how (polite)</vocabulary> he can help you today.
ikaga.description: This is the polite version of the plain how, used when making an offer or asking someone's preference, such as with a guest or customer. The plain form is what you would use with close friends instead.

ikaseru.meaning_mnemonic: At its core this word is still the <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji. The tail added on means you <vocabulary form="行かせる">make or let someone go</vocabulary>, whether they want to or not.
ikaseru.reading_mnemonic: Same 「い」 as in 行く, so <vocabulary form="行かせる">to make/let go</vocabulary> keeps that opening sound and becomes <reading>いかせる</reading>.

ike.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="池">pond</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary> word are the same character, so of course they mean exactly the same thing.
ike.reading_mnemonic: Water that goes nowhere, curling back on itself like a snake's tail, turns green and <reading>icky</reading> by August, and the frogs croak <reading>いけ</reading> from that <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary>.

iken.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>idea</kanji> stuck on loop in your heart only turns into an <vocabulary>opinion</vocabulary> once you make other people <kanji>see</kanji> it too.

ikeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji stands on its own here, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> is that same kanji and not one idea more.
ikeru.reading_mnemonic: The 「い」 in this word is the one from 行く that you already know, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>いける</reading>.

iku-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>go</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to go</vocabulary> word are the same word, so they mean the same thing. It is intransitive: you just go, with no object tagging along.
iku-v.reading_mnemonic: Standing at the crossroads, a hiker grins that <reading>I could</reading> take any road, shouts 「<reading>いく</reading>」, and her feet start <vocabulary form="行く">to go</vocabulary> down the left one.

ikura.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tub of salmon roe sits with no price tag, so you hold it up to the cashier and ask <vocabulary>how much</vocabulary>.
ikura.description: いくら for how much is an exact homophone of いくら, the everyday word for salmon roe — a genuine coincidence in real Japanese, not just this story's invention.

ikutsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank you keep saying eek at every coot that paddles past, until you've lost all track of <vocabulary>how many / how old</vocabulary> the chicks trailing behind them are.
ikutsu.description: This one question word covers two different English words: asking how many of something there is, and asking someone's age. Context tells you which sense is meant, since there is no separate word for each.

ima.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>now</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so whenever you say it, that is the only moment it ever points to.
ima.reading_mnemonic: Under the giant arrow tip hanging in the air, a passer-by shouts <reading>いま</reading>, like <reading>I'm-a</reading> grab it, and snatches the coin <vocabulary form="今">now</vocabulary>.

imi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>idea</kanji> you can almost <kanji>taste</kanji> when a word is used just right is that word's <vocabulary>meaning</vocabulary>.

imouto.meaning_mnemonic: She barges into your room without knocking and steals your snacks, which is just what a <vocabulary>younger sister</vocabulary> does.
imouto.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, your <vocabulary>younger sister</vocabulary> squeals 「<reading>いもうと</reading>」, sounding just like <reading>ee-moh-oh-toh</reading>, every time she swipes your onigiri before you can pay.

inaka.meaning_mnemonic: A view that is nothing but flooded <kanji form="田">rice paddy</kanji> and one lonely <kanji form="舎">hut</kanji> at its edge is the <vocabulary form="田舎">countryside</vocabulary>.
inaka.reading_mnemonic: Past flooded paddy after flooded paddy, you sit three hours <reading>in a car</reading> to reach one lonely hut at the edge, and the driver yawns <reading>いなか</reading>: the deep <vocabulary form="田舎">countryside</vocabulary>.
