inoru.meaning_mnemonic: Bow your head, close your eyes, and quietly ask a power you cannot see to keep someone safe. That asking, with nothing but words, is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>.
inoru.reading_mnemonic: At dawn a line of pilgrims kneels in one long <reading>row</reading> on the shrine steps, foreheads to the stone, each asking an unseen power for rain. Kneeling in a <reading>row</reading> and begging like that is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いのる</reading>.

intaanetto.meaning_mnemonic: You <reading>enter a net</reading> stretched over the whole planet, and every fact anyone ever wrote hangs caught in its mesh, in reach from wherever you stand. That worldwide catch is the <vocabulary form="インターネット">internet</vocabulary>, and its name is the sound of stepping in: <reading>インターネット</reading>.

inu.meaning_mnemonic: The animal that hears your car three streets away and is losing its mind at the door before your key is out is a <vocabulary>dog</vocabulary>.
inu.reading_mnemonic: Your car is heard three streets away, and by the time your key is out the thing behind the door yelps <reading>a new</reading> arrival, <reading>いぬ</reading>, again and again. That furry doorbell is your <vocabulary form="犬">dog</vocabulary>.

ippan.meaning_mnemonic: When <kanji form="一">one</kanji> single rule is broad enough to <kanji form="般">carry</kanji> every person under it, that rule is <vocabulary form="一般">general / common</vocabulary>.

irassharu.meaning_mnemonic: The white-gloved <reading>usher</reading> at the theatre glides over to walk each important guest in, out, and to their seat without a wasted step. That smooth, honored coming and going is <vocabulary form="いらっしゃる">to be, go, or come, honorifically</vocabulary>, and it sounds like <reading>いらっしゃる</reading>.

ireru-v.meaning_mnemonic: You take the coin and make it <kanji>enter</kanji> the narrow slot, pushing where it does not want to go. Doing the entering to something else, not yourself, is to <vocabulary>put in</vocabulary>.
ireru-v.reading_mnemonic: The coin slot on the <reading>eerie loo</reading> at the station jams, so you thumb the coin in hard, past where it wants to go, with a <reading>いれる</reading> clunk: that is to <vocabulary form="入れる">put in</vocabulary>.

iriguchi.meaning_mnemonic: The single <kanji>mouth</kanji> in a building's front wall that people <kanji>enter</kanji> through is its <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary>.
iriguchi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi stands at the front door chanting <reading>ee-ree-goo-chee</reading> at everyone who walks past. That doorway is the <reading>いりぐち</reading>, the one <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary> into his konbini.

iro.meaning_mnemonic: Take it all out and the world is a grey photocopy. The red of a stop sign or the green of a leaf, dropped back in, is <vocabulary>color</vocabulary>.
iro.reading_mnemonic: A tourist fans out a stack of <reading>Euro</reading> notes, one orange, one purple, one blue, far louder than the grey money back home, and laughs 「<reading>いろ</reading>」. Whatever makes one note orange and the next blue is <vocabulary>color</vocabulary>.

iroiro.meaning_mnemonic: Keep adding one more <kanji>color</kanji> to the heap until nothing in it matches anything else, and the heap counts as <vocabulary>various</vocabulary>. Being a な adjective, it needs な before the noun it describes.
iroiro.reading_mnemonic: A market trader keeps tossing one more colour of cloth onto the heap, chanting <reading>ee-ro, ee-ro</reading> until nothing matches. Shoppers hear <reading>いろいろ</reading> and know the pile is <vocabulary form="色々">various</vocabulary>.

iru-exist.meaning_mnemonic: Peer into the bait bucket at the riverbank and one fat <reading>eel</reading> is coiled in the bottom, blinking up at you. It is alive and it is right there, and a living thing being right there is what it means to <vocabulary>exist</vocabulary> — <reading>いる</reading>.

iru-need.meaning_mnemonic: High on the mountain trail, the lone vending machine will not open until the exact right coin drops in. That coin is the one thing <vocabulary>needed</vocabulary> to get a hot drink, and nothing else counts.
iru-need.reading_mnemonic: An eel tossed onto the dry trail flaps in the dust, and a bucket of river water is the one thing it <vocabulary>needs</vocabulary> before it stops moving. It wheezes that demand as <reading>いる</reading>, almost the word <reading>eel</reading>.

isha.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever pulls the arrow out and shuts it away already practices <kanji>medicine</kanji>. Add the <kanji>person</kanji> doing it and you have a <vocabulary>doctor</vocabulary>.

isogashii.meaning_mnemonic: You are cooking on every burner when the phone starts ringing and both oven timers go off. Never finishing one job before the next lands on you is <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary>.
isogashii.reading_mnemonic: With every burner going, the phone ringing and both oven timers shrieking, Sora gasps <reading>'Easy, gosh, gee'</reading> at anyone who asks. That gasp, <reading>いそがしい</reading>, means <vocabulary form="忙しい">busy</vocabulary>.

isogu.meaning_mnemonic: Two minutes on the clock, one long staircase up to the platform. Your legs go into overdrive, and driving your own pace up hard is to <vocabulary>hurry</vocabulary>.
isogu.reading_mnemonic: Two minutes on the clock and the long staircase still ahead, Koichi yells <reading>I so gotta go</reading>, 「<reading>いそぐ</reading>」, and drives his legs up three steps at a time to <vocabulary form="急ぐ">hurry</vocabulary>.

issho-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Lash the whole load onto a single leather <kanji>thong</kanji> and cinch it into <kanji>one</kanji> tight bundle. Everything that now rides that one strap travels <vocabulary>together</vocabulary>.

issou.meaning_mnemonic: Stack <kanji form="一">one</kanji> more <kanji form="層">layer</kanji> onto a pile that is already high, and the whole thing presses down <vocabulary form="一層">even more</vocabulary>.

isu.meaning_mnemonic: Shrink a grand throne until it seats just one ordinary person and what is left is the throne's <kanji>child</kanji>. That small single seat with a back is a <vocabulary>chair</vocabulary>.

itadakimasu.meaning_mnemonic: Lift your chopsticks over a steaming bowl and say <reading>いただきます</reading>, close enough to <reading>eat-a-duck-ee</reading> to stick. It is the set phrase you say before eating, <vocabulary>let's eat</vocabulary>, with a nod of thanks for the food.

itadaku.meaning_mnemonic: You take the gift in both hands and lift it up past your forehead, putting yourself lower than the thing you were just given. Receiving or eating anything from that bowed-under position is to <vocabulary form="頂く">receive it, humbly</vocabulary>.
itadaku.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine a tame duck waddles up and drops a rice cracker into your cupped hands, and you bow lower than the bird to take it. That <reading>eat a duck</reading> moment, receiving with your head down, is <vocabulary form="頂く">to receive and eat, humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>いただく</reading>.

itai.meaning_mnemonic: Step on a plug lying prongs-up in a dark room and the white spark that shoots up your foot is exactly <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary>. That final い marks it as an adjective.
itai.reading_mnemonic: Koichi crosses the dark room, steps square on a plug lying prongs-up, and howls <reading>eye-tie</reading>, <reading>いたい</reading>, because that white spark shooting up his foot is <vocabulary form="痛い">painful</vocabulary>.

itamu.meaning_mnemonic: A back tooth starts to throb late at night with nobody near it and nothing pressing on it. When a part of you sends up that steady, unasked-for pain on its own, it has begun <vocabulary form="痛む">to hurt / ache</vocabulary>.
itamu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 痛 is 「いた」 from 痛い, so for a sore knee <vocabulary form="痛む">to hurt / ache</vocabulary> on its own is <reading>いたむ</reading>.

itasu.meaning_mnemonic: A servant finishes every task before anyone notices it needed doing, then sweeps away their own footprints so no one sees the work. Getting the whole job done while keeping yourself invisible is to <vocabulary form="致す">do it, humbly</vocabulary>.
itasu.reading_mnemonic: Two overalled helpers answer every call at the back door with a soft <reading>it's us</reading>, then quietly fix whatever broke and slip out again. Doing the work for someone while staying that far in the background is <vocabulary form="致す">to do, humbly</vocabulary>, spoken as <reading>いたす</reading>.

itsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat sits under the enormous bell all day. It keeps asking いつ, itchy to know exactly <vocabulary>when</vocabulary> the bell will ring.

itsu-demo.meaning_mnemonic: The tasting stand by the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini never shuts down; walk in at three in the morning and <reading>it's a demo</reading> running, same as noon. That round-the-clock sampling is <reading>いつでも</reading>, meaning <vocabulary form="いつでも">anytime</vocabulary>.

itsuka.meaning_mnemonic: Watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> rise <kanji>five</kanji> separate times over the konbini roof, and you have counted <vocabulary>five days</vocabulary>.

itsumo.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail the same grizzled vendor is <vocabulary>always</vocabulary> restocking that one vending machine, dawn or dusk, so hikers call it <reading>いつも</reading> — <reading>it's more</reading> — ridge.

itsutsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>five</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>five things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
itsutsu.reading_mnemonic: Hand stuck flat to the low ceiling after a failed high-five, you feel <reading>itchy</reading> under each spread finger and count <reading>いつつ</reading>: <vocabulary form="五つ">five things</vocabulary> you cannot scratch.

ittekimasu.meaning_mnemonic: You pause at the <kanji>go</kanji> crossroads and call back to the house before you step out. That call is <vocabulary>I'm off (going and coming back)</vocabulary>, and the crossroads is your promise to walk back through it by evening.
ittekimasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know 行 is 「い」 from 行く, so <vocabulary>I'm off (going and coming back)</vocabulary> is <reading>いってきます</reading>.

iu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>say</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
iu-v.reading_mnemonic: A fussy heron opens its small mouth and floats just one line of words up into the air, a sniffy 「<reading>いう</reading>」, <reading>ew</reading>, the only thing it ever bothers <vocabulary form="言う">to say</vocabulary>.

iwa.meaning_mnemonic: A single stone in the field is too big to lift, too heavy to roll, and was sitting there before the farm was. A stone that large and that settled is a <vocabulary form="岩">rock / boulder</vocabulary>.
iwa.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>Iowa</reading> farmer plows around the same stone every spring, too big to lift and older than his farm, and kicks it with a grunt of <reading>いわ</reading>: his field's <vocabulary form="岩">boulder</vocabulary>.

iwau.meaning_mnemonic: Good news lands, so you deliberately gather people, food and noise around the one it happened to. That staged happiness is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>.
iwau.reading_mnemonic: The team wins and Sei's whole class erupts, caps in the air, everyone shouting 'I <reading>wow</reading>' around a cake nobody planned. Making that much noise on purpose for one person is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いわう</reading>.

izen.meaning_mnemonic: A museum lets you place any memory on its long wall timeline, measured only <kanji form="以">by means of</kanji> one brass marker peg. Everything you pin in <kanji form="前">front</kanji> of that peg counts as <vocabulary form="以前">before</vocabulary>.

ji-oclock.meaning_mnemonic: Stop the <kanji>hour</kanji> hand dead on one mark of the dial and say the number it points at out loud. That spoken-aloud hour is what <vocabulary>o'clock</vocabulary> names.

jibun.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>self</kanji> is the one <kanji>part</kanji> you can never hand off to someone else, which makes it entirely <vocabulary>oneself</vocabulary>.

jibun-time.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>minute</kanji> sliced off of <kanji>time</kanji> tells you exactly what <vocabulary>time (of day)</vocabulary> it is.

jijou.meaning_mnemonic: A single <kanji form="事">matter</kanji> sitting at the centre of an event drags a whole knot of <kanji form="情">feelings</kanji> in behind it. That full tangle around it is the <vocabulary form="事情">circumstances</vocabulary>.

jikan.meaning_mnemonic: How much <kanji>time</kanji> sits in the <kanji>between</kanji> of two moments is exactly <vocabulary>time / hours</vocabulary>.

jikan-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Measure everything that sits <kanji>between</kanji> one clock <kanji>time</kanji> and the next one. Stack those measured spans up and the total is so many <vocabulary>hours</vocabulary> of duration.

jikken.meaning_mnemonic: To run an <vocabulary form="実験">experiment</vocabulary> is to <kanji form="験">examine</kanji>, under controlled conditions, whether an idea holds up against <kanji form="実">reality</kanji>.

jishin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="地">ground</kanji> is the one thing built to stay still, so when it starts to <kanji form="震">shake</kanji> hard enough to knock cups off the shelf, you have an <vocabulary form="地震">earthquake</vocabulary>.

jisho.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>write</kanji> down every <kanji>word</kanji> there is and put them in order, the book you end up with is a <vocabulary>dictionary</vocabulary>.

jitensha.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>car</kanji> with no engine leaves the pedalling to you. Your own legs make the wheels <kanji>revolve</kanji>, so the whole thing is <kanji>self</kanji>-propelled, which is what a <vocabulary>bicycle</vocabulary> is.

jiyuu.meaning_mnemonic: When your <kanji form="自">self</kanji> is the only <kanji form="由">reason</kanji> you need for what you do, you have <vocabulary form="自由">freedom</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so it takes な before the noun it describes.

josei.meaning_mnemonic: In biology class the <kanji>woman</kanji> is the worked example of the other <kanji>gender</kanji>, the one marked <vocabulary>female (gender)</vocabulary>.

jouken.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji form="条">clause</kanji> written into the agreement names one <kanji form="件">matter</kanji> that has to be settled before anything moves ahead. Every one of those clauses is a <vocabulary form="条件">condition</vocabulary>.

jouzu.meaning_mnemonic: When your <kanji>hand</kanji> at a task sits a clear notch <kanji>above</kanji> everyone else's, you are <vocabulary>skillful / good at</vocabulary> it. That な goes between the word and the noun it praises.

jugyou.meaning_mnemonic: A set hour in which a teacher will <kanji>impart</kanji> the skills of a trade or <kanji>business</kanji> to you is a <vocabulary>class / lesson</vocabulary>.

junbi-suru.meaning_mnemonic: While the room is still empty you <kanji>lay in every provision</kanji> the day is going to need. Having it all standing ready before anyone arrives is what it means <vocabulary>to prepare</vocabulary>.

juu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji is simply the <vocabulary>ten</vocabulary> word. There is one mark and one meaning, nothing extra to remember.

juubun.meaning_mnemonic: Ten <kanji form="分">part</kanji>s out of <kanji form="十">ten</kanji> make up the whole, and having the whole of something is having <vocabulary form="十分">sufficient / enough</vocabulary> of it. As a な adjective, な comes before the noun it describes.

juubun-na.meaning_mnemonic: Cut something into <kanji form="十">ten</kanji> <kanji form="分">part</kanji>s and hand someone all ten. Getting the whole set with none missing is what <vocabulary form="十分な">sufficient (attributive)</vocabulary> describes.

juusho.meaning_mnemonic: Your <vocabulary>address</vocabulary> is the named <kanji>place</kanji> where you <kanji>live</kanji>, spelled out house, street and town.

juusu.meaning_mnemonic: <reading>Zeus</reading> squeezes a whole storm cloud full of oranges until it rains down into one tall glass. What fills the glass is <vocabulary form="ジュース">juice</vocabulary>, <reading>ジュース</reading>.

juuyou.meaning_mnemonic: Pile a thousand rice sacks onto something you already <kanji form="要">need</kanji>, and the <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> load makes it impossible to set aside. A need that weighs that much is <vocabulary form="重要">important</vocabulary>, and as a な adjective it takes な before its noun.

ka-mosquito.meaning_mnemonic: The high thin whine circles your ear in the dark, stops, and a second later a hot itch rises on your arm. The thing that bit you and left that whine is a <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary>.
ka-mosquito.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kaa</reading> the crow hears the thin whine circling your ear in the dark, puffs one spark at it and caws <reading>か</reading> as the <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary> drops off your itching arm.

kaban.meaning_mnemonic: A <reading>cabin</reading> is a wooden box big enough to walk into, holding everything you packed for the trip. Shrink it until it hangs off one shoulder and you get a <reading>かばん</reading>, an everyday <vocabulary>bag</vocabulary>.

kado.meaning_mnemonic: Every <vocabulary>corner</vocabulary> in the house is the spot where two walls give up going straight and slam into each other at a hard right angle.
kado.reading_mnemonic: Movers swing an old <reading>car door</reading> through the house and jam it where two walls slam together at a hard right angle, and it sticks with a 「<reading>かど</reading>」 in that <vocabulary form="角">corner</vocabulary>.

kaeru-change.meaning_mnemonic: You swap the batteries, reset the clock, repaint the door. Making a thing become different by your own hand is to <vocabulary>change</vocabulary> it.
kaeru-change.reading_mnemonic: You already know this reading of 変 from 変わる, so when it is your hand doing it, <vocabulary>to change</vocabulary> something, the word is <reading>かえる</reading>.

kaeru-potential.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="買">buy</kanji> kanji carries straight over into this word, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> holds no meaning the kanji did not already.
kaeru-potential.reading_mnemonic: That 「か」 is the reading 買う already gave you, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> lands as <reading>かえる</reading>.

kaeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>return</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to return home</vocabulary> word are the same, so they mean the same thing. You do it under your own steam — it is intransitive.
kaeru-v.reading_mnemonic: The hour a <reading>frog</reading> gets <vocabulary form="帰る">to return home</vocabulary>, it drops its little knife by the door, picks up the sweeper and croaks 「<reading>かえる</reading>」 with every sweep.

kaesu.meaning_mnemonic: You borrowed the umbrella, so now you carry it back to its owner. Putting a thing back in the hand it came from is to <vocabulary>return</vocabulary> it.
kaesu.reading_mnemonic: Sei borrows Kai's spare gym shoes, then walks the whole way back to leave <reading>Kai's shoes</reading> at his locker, 「<reading>かえす</reading>」, and handing them straight back is to <vocabulary>return</vocabulary> them.

kagaku.meaning_mnemonic: Split all human <kanji>learning</kanji> into labelled <kanji>department</kanji>s, then keep only the ones that test what they claim, and what is left on the shelf is <vocabulary>science</vocabulary>.

kagakusha.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="者">person</kanji> who spends every day turning pages in one narrow <kanji form="科">department</kanji> of <kanji form="学">study</kanji> is a <vocabulary form="科学者">scientist</vocabulary>.

kagetsu.meaning_mnemonic: That small <kanji>month</kanji> kanji riding on the end is the whole word, so ticking these off just counts <vocabulary>months</vocabulary> of elapsed time.
kagetsu.reading_mnemonic: A heavy <reading>cargo jet</reading> grinds across the sky so slowly that one lap of its route eats a whole month. Count enough laps and the number you reach is how many <vocabulary>months</vocabulary> have gone by; every slow pass sounds like 「<reading>かげつ</reading>」.

kagi.meaning_mnemonic: Every locked door has just one small metal shape that will turn it, and that shape is a <vocabulary>key / lock</vocabulary>.
kagi.reading_mnemonic: The landlord turns <reading>cagey</reading> when you ask which small metal shape will turn your locked door, mutters 「<reading>かぎ</reading>」 and pockets the only <vocabulary form="鍵">key</vocabulary>.

kai-floor.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>storey</kanji> of a building is one flat slab dropped on top of the last, linked by a flight of stairs. Count the slabs from street level upward and the running total is how many <vocabulary>floors</vocabulary> you have gone up.

kai-times.meaning_mnemonic: Push a revolving door and count each full circle it carries you through before you step out. Every completed circle around is one <vocabulary>times (counter)</vocabulary>.

kaidan.meaning_mnemonic: Stack a row of narrow ledges so each sits one step higher than the last, then lean the whole run against a wall. What you have built is <vocabulary>stairs</vocabulary>.

kaigan.meaning_mnemonic: Where the <kanji form="海">sea</kanji> that every river drains into finally meets the <kanji form="岸">beach</kanji>, you are standing on the <vocabulary form="海岸">coast / seashore</vocabulary>.

kaigi.meaning_mnemonic: Trap eight people around one table in slow formal <kanji>deliberation</kanji>, refill the coffee twice, and what you are left with is a <vocabulary>meeting</vocabulary>.

kaigi-shitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Every hallway in the building ends at one <kanji form="室">room</kanji> kept for people to <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> and <kanji form="議">debate</kanji> in. That is the <vocabulary form="会議室">meeting room</vocabulary>.

kaigou.meaning_mnemonic: When enough people <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> in one room that the chairs and the heads finally <kanji form="合">fit</kanji> the same count, that filled room is a <vocabulary form="会合">gathering</vocabulary>.

kaimono.meaning_mnemonic: You sling your net over stall after stall and drop a shell on each counter to <kanji>buy</kanji> every <kanji>thing</kanji> that is not nailed down. Hauling that catch home is <vocabulary>shopping</vocabulary>.

kaimono-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You throw a net over one <kanji>thing</kanji> after another and drop clam-shell coins on the counter to <kanji>buy</kanji> each one. Keep that up stall after stall and you are out to <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>.

kaisha.meaning_mnemonic: The building you travel to each morning to <kanji>meet</kanji> the same coworkers and do the same job is your <vocabulary>company / office</vocabulary>.

kaishain.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone who <kanji>meets</kanji> here for a paycheck is an <kanji>employee</kanji>, one more mouth this place must feed. That makes them a <vocabulary>company employee</vocabulary>.

kaite-ageru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning does not change.
kaite-ageru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is 「か」 from 書く, the verb to write, so <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>かいてあげる</reading>.

kakaku.meaning_mnemonic: Every shop <kanji>rank</kanji>s its goods with a number on a little tag, and that number, the one every customer pays, is the <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

kakaru-v.meaning_mnemonic: A coat on a hook stays put with no one holding it, and an hour spent on a job slips by the same way. Either one just <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> there and takes the time it takes.
kakaru-v.reading_mnemonic: A crow perches on the coat that <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> on its hook with no one holding it, and croaks <reading>caw-caw-roo</reading>, <reading>かかる</reading>, once for every hour the job takes.

kakeru-call.meaning_mnemonic: You jab in the number and cackle your hello far too loudly down the line. That <reading>cackle-rue</reading> of a greeting is <reading>かける</reading>, which is <vocabulary>to make a call</vocabulary>.

kakeru-hang.meaning_mnemonic: You reach up and set the frame on the nail yourself; you choose to put a full hour into the work. Doing either by your own hand is to <vocabulary form="掛ける">hang</vocabulary> a thing or spend the time on it.
kakeru-hang.reading_mnemonic: You already met 掛かる, so its hands-on twin <vocabulary form="掛ける">to hang or spend</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かける</reading>.

kakeru-write-potential.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. The added ending only shifts it from doing the writing to being able to do it.
kakeru-write-potential.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is read 「か」 from 書く, so <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>かける</reading>.

kaku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to write</vocabulary> word are the same character doing the same job, so they mean the same thing.
kaku.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>cackling</reading> old calligrapher keeps his brush moving all day, going 「<reading>かく</reading>」 with each stroke until the page is all marks, which is what it means <vocabulary form="書く">to write</vocabulary>.

kamaimasen.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever option you pick, this person's <kanji form="構">stance</kanji> does not shift even slightly. A body that stays relaxed no matter what you choose is telling you <vocabulary form="構いません">it doesn't matter</vocabulary>.
kamaimasen.reading_mnemonic: Offer the mason any option you like and his relaxed stance never shifts; he just shrugs <reading>come, I'm a mason</reading>, <reading>かまいません</reading>, meaning <vocabulary form="構いません">it doesn't matter</vocabulary>.

kamera.meaning_mnemonic: A <reading>camel</reading> plods past the mossy shrine steps and every tourist lifts a little black machine to one eye and clicks. The gadget that freezes the camel mid-chew is a <vocabulary>camera</vocabulary>, so they shout for the <reading>カメラ</reading> before it wanders off.

kami-hair.meaning_mnemonic: The stuff that clogs the shower drain and slips out of every ponytail by noon is <vocabulary>hair</vocabulary>.
kami-hair.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Cammy</reading> fishes a fat wet clump of <vocabulary form="髪">hair</vocabulary> out of the clogged shower drain, then feels her ponytail slipping loose again and sighs 「<reading>かみ</reading>」.
kami-hair.description: 髪 is specifically the hair on your head. Hair elsewhere on the body, or an animal's coat, is a different word, so do not stretch 髪 to cover it.

kami-paper.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>paper</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>paper</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
kami-paper.reading_mnemonic: Cammy the goat eats anything, but what she loves most is <vocabulary>paper</vocabulary>. Hand her a page and <reading>Cammy</reading> grinds it to pulp, bleating <reading>かみ</reading>.

kanarazu.meaning_mnemonic: Dodging a slash aimed at your heart is not a choice your body makes. It happens every time because the move is <kanji form="必">necessary</kanji>, and something that locked-in happens <vocabulary form="必ず">definitely / without fail</vocabulary>.
kanarazu.reading_mnemonic: When the slash comes at her heart, <reading>Kana rushes</reading> aside before she can think, every single time, <reading>かならず</reading>: her body dodges <vocabulary form="必ず">without fail</vocabulary>.

kanari.meaning_mnemonic: The pet shop <reading>canary</reading> is louder than a normal bird by a wide margin. Naming that wide margin above ordinary is <reading>かなり</reading>, meaning <vocabulary form="かなり">quite / considerably</vocabulary>.
kanari.description: Usually an adverb placed right before an adjective, close to fairly or pretty in English. It can also act as a na-adjective before a noun, but that use is much rarer.

kanashii.meaning_mnemonic: A kid watches a balloon slip its string and float up past the rooftops. There is nothing to chase and nothing to do, and that empty feeling is <vocabulary>sad</vocabulary>.
kanashii.reading_mnemonic: The kid's balloon slips its string and drifts up past the <reading>cannery</reading> roof, and Nana, on her break, can only watch it go. That empty <reading>かなしい</reading> feeling is <vocabulary form="悲しい">sad</vocabulary>.

kanban.meaning_mnemonic: A flat <kanji>board</kanji> hung up high where every passer-by is forced to <kanji>see</kanji> it is a <vocabulary>sign / signboard</vocabulary>.

kangaedasu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="考">think</kanji>, tracing one old thought down its kinked track until a new idea works loose. Forcing that idea to <kanji form="出">exit</kanji> into the open is <vocabulary form="考え出す">to think up / devise</vocabulary>.

kangaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You take a hard problem, turn it over in your hands like a stuck jar lid, and work at it until it gives. That patient working-at-a-thing until it opens is to <vocabulary>think it through, to consider</vocabulary> it.
kangaeru.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>kangaroo</reading> turns a stuck jar lid over and over in its paws, working at it until it gives with a 「<reading>かんがえる</reading>」, the patient way you <vocabulary form="考える">think</vocabulary> a problem through.

kanji-word.meaning_mnemonic: A written <kanji>character</kanji> that walked over from <kanji>China</kanji> and settled in Japan for good is a <vocabulary>kanji</vocabulary>.

kanjiru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">emotion</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="感じる">to feel</vocabulary> word are the same; the added kana just turns that emotion into something you actively do.

kanjou.meaning_mnemonic: The whole <kanji form="感">feeling</kanji> hitting you at once, with the head left out of it entirely, settles into one named <vocabulary form="感情">emotion</vocabulary>.

kankei.meaning_mnemonic: Run a cord from one person to another and pull your end of it. Whatever happens to the one is felt straight down the line by the other, and that living line between them is a <vocabulary form="関係">relationship / connection</vocabulary>.

kankyou.meaning_mnemonic: Draw a <kanji>ring</kanji> around yourself and walk it out to the <kanji>boundary</kanji> where your surroundings stop; everything caught inside is your <vocabulary>environment</vocabulary>.

kanojo.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>he</kanji> walking off down the road turns out to be a <kanji>woman</kanji>, and now she's the one you point at and simply call <vocabulary>she / girlfriend</vocabulary>.
kanojo.description: Context decides the sense: introduced as someone's partner it means girlfriend, used as a plain pronoun it just means she.

kanou.meaning_mnemonic: Set an <kanji form="可">approval</kanji> stamp beside the <kanji form="能">ability</kanji> to do the job, and the thing can be done. That is <vocabulary form="可能">possible</vocabulary>, and as a な adjective it takes な before its noun.

kansha-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">feeling</kanji> that wells up and makes you want to <kanji form="謝">thank</kanji> someone to their face is being <vocabulary form="感謝する">grateful</vocabulary>.

kantan-n4.meaning_mnemonic: A job cut back to pure <kanji form="簡">brevity</kanji>, with nothing left over to explain, is a <vocabulary form="簡単">simple</vocabulary> one. As a な adjective, it takes な before the noun it describes.

kanzen.meaning_mnemonic: Once Koichi has swept the <kanji form="全">whole</kanji> shelf into the basket with not one rice ball left behind, the set is <vocabulary form="完全">perfect / complete</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な comes before the noun it describes.

kao.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi hangs a mirror by the onigiri shelf so no customer walks past the beeping till without seeing their own <vocabulary>face</vocabulary> first.
kao.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>cow</reading> wanders into Koichi's konbini, stops at the mirror by the onigiri shelf and moos 「<reading>かお</reading>」 at the big hairy <vocabulary form="顔">face</vocabulary> staring back.

karada.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>body</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>body</vocabulary> word are the same character, so the meaning carries straight across with nothing added.
karada.reading_mnemonic: Nurse Cara reads each patient's <vocabulary form="体">body</vocabulary> like the one book they were born holding, finds the newest aching page and announces it with a proud 「<reading>からだ</reading>」, <reading>Cara-ta-da</reading>.

karai.meaning_mnemonic: Bite a chilli the colour of a fire hydrant, then chase it with a fistful of rock salt, and your whole mouth is on fire either way. Either burn is <vocabulary>spicy / salty</vocabulary>, and that final い lets you hang it on a noun like any adjective.
karai.reading_mnemonic: A hungry pilgrim at Grandma Kane's shrine wolfs a bowl of <reading>curry</reading> left as an offering, gets three steps, and dives into the water trough. A mouth that reacts like that has met something truly <reading>からい</reading>, blazing <vocabulary>spicy / salty</vocabulary>.

kare.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>he</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> are exactly the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
kare.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker points at a shape trudging up and asks <reading>かれ</reading>. It sounds just like <reading>car, eh</reading>, and she means only the <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> who promised to meet her there.

karee.meaning_mnemonic: Every Friday <reading>Carrie</reading> ladles a thick brown spiced stew over a mound of rice for the whole house. Her Friday dish is <vocabulary form="カレー">curry</vocabulary>, <reading>カレー</reading>.

kariru.meaning_mnemonic: You carry a neighbour's ladder home, use it for one afternoon, and promise it back by dark. Taking a thing on the promise you give it back is to <vocabulary>borrow</vocabulary> it.
kariru.reading_mnemonic: You <reading>carry</reading> the neighbour's ladder home on one shoulder, calling <reading>かりる</reading> over the fence and promising it back by dark, which is what it is to <vocabulary form="借りる">borrow</vocabulary>.

karui.meaning_mnemonic: You brace hard to heave the box, but it is empty, and it flies up so fast you stumble backwards. Anything that easy to lift is <vocabulary>light (weight)</vocabulary>, and the い ending marks it as an adjective.
karui.reading_mnemonic: You brace to heave the box, but it is empty and flies up so fast you stumble backwards. Now you can <reading>carry</reading> it on one finger, because a box that <reading>かるい</reading> is <vocabulary form="軽い">light</vocabulary>.

kasa.meaning_mnemonic: Pop open a dome of cloth on a thin pole and hold it overhead, and the rain drums on the fabric instead of on you. That portable roof is an <vocabulary>umbrella</vocabulary>.
kasa.reading_mnemonic: The old angler at the riverbank refuses to <reading>cast a</reading> line in the rain until he has popped open his patched <vocabulary>umbrella</vocabulary>. He calls that leaky dome on a stick his <reading>かさ</reading>.

kasanaru.meaning_mnemonic: Loose sheets keep drifting down onto each other with no hand guiding them, and the stack grows <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> as each one lands. Left to themselves they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> and settle into a pile.
kasanaru.reading_mnemonic: A dancer clacks her <reading>castanets</reading> over the desk, and with every clack another loose sheet drifts down onto the last until they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> in a heavy pile: <reading>かさなる</reading>.

kasaneru.meaning_mnemonic: You set plate on plate by hand, squaring each one on the last, every <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> disc pushing the stack down harder. Doing it on purpose like that is to <vocabulary form="重ねる">pile up</vocabulary>.
kasaneru.reading_mnemonic: You already met 重なる, so its by-hand partner <vocabulary form="重ねる">to pile things up</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かさねる</reading>.

kashite-morau.meaning_mnemonic: You ask, and the owner agrees to <kanji form="貸">lend</kanji> you the thing you need. Walking off with it on that promise is to <vocabulary form="貸してもらう">have (something) lent</vocabulary>.
kashite-morau.reading_mnemonic: You already know 貸 is 「か」 from 貸す, the verb to lend, so <vocabulary form="貸してもらう">to have (something) lent</vocabulary> is <reading>かしてもらう</reading>.

kasu.meaning_mnemonic: A friend's phone is dead, so you unplug your charger and hand it over until lunch. Handing your own thing to someone else for a bit, knowing it comes back, is to <vocabulary>lend</vocabulary> it.
kasu.reading_mnemonic: Your friend offers you <reading>cash</reading> for the charger, but you just unplug it and hand it over till lunch with a <reading>かす</reading>, no money needed; you only <vocabulary form="貸す">lend</vocabulary> it.

kata-person.meaning_mnemonic: The new receptionist at the school is painfully formal. She greets every student, even the smallest, as an honoured <vocabulary>person (polite)</vocabulary>, bowing before she hands back a dropped pencil.
kata-person.reading_mnemonic: The receptionist summons the school's gruff hedge <reading>cutter</reading> to shape the entrance bushes. Even he is welcomed as an honoured <vocabulary>person (polite)</vocabulary>, with a deep bow and a careful 「<reading>かた</reading>」.

katakana.meaning_mnemonic: The letters look like someone took a ruler and decided to <reading>cut a corner</reading> on every curve, leaving nothing but sharp straight angles. That stiff script for foreign words is <vocabulary>katakana</vocabulary>, and <reading>カタカナ</reading> is that phrase said fast.

kau-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>buy</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to buy</vocabulary> word are the same character, so the meaning is identical.
kau-v.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>cow</reading> throws a net over the whole fish stall and moos 「<reading>かう</reading>」 as she tips a pile of clam-shell money on the counter <vocabulary form="買う">to buy</vocabulary> her catch.

kawa-v.meaning_mnemonic: Those three flowing strokes are the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji, and the <vocabulary>river</vocabulary> word is that same character unchanged: one drawing, one meaning.
kawa-v.reading_mnemonic: A soggy dog hauls itself out where three streams flow side by side, then <reading>cower</reading>s on the bank whimpering <reading>かわ</reading> at the fast water the three make together, the <vocabulary form="川">river</vocabulary>.

kawaii.meaning_mnemonic: A muddy calf at the riverbank lifts its huge wet <reading>cow eye</reading> to you and you forget you were ever annoyed. That helpless, melting feeling is <reading>かわいい</reading>, the word for <vocabulary>cute</vocabulary>.

kawakasu.meaning_mnemonic: You hold a soaked towel flat in front of the heater and keep it there until not one drop is left. Forcing all the water out of a wet thing like that is what it is to <vocabulary form="乾かす">dry</vocabulary> it.
kawakasu.reading_mnemonic: You hold the soaked towel in front of the heater, and it roars like the blower at a <reading>car wash</reading> until not one drop is left. That is how you <vocabulary form="乾かす">dry</vocabulary> it, <reading>かわかす</reading>.

kawaku.meaning_mnemonic: You peg the washing out in the midday sun and come back to sheets that are stiff, warm, and holding no water at all. A thing losing every drop on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="乾く">dry</vocabulary>.
kawaku.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 乾かす, so the twin where something goes <vocabulary form="乾く">dry</vocabulary> on its own, with no heater on it, is <reading>かわく</reading>.

kawaru.meaning_mnemonic: A chameleon crosses a warm rock and drifts from green to brown, with nothing done to it. Turning into a new version of itself on its own is to <vocabulary>change</vocabulary>.
kawaru.reading_mnemonic: A shy octopus at the riverbank seems to <reading>cower</reading> and shift colour every few seconds without deciding to, 「<reading>かわる</reading>」, and going from one state to another on its own is to <vocabulary>change</vocabulary>.

kayou.meaning_mnemonic: Slip into the <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> that pours down one road every morning and back every night. Making that same trip over and over, day after day, is what it means <vocabulary form="通う">to commute</vocabulary>.
kayou.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the same man slips into the traffic pouring down the one road, and the crossing guard sighs <reading>Kai, you</reading> again. Kai making that trip daily is <reading>かよう</reading>, what it means <vocabulary form="通う">to commute</vocabulary>.

kayoubi.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Fire</kanji> catches on the next <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> it can reach and burns straight through it, leaving <vocabulary>Tuesday</vocabulary> scorched.

kayui.meaning_mnemonic: One mosquito gets into the tent at the riverbank and finds the strip of skin behind your knee. By dawn that spot is so <vocabulary form="痒い">itchy</vocabulary> you have scratched it raw in your sleep.
kayui.reading_mnemonic: In the tent by the river you wake with that bite behind your knee burning, and you beg your friend <reading>can you</reading> scratch it. You groan <reading>かゆい</reading>, it is so <vocabulary form="痒い">itchy</vocabulary>.

kaze-cold.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>wind</kanji> strong enough to flick a bug off the picnic table turns <kanji>wicked</kanji> and slips down your collar. The chill it leaves behind is a <vocabulary>cold</vocabulary>.
kaze-cold.reading_mnemonic: At the picnic table Grandma Kane sneezes and names the wicked wind that slipped down her collar as the <reading>cause</reading> of her <vocabulary form="風邪">cold</vocabulary>: 「<reading>かぜ</reading>」.
kaze-cold.description: Identical in sound to the everyday word for wind, and written with that same first character, so only context tells the two apart.

kaze-illness.meaning_mnemonic: Pull a <kanji form="邪">wicked</kanji> <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> deep into your chest and let it settle in as a three-day fever. Drawing bad air right inside you like that is what it means <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.
kaze-illness.reading_mnemonic: A cold gust off the river hooks Kaz like a fish on a line and reels him straight into bed. When chilled air <reading>hooks</reading> into you and holds on, that is <reading>かぜをひく</reading>, <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.

kaze-wind.meaning_mnemonic: This character is an old friend by now: the <kanji>wind</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>wind</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so nothing about the meaning changes.
kaze-wind.reading_mnemonic: One slash of air lifts a beetle off the picnic table along with the strip of <reading>gauze</reading> it sat on, and the gauze snaps out flat: 「<reading>かぜ</reading>」, real <vocabulary form="風">wind</vocabulary>.

kazoku.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone crammed under one <kanji>house</kanji>'s roof, sharing meals and arguments, is what makes a <vocabulary>family</vocabulary>.

keeki.meaning_mnemonic: The sponge comes out of the oven the exact dull brown-green of <reading>khaki</reading> trousers, yet it is soft and sweet. That baked sweet is a <vocabulary form="ケーキ">cake</vocabulary>, <reading>ケーキ</reading>.

kega.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="怪">mysterious</kanji> shape swings out of the dark and catches the one <kanji form="我">self</kanji> you were busy minding. Whatever it leaves on you afterward, a gash or a sprain or a spreading bruise, is an <vocabulary form="怪我">injury</vocabulary>.

kegasuru.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji form="怪">suspicious</kanji> force blindsides your own <kanji form="我">self</kanji> and something tears or swells with nobody's hand on it, that event is what it means <vocabulary form="怪我する">to get injured</vocabulary>.

keihi.meaning_mnemonic: Every yen the business earns must first <kanji form="経">pass through</kanji> a line of costs, rent and power and supplies, and the total it loses on the way is its <vocabulary form="経費">expenses</vocabulary>.

keikaku.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="計">plot</kanji> you have only worked out in your head turns into a <vocabulary form="計画">plan</vocabulary> the moment you lay it out in clear <kanji form="画">brush-strokes</kanji> on paper.

keikan.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>government</kanji> official whose whole job is to <kanji>admonish</kanji> you is a <vocabulary>police officer</vocabulary>.

keisatsukan.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="官">bureaucrat</kanji> paid to <kanji form="警">admonish</kanji> lawbreakers and <kanji form="察">surmise</kanji> which of them did it is a <vocabulary form="警察官">police officer</vocabulary>.

keitai.meaning_mnemonic: Strap a phone to your <kanji>sash</kanji> to keep it <kanji>portable</kanji>, bouncing on your hip through every train and every queue. That belt-worn phone is a <vocabulary>mobile phone</vocabulary>.

keiyaku.meaning_mnemonic: Two people each make a <kanji form="契">pledge</kanji>, write the matching <kanji form="約">promise</kanji> down, and sign it. That signed pair of promises is a <vocabulary form="契約">contract</vocabulary>.

keizai.meaning_mnemonic: Track how money <kanji form="経">passes through</kanji> every shop, wage and loan until each debt is <kanji form="済">settle</kanji>d, and that whole churn of payments is a country's <vocabulary form="経済">economy</vocabulary>.

kekka.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Tie</kanji> off the last knot of a long job and cut open whatever <kanji>fruit</kanji> it grew; that payoff is the <vocabulary>result</vocabulary>.

kekkon-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Two people <kanji>knot</kanji> their lives together into one <kanji>marriage</kanji> that is built never to come undone. Tie that knot and you <vocabulary>marry</vocabulary>.

kemuri.meaning_mnemonic: When something burns, part of it leaves as a grey cloud that climbs, spreads flat under the ceiling, and stings your eyes. That rising grey cloud off a fire is <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary>.
kemuri.reading_mnemonic: The grey cloud off the burnt toast climbs, spreads flat under the ceiling and stings the cook's eyes, so he finds the stove only from <reading>memory</reading>, coughing <reading>けむり</reading> through the <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary>.

kenkou.meaning_mnemonic: When every part of your body has settled into <kanji form="康">ease</kanji> and nothing in it aches or strains, the single word for that whole calm state is <vocabulary form="健康">health</vocabulary>.

kenkoushindan.meaning_mnemonic: Once a year a doctor checks whether every part of you is running at <kanji form="康">ease</kanji>, then draws a firm <kanji form="断">severance</kanji> line between what passed and what a specialist must chase. That whole yearly review is a <vocabulary form="健康診断">health checkup</vocabulary>.

kenkyuu.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="研">polish</kanji> one question for years and dig in a cave for its bottom. That patient <kanji form="究">study</kanji> of a thing down to its base is <vocabulary form="研究">research</vocabulary>.

kenri.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>benefit</kanji> the law guarantees you from birth, one that no ruler or vote is allowed to strip away, is a <vocabulary>right (entitlement)</vocabulary>.

kesseki-suru.meaning_mnemonic: When your <kanji form="席">seat</kanji> on the team bench shows a <kanji form="欠">gap</kanji> where you should be sitting, you <vocabulary form="欠席する">are absent</vocabulary>.

kesu.meaning_mnemonic: Your thumb smears across the glowing screen and every picture it touches goes black. Rubbing the light out of a thing like that is how you <vocabulary>turn off / erase</vocabulary> it.
kesu.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>kestrel</reading> lands on your glowing phone and drags one talon across it, and every picture under the claw goes black with a dry <reading>けす</reading>. That bird knows how to <vocabulary form="消す">erase</vocabulary>.

ki-tree-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tree</kanji> kanji, trunk and branches and roots in the dirt, is exactly the <vocabulary>tree</vocabulary> word, the same character standing for the same thing.
ki-tree-v.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, slides down the trunk, swings on the one flat branch and tickles the two slanted roots, giggling <reading>key</reading>, <reading>き</reading>, all over her <vocabulary form="木">tree</vocabulary>.

kibishii.meaning_mnemonic: Your piano teacher stops you at the first wrong note, every time, and will not let you move on until the bar is perfect. Being held to a standard that hard, with nothing let slide, is <vocabulary form="厳しい">strict</vocabulary>.
kibishii.reading_mnemonic: Your piano teacher, a bee named <reading>Kibi</reading>, buzzes <reading>きびしい</reading> and stops you at the first wrong note, never letting a single bar slide, because she is that <vocabulary form="厳しい">strict</vocabulary>.

kibou.meaning_mnemonic: Fix your mind on the thing you want and hold the picture of it bright even while it is still far off. Refusing to let that picture go dim is <vocabulary form="希望">hope / wish</vocabulary>.

kibun.meaning_mnemonic: Check one <kanji>part</kanji> of the <kanji>spirit</kanji> you are running on today, and that single slice of it is your <vocabulary>mood</vocabulary>.

kigyou.meaning_mnemonic: A tree-stump <kanji>business</kanji> that someone <kanji>scheme</kanji>s up into offices, payroll and a logo has grown into an <vocabulary>enterprise / business</vocabulary>.

kiiro.meaning_mnemonic: The single <kanji>color</kanji> that screams warning on wasps, road signs, and hazard tape is <vocabulary>yellow</vocabulary>. It behaves as a な adjective, so you slot な in before whatever noun it describes.

kiji.meaning_mnemonic: An <vocabulary form="記事">article</vocabulary> is a <kanji form="記">written account</kanji> of exactly one <kanji form="事">matter</kanji>, pinned down so hard it cannot wriggle off the page before you finish reading.

kikai-chance.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="機">mechanism</kanji> of events turns, and for one moment a gap in it lines up with you. Step through and <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> it and you have taken an <vocabulary form="機会">opportunity</vocabulary>.

kikai-machine.meaning_mnemonic: A cabinet packed with gears and levers that turns one small push at the handle into the same heavy job done over and over is a <vocabulary form="機械">machine</vocabulary>.

kiken.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="険">precipitous</kanji> place is all sheer drops and loose footing, so setting foot on one is plainly <vocabulary form="危険">dangerous</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な goes before the noun it describes.

kikoeru.meaning_mnemonic: Your ear is still jammed against that cold gate, but now the sounds push through the wood on their own. A noise that reaches you with no <kanji>hearing</kanji> on your part is <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary>.
kikoeru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 聞 is read 「き」 from 聞く, so this word for <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary> is simply <reading>きこえる</reading>.

kiku-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hear</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to listen</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries over. Leaning your ear in to catch more is also how you ask someone a question.
kiku-v.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon presses its ear to the crack in the gate, mutters <reading>key, coo</reading> once, then goes silent <vocabulary form="聞く">to listen</vocabulary>, breathing 「<reading>きく</reading>」 as voices drift through.

kimaru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="決">decide</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="決まる">to be decided</vocabulary> word are the same word. This form just means the matter settles on its own, with nobody there to make the call.
kimaru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kiki</reading> the tree spirit watches the water drop leave the brush and the hooked stroke swing. Once neither can be pulled back, she sighs <reading>きまる</reading>, for the matter has come <vocabulary form="決まる">to be decided</vocabulary>.

kimeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="決">decide</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="決める">to decide</vocabulary> word are the same word. This form adds a person to the scene: you are the one who makes the call and fixes the outcome.
kimeru-v.reading_mnemonic: You already know 決 is 「き」 from 決まる, so for you <vocabulary form="決める">to decide</vocabulary> the outcome yourself is <reading>きめる</reading>.

kimi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mister</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>you (familiar)</vocabulary> are exactly the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
kimi.reading_mnemonic: The official, mouth still hanging open mid-order, jabs a finger at your chest and barks <reading>きみ</reading>, like <reading>key, me</reading>, demanding the office key from <vocabulary form="君">you</vocabulary>.

kimochi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>spirit</kanji> you happen to be <kanji>holding</kanji> onto at any given moment, good or bad, is your <vocabulary>feeling</vocabulary>.

kinou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>day</kanji> that already slipped past you, gone before you could grab it, is <vocabulary>yesterday</vocabulary>.
kinou.reading_mnemonic: You lunge for the day slipping past, but it locks its door with a rusty <reading>key</reading> that clicks <reading>きのう</reading>, and it is already <vocabulary form="昨日">yesterday</vocabulary>.

kinyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> finally pays out in solid <kanji>gold</kanji>, and that payday is <vocabulary>Friday</vocabulary>.

kippu.meaning_mnemonic: A paper <kanji>token</kanji> gets one clean <kanji>cut</kanji> from the conductor's punch as you board, and that notched stub is your <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary>.
kippu.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit blocks the platform gate until you trade her a smoked <reading>kipper</reading> for the <reading>きっぷ</reading> she keeps calling your <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary>.

kirai.meaning_mnemonic: The instant curl of your lip at a smell you cannot stand is the whole of being <vocabulary>disliked</vocabulary>. Like every な word, it drops な in front of the noun.
kirai.reading_mnemonic: Sei sniffs the sour old <reading>clay</reading> at the pottery table and her lip curls at once, the way it does at any smell she cannot stand. That curl, <reading>きらい</reading>, means <vocabulary form="嫌い">disliked</vocabulary>.

kiraku.meaning_mnemonic: Let your <kanji form="気">spirit</kanji> rise off you light as steam and everything within reach feel like plain <kanji form="楽">ease</kanji>, and that is what being <vocabulary form="気楽">carefree / relaxed</vocabulary> is. As a な adjective, な comes before the noun it modifies.

kirei.meaning_mnemonic: A cleaner named <reading>Kelly</reading> scrubs every train window on the line until you could photograph your face in it. Spotless and <vocabulary>pretty / clean</vocabulary> is what <reading>きれい</reading> means.

kiroku.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="記">scribe</kanji> writes down exactly what happened and keeps himself out of every line. That filed account, kept for checking years later, is a <vocabulary form="記録">record</vocabulary>.

kiru-cut.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cut</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to cut</vocabulary> word are the very same thing, so the る on the end just makes it the verb you do to something.
kiru-cut.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit takes a sword to one carrot seven times, then <reading>keel</reading>s over giggling at the bits on the board, <reading>きる</reading>: that is what it means to <vocabulary form="切る">cut</vocabulary>.

kiru-wear.meaning_mnemonic: You drag a jumper down over your head and force both arms through the sleeves until your face pops out the top. Winning that wrestling match with a shirt is what it means to <vocabulary>wear (top)</vocabulary>.
kiru-wear.reading_mnemonic: A heron on the mountain trail is so cold it feeds coins to the vending machine and drags on a whole <reading>kilo</reading> of knitted jumpers. It squawks 「<reading>きる</reading>」 and will <vocabulary>wear (top)</vocabulary> anything with sleeves.

kissaten.meaning_mnemonic: Set aside a whole room where the only thing to do is <kanji>drink</kanji> from a steaming <kanji>tea</kanji> cup and watch the afternoon crawl past. That room is a <vocabulary>coffee shop</vocabulary>.

kita-v.meaning_mnemonic: This word is just the <kanji>north</kanji> kanji standing on its own, so the <vocabulary>north</vocabulary> word means exactly what the kanji does.
kita-v.reading_mnemonic: Two campers sit back to back against the cold wind from the <vocabulary form="北">north</vocabulary>, and the one called <reading>Keeta</reading> shouts 「<reading>きた</reading>」 at it to make it stop.

kitaisuru.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji form="待">wait</kanji> out a fixed <kanji form="期">period</kanji>, sure the thing is coming, is to <vocabulary form="期待する">expect</vocabulary> it.

kitanai.meaning_mnemonic: You haul your one white shirt out of the river and it comes up streaked brown and reeking of pondweed, somehow worse than before the wash. A shirt in that state is <vocabulary>dirty</vocabulary>, and the trailing い tags it as an adjective.
kitanai.reading_mnemonic: A stray kitten drags itself out of the riverbank mud with one <reading>kitten eye</reading> gummed shut and its fur matted into grey clumps. You reach to lift it, but it is <reading>きたない</reading> to the bone, far too <vocabulary>dirty</vocabulary> for your lap.

kitsui.meaning_mnemonic: The zip-tie on that parcel is pulled so <vocabulary form="きつい">tight / harsh</vocabulary> it <reading>cuts you</reading> when you lift it. That bite into your fingers is what <reading>きつい</reading> means.

kitsune.meaning_mnemonic: At dusk a low red-brown shape slips along the treeline by the school field, quick and quiet, a white-tipped tail held straight out behind. That build and that tail mean a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>.
kitsune.reading_mnemonic: By the school field at dusk, a girl watches the white-tipped tail slip along the treeline and whispers <reading>Kit, so neat</reading> to her brother: a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>, <reading>きつね</reading>.

kitte.meaning_mnemonic: Stamps come joined in a big sheet, so you <kanji>cut</kanji> one free by <kanji>hand</kanji> along the row of little holes. That torn-off square you lick and stick is a <vocabulary>postage stamp</vocabulary>.
kitte.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit licks the back of a tiny <reading>kitty</reading> sticker and smooths it onto a letter. She giggles 「<reading>きって</reading>」, because to her that lickable little square is a <vocabulary>postage stamp</vocabulary>.

kitto.meaning_mnemonic: The locksmith lifts one blank off the ring, holds it to the light, and says it is <reading>key to</reading> this lock with no doubt at all. That flat certainty before he has even tried it is <reading>きっと</reading>, <vocabulary form="きっと">surely / certainly</vocabulary>.

ko-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Tip a jar of buttons, beads and dice onto the table, then point at each <kanji>individual</kanji> one as you drop it back in. Anything small enough to pinch between two fingers is one <vocabulary>small objects (counter)</vocabulary>.

kochira.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sweeps one arm toward the shrine steps and the stranger beside her in one motion. Wherever that arm lands, path or person, is <vocabulary>this way / this person</vocabulary>.

kodomo-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>child</kanji> you proudly <kanji>offer</kanji> up to the neighbors, freshly bathed and squirming, is simply your <vocabulary>child</vocabulary>.
kodomo-v.description: Sometimes written partly in hiragana, since the second kanji once meant "servant."

koe.meaning_mnemonic: A ventriloquist's dummy sits alone on the stage and starts talking. The sound has to come from somewhere, and that somewhere, a throat pushing air, is a <vocabulary>voice</vocabulary>.
koe.reading_mnemonic: The dummy alone on the stage calls <reading>cooee</reading> to the empty seats, one long 「<reading>こえ</reading>」 with no throat behind it, and still the hall fills with a <vocabulary form="声">voice</vocabulary>.

koibito.meaning_mnemonic: The single <kanji>person</kanji> your heart keeps circling back to, the one you actually picked, is your <vocabulary>lover / partner</vocabulary>.

kojin.meaning_mnemonic: Pull one <kanji>person</kanji> out of the crowd and weigh them on their own, and what you are looking at is an <vocabulary>individual</vocabulary>.

kokka.meaning_mnemonic: Treat the whole <kanji form="国">country</kanji>, walls and shared jewel and all, as one <kanji form="家">house</kanji> that everyone inside it belongs to, and you have a <vocabulary form="国家">nation / state</vocabulary>.

koko.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine you stop on one mossy step and plant both feet. You thump the stone under you and mean exactly <vocabulary>here</vocabulary>, nowhere else.

kokonoka.meaning_mnemonic: Cross off <kanji>nine</kanji> boxes on the calendar, one for every <kanji>day</kanji>, and you have marked off <vocabulary>nine days</vocabulary>.

kokonotsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji still means the same nine, and adding つ turns it into <vocabulary>nine things</vocabulary>. You're counting objects now, not just naming the number.
kokonotsu.reading_mnemonic: The fishing line curls into its hook and pulls up <reading>coconuts</reading> instead of fish, until the bucket holds <reading>ここのつ</reading>: <vocabulary form="九つ">nine things</vocabulary>, one short of ten.

kokuban.meaning_mnemonic: Smoke a flat <kanji>board</kanji> over that village fire pit until the whole face of it goes <kanji>black</kanji>, then nail it to the classroom wall as a <vocabulary>blackboard</vocabulary>.

kokusai.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that happens right on the <kanji>edge</kanji> where one <kanji>country</kanji>'s wall butts against the next one's is, by definition, <vocabulary>international</vocabulary>.
kokusai.description: Almost always used stuck in front of another noun, the way a label is, rather than standing on its own as a full noun.

komaru.meaning_mnemonic: Your card is declined and the queue behind you keeps growing. There is nothing you can do about it, and being stuck with no way out is to <vocabulary>be troubled</vocabulary>.
komaru.reading_mnemonic: Your card is declined over one stray <reading>comma</reading> in the total, the queue behind you keeps growing, and all you can mutter is 「<reading>こまる</reading>」, stuck and <vocabulary form="困る">troubled</vocabulary>.

kome-v.meaning_mnemonic: The hard little grains straight from the sack, before a drop of water or any heat reaches them, are <vocabulary>uncooked rice</vocabulary>.
kome-v.reading_mnemonic: Old Mei pours the hard grains straight from the sack and drags a bamboo <reading>comb</reading> through them, muttering 「<reading>こめ</reading>」 before any water or heat touches her <vocabulary form="米">uncooked rice</vocabulary>.

konbanwa.meaning_mnemonic: The night baker leaves one leftover <reading>cone bun</reading> on the counter and says <reading>こんばんは</reading> to whoever comes in last. That after-dark greeting is <vocabulary>good evening</vocabulary>.

konbini.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's shop sells socks, stamps and hot coffee at three in the morning without blinking. A store built entirely around being that <reading>convenient</reading> is a <vocabulary>convenience store</vocabulary>, a <reading>コンビニ</reading>.

kongetsu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Now</kanji> lands on whichever lap of the <kanji>month</kanji> the moon is currently making, and that lap is <vocabulary>this month</vocabulary>.

konna.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi holds up a rice ball that got sat on and refuses to sell <vocabulary>this kind of</vocabulary> onigiri. He waves it at the shelf like evidence.

konnichiwa.meaning_mnemonic: A delivery guy with a <reading>corn-itchy</reading> sunburn across his neck tips his cap at the door and says <reading>こんにちは</reading>. It is the plain daytime <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary> you switch to once the morning is over.

kono.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school you snatch up your own notebook and refuse to loosen your grip, because <vocabulary>this (+ noun)</vocabulary> only works with something actually in your hand.

konpyuutaa.meaning_mnemonic: A grey desk machine that grinds through a million sums a second is a thing that <reading>computes</reading>, and the flat everyday name for it is <vocabulary form="コンピューター">computer</vocabulary>, <reading>コンピューター</reading>.

konshuu.meaning_mnemonic: The moment <kanji>now</kanji> falls on is always inside one lap of the <kanji>week</kanji>, and that lap is <vocabulary>this week</vocabulary>.

koohii.meaning_mnemonic: Punch the top button on the mountain-trail vending machine and it drops a scalding can with a hiss that sounds like <reading>koh-hee</reading>. That hiss is <reading>コーヒー</reading>, and the can is bitter black <vocabulary>coffee</vocabulary>.

koori.meaning_mnemonic: Water held cold enough for long enough stops behaving like a liquid and turns hard, clear and slippery. Water in that solid state is <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary>.
koori.reading_mnemonic: The lake held cold all winter has turned hard, clear and slippery, so the crew saws it out in blocks like a <reading>quarry</reading>, shouting <reading>こおり</reading> over each slab of <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary>.

kooru.meaning_mnemonic: Leave water still in the cold long enough and it turns hard and <kanji form="凍">frozen</kanji> all by itself. Water going solid like that, with nobody freezing it, is <vocabulary form="凍る">to freeze</vocabulary>.
kooru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Cora</reading> leaves a bucket of water sitting still in the cold overnight, and by dawn it has turned hard all by itself. She taps the ice and says <reading>こおる</reading>, having watched water <vocabulary form="凍る">freeze</vocabulary>.

kooto.meaning_mnemonic: On a tennis <reading>court</reading> frozen solid in January, both players keep rallying in a full <vocabulary>coat</vocabulary> and thick gloves, because 「<reading>コート</reading>」 is too cold to play in anything less.

koppu.meaning_mnemonic: A traffic <reading>cop</reading> waves cars past all afternoon while nursing one paper 「<reading>コップ</reading>」 of water, the only <vocabulary>cup / glass</vocabulary> in his booth.

kore.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi grabs the onigiri closest to his hand at the register and holds it straight up without even glancing at the shelf. Whatever sits right beside you is always <vocabulary>this one</vocabulary>.

koreru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
koreru.reading_mnemonic: As the burst rice grain scatters over the flat ground, the farmer asks his wife <reading>Cora, really?</reading> and she nods: a whole crop <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> up from that, <reading>こられる</reading>.

korosareru.meaning_mnemonic: A beetle wanders onto the train track at exactly the wrong second. The 8:15 does not slow down, and being the one it happens to is <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary>.
korosareru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 殺 is 「ころ」 from 殺す, the verb you first met it in, so <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary> is <reading>ころされる</reading>.

korosu.meaning_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower and the motor goes quiet for good under your hands. Ending a running thing on purpose like that is what it means <vocabulary form="殺す">to kill</vocabulary> it.
korosu.reading_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower in the middle of its roaring <reading>chorus</reading>, and the motor goes quiet under your hands for good: <reading>ころす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="殺す">kill</vocabulary> it.

kotae.meaning_mnemonic: The hand that shoots up, the words that make the teacher stop scanning the room and nod, is the <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary>.
kotae.reading_mnemonic: You already know 答 is 「こた」 from 答える, so the <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> you fill the blank with is <reading>こたえ</reading>.

kotaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Call a question into the school's empty, echoing hallway and just wait. The reply that comes bouncing back on its own, with nobody standing there to give it, is the hall beginning <vocabulary>to answer</vocabulary>.
kotaeru.reading_mnemonic: The kangaroo mascot <reading>Cot-a-roo</reading> hops down the empty school hallway; yell a question at it and the hall bounces back 「<reading>こたえる</reading>」, as if the walls had learned <vocabulary form="答える">to answer</vocabulary>.

koto.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine a lantern tips over and an offering goes missing the same morning. Grandma Kane writes each mishap on a slip and calls it one more <vocabulary>thing (matter)</vocabulary> to deal with.
koto.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane winds a <reading>cotton</reading> string round her finger for every unfinished <vocabulary>thing (matter)</vocabulary> on her mind. By noon her hand is a fat white ball she taps while muttering 「<reading>こと</reading>」.

kotoba.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>leaf</kanji> on the tree is one thing a person once chose to <kanji>say</kanji>, and the whole crown of them together is <vocabulary>language</vocabulary>.

kotoshi.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever year is <kanji>now</kanji> is simply this <kanji>year</kanji> — nothing else counts as <vocabulary>this year</vocabulary>.
kotoshi.reading_mnemonic: The tailor <reading>Coat, She</reading> stitches <reading>ことし</reading> into a coat for whatever year it is now and burns every other date, because only <vocabulary form="今年">this year</vocabulary> counts.

kotowaru.meaning_mnemonic: The host holds out the good sweets and you put a flat hand over your cup and say no until she takes the plate back. Turning down what someone offers, out loud and on purpose, is what it means <vocabulary form="断る">to refuse / decline</vocabulary>.
kotowaru.reading_mnemonic: Even when the host offers sweets as soft as <reading>cotton wool</reading>, your flat hand stays over the cup until she takes the plate back: <reading>ことわる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="断る">refuse</vocabulary>.

kouban.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>police box</vocabulary> is one street-corner spot where police and the public <kanji>mingle</kanji> all day long. Officers keep it staffed by each taking a <kanji>turn</kanji> on duty there.

kouen.meaning_mnemonic: Take a patch of trees and mown grass, then make it <kanji>public</kanji> so any stranger can wander in and sit down. That open ground is a <vocabulary>park</vocabulary>.

koufuku.meaning_mnemonic: Set the homegrown <kanji form="幸">happiness</kanji> of a stalk in your own soil next to an outright <kanji form="福">blessing</kanji> dropped in your lap, and stacked together they are <vocabulary form="幸福">formal happiness</vocabulary>. This is a な adjective, so な goes in front of the noun it describes.

koujou.meaning_mnemonic: Wall off a flat <kanji>place</kanji>, pack it with machines doing heavy <kanji>craft</kanji> all day, and the shed you built is a <vocabulary>factory</vocabulary>.

koukan-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Two people let their goods <kanji form="交">mingle</kanji> on the table, then <kanji form="換">change</kanji> which one each takes home. What they do is <vocabulary form="交換する">to exchange</vocabulary> them.

koumuin.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>employee</kanji> whose <kanji>duties</kanji> are <kanji>public</kanji> is a <vocabulary>civil servant</vocabulary>. The public purse feeds this one, not a single company's till.

koutei.meaning_mnemonic: Take the shaded <kanji>school</kanji> where paths cross and fence off the bare <kanji>yard</kanji> beside it for running laps, and that dusty patch is the <vocabulary>schoolyard</vocabulary>.

kouza.meaning_mnemonic: At the bank your money gets a reserved place to <kanji form="座">sit</kanji>, and a slot shaped like a <kanji form="口">mouth</kanji> in the counter is where you feed it in. That spot where your money sits is your <vocabulary form="口座">bank account</vocabulary>.

kowai.meaning_mnemonic: A thing so <kanji form="怖">dreadful</kanji> that your legs lock and your breath stops before you can even run from it is what <vocabulary form="怖い">scary</vocabulary> means.
kowai.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>koala</reading> drops from a branch right in front of you, ears flat and hissing, and your legs lock and your breath stops before you can run. You can only gasp <reading>こわい</reading>, because that is <vocabulary form="怖い">scary</vocabulary>.

kowareru.meaning_mnemonic: One morning the old radio just goes silent, and no switch brings it back. A thing that stops working with nobody laying a hand on it has come to <vocabulary form="壊れる">break</vocabulary>.
kowareru.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 壊す, so the twin where a thing <vocabulary form="壊れる">breaks</vocabulary> on its own, with no one touching it, is <reading>こわれる</reading>.

kowasu.meaning_mnemonic: Take something that works fine, swing a hammer at it, and leave it in pieces on the floor. Doing that to an object on purpose is what it is to <vocabulary form="壊す">break</vocabulary> it.
kowasu.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>cow</reading> grips your hammer in her teeth, swings it at the perfectly good radio and leaves it in pieces on the floor. She moos <reading>こわす</reading>, proud of how hard she can <vocabulary form="壊す">break</vocabulary> things.

ku-num.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>nine (alt)</vocabulary> word point at the same idea, character for character.

kubi.meaning_mnemonic: An owl swivels its head almost all the way around. The bendy stalk that lets it do that, the piece joining head to shoulders, is the <vocabulary>neck</vocabulary>.
kubi.reading_mnemonic: The owl backs into a wooden <reading>cubby</reading> and swivels its head almost all the way round on its bendy <vocabulary form="首">neck</vocabulary>, hooting a muffled 「<reading>くび</reading>」 from inside.

kuchi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mouth</kanji> kanji you already know and the <vocabulary>mouth</vocabulary> word are the exact same character, unchanged.
kuchi-v.reading_mnemonic: A kid mid-yawn has his small square <vocabulary form="口">mouth</vocabulary> stretched so wide that his sister claps a hand over the open hole and shrieks 「<reading>くち</reading>」, sure a <reading>cootie</reading> will fly in.

kudamono.meaning_mnemonic: Out of everything hanging in a tree, the one <kanji>thing</kanji> sweet enough to be worth climbing for is <vocabulary>fruit</vocabulary>.
kudamono.reading_mnemonic: The farmer yells <reading>Cooda Moe, no!</reading> as his monkey climbs to the top of the tree for the one sweet <vocabulary form="果物">fruit</vocabulary> worth the climb, and 「<reading>くだもの</reading>」 echoes through the orchard.

kudasaru.meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
kudasaru.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

kuma.meaning_mnemonic: The beekeeper finds three hives smashed flat, the honey frames licked clean and claw marks gouged deep in the wood. Only a <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary> robs hives like that.
kuma.reading_mnemonic: The beekeeper follows the claw marks to a hollow log where the thief lies curled in a furry <reading>comma</reading>, honey on its snout, and hisses <reading>くま</reading> at the <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary> that licked his frames clean.

kumo.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi leaves a bag of cotton balls open by the till, the ceiling fan catches them, and a grey clump ends up hovering over the onigiri shelf where nobody can reach it. That floating, unreachable fluff is a <vocabulary>cloud</vocabulary>.
kumo.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon perched on Koichi's onigiri shelf coos 「<reading>くも</reading>」, <reading>coo-moh</reading>, at the grey cotton fluff the ceiling fan keeps spinning just out of reach, its own little <vocabulary form="雲">cloud</vocabulary>.

kumo-spider.meaning_mnemonic: You step off the porch at dawn and walk face-first through a wide sticky net strung across the doorway. Sitting dead centre with its legs spread is the <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary> that spun it overnight.
kumo-spider.reading_mnemonic: Mo walks the mountain trail into the same face-height web every dawn and yells <reading>come, Mo</reading> at nobody. The weaver that keeps rebuilding it is a <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary>, 「<reading>くも</reading>」.

kurai.meaning_mnemonic: Someone unscrews the last working bulb in the basement and now you cannot see your own hand in front of your face. A room like that is <vocabulary>dark</vocabulary>, and the trailing い makes it an adjective.
kurai.reading_mnemonic: Someone unscrews the last bulb in the basement and little Kura cannot see her own hand, so she sits on the stairs to <reading>cry</reading>. A basement that <reading>くらい</reading> is truly <vocabulary form="暗い">dark</vocabulary>.

kureru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the curry machine skips the whole queue and fires a hot pouch straight into your hands. Something that rams a packet at you unasked <vocabulary>gives</vocabulary> it to you, so say <reading>curry roo</reading> fast and you land on <reading>くれる</reading>.

kurikaesu.meaning_mnemonic: You set the reel <kanji form="繰">winding</kanji> forward, it <kanji form="返">return</kanji>s to the very same mark, and your hand starts it winding again. Motion that keeps coming back to its start is <vocabulary form="繰り返す">to repeat</vocabulary>.

kuro-color.meaning_mnemonic: This <vocabulary>black</vocabulary> word is just the <kanji>black</kanji> kanji you already know, standing on its own with the meaning unchanged.
kuro-color.reading_mnemonic: Over the village built on the fire pit, a <reading>crow</reading> lands on a smoking roof and caws <reading>くろ</reading>, so sooty now that it matches every roof and paddy: all <vocabulary form="黒">black</vocabulary>.

kuroi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>black</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>black</vocabulary> word are the same character. The い tacked on the end is just what turns it into an adjective.
kuroi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 黒 is read 「くろ」 from the word 黒, so this adjective meaning <vocabulary>black</vocabulary> is just <reading>くろい</reading>.

kuru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>come</kanji> kanji standing on its own is exactly the <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> word, so they mean the same thing. No one makes it happen; it is intransitive.
