kuru-v.reading_mnemonic: Where the burst rice grain scattered, a <reading>crew</reading> of green shoots pokes up through the ground, each one piping 「<reading>くる</reading>」 as the crop starts <vocabulary form="来る">to come</vocabulary> up.

kuruma.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>car</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>car</vocabulary> word are the same single character, meaning the same thing.
kuruma.reading_mnemonic: Seen from above, a little cart with a box body and bar wheels <reading>caroms</reading> off the curb, and its driver checks the bent axle, muttering 「<reading>くるま</reading>」 over his battered <vocabulary form="車">car</vocabulary>.

kusaru.meaning_mnemonic: Shove a tub of rice to the back of the fridge and forget it for three weeks. The smell hits before you see the domed, slimy lid, and food left to turn that far is what <vocabulary form="腐る">to rot / spoil</vocabulary> means.
kusaru.reading_mnemonic: Three weeks on, you pry the slimy domed lid off the forgotten rice tub and find it grey and lumpy as old <reading>couscous</reading>. You gag <reading>くさる</reading>: the rice has begun to <vocabulary form="腐る">rot</vocabulary>.

kusuri.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>medicine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>medicine</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning.
kusuri.reading_mnemonic: The herbalist gives your sore knee one <reading>cursory</reading> glance, then brews grass until it hums its gentle music and hands you 「<reading>くすり</reading>」, the oldest <vocabulary form="薬">medicine</vocabulary>.

kusuri-o-nomu.meaning_mnemonic: English says you take a pill; Japanese says you <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> it. So even a dry tablet of <kanji form="薬">medicine</kanji> goes down the same way water does, and that is what it means <vocabulary form="薬を飲む">to take medicine</vocabulary>.

kutsu.meaning_mnemonic: The two leather cages you lock your feet into every morning, so you can stomp across gravel without a second thought, are your <vocabulary>shoes</vocabulary>.
kutsu.reading_mnemonic: A barefoot hiker crosses the riverbank stones and picks up sharp <reading>cuts</reading> on both soles. She pulls on 「<reading>くつ</reading>」 so the next crossing scratches the <vocabulary>shoes</vocabulary>, not her feet.

kutsushita.meaning_mnemonic: Hidden <kanji form="下">below</kanji> your <kanji form="靴">shoes</kanji> all day where nobody sees them, wrapped straight onto the foot, are your <vocabulary form="靴下">socks</vocabulary>.

kuukou.meaning_mnemonic: Swap the sea out of a <kanji>harbor</kanji> for a stretch of <kanji>empty</kanji> sky, and the boats that dock there become planes at an <vocabulary>airport</vocabulary>.

kyaku.meaning_mnemonic: Anyone who comes through your door expecting to be seated, served and fussed over before they leave again is a <vocabulary>guest / customer</vocabulary>.

kyonen.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>year</kanji> already scratched onto the shield-board and left behind you is <vocabulary>last year</vocabulary>.

kyou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> you are standing in belongs to whichever <kanji>day</kanji> the sun happens to be up, and that day is <vocabulary>today</vocabulary>.
kyou.reading_mnemonic: The moment the sun is up is your <reading>cue</reading>: a rooster crows <reading>きょう</reading> to claim the day you are standing in as <vocabulary form="今日">today</vocabulary>.

kyoudai.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>older brother</kanji> and a <kanji>younger brother</kanji> together are what everyone calls <vocabulary>siblings</vocabulary>.
kyoudai.description: Covers siblings in general, including sisters, even though both kanji individually mean brother.

kyoukasho.meaning_mnemonic: Someone <kanji>write</kanji>s down exactly what each <kanji>department</kanji> has to <kanji>teach</kanji>, binds the pages, and hands you the result as a <vocabulary>textbook</vocabulary>.

kyoumi.meaning_mnemonic: A subject that keeps <kanji form="興">entertaining</kanji> you and leaves a <kanji form="味">taste</kanji> you go back for again has a hold on you. That hold is your <vocabulary form="興味">interest</vocabulary> in it.

kyouryoku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: When several people aim their <kanji form="力">strength</kanji> at the same task and merge it into one shared push, that <kanji form="協">cooperation</kanji> is what it means to <vocabulary form="協力する">cooperate</vocabulary>.

kyoushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Put a <kanji>room</kanji> around the act of <kanji>teach</kanji>ing, with desks bolted down facing one wall, and you have built a <vocabulary>classroom</vocabulary>.

kyuu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>nine</vocabulary> word are the exact same character, doing the exact same job.

kyuuka.meaning_mnemonic: Line up a run of <kanji form="休">rest</kanji> days with enough <kanji form="暇">spare time</kanji> stacked behind them to do nothing at all, and the stretch you get away from work is a <vocabulary form="休暇">vacation / leave</vocabulary>.

kyuuryou.meaning_mnemonic: Once a month your <kanji form="料">fee</kanji> for showing up arrives, paid to you by the firm and not by you, and that regular sum is your <vocabulary form="給料">salary</vocabulary>.

machi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>town</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>town</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries straight over.
machi-v.reading_mnemonic: Sei strikes a <reading>match</reading> on the dark mountain trail, and the flame shows her she is standing in the main square of a whole <vocabulary>town</vocabulary> that was empty fields at dusk. She keeps the 「<reading>まち</reading>」 lit so it cannot slip back into the dark.

machigaeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>space between</kanji> two pigeonhole dividers is a mail slot, and you shove your letter into the one that <kanji>differs</kanji> from yours by a single room number. Feeding that wrong slot is what it means to <vocabulary>make a mistake</vocabulary>.

machigau.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji form="間">gap between</kanji> what you believe and what is true turns out to <kanji form="違">differ</kanji>, you are <vocabulary form="間違う">mistaken</vocabulary>.

mada.meaning_mnemonic: Ask the teenager if his homework is finished and he groans <reading>まだ</reading>. That groan is his flat <reading>'Ma, duh'</reading> for <vocabulary>still / not yet</vocabulary>.

mado.meaning_mnemonic: Punch a square hole in a solid wall and fill it with a sheet of glass. Now you can watch the storm without a single drop landing on you, and that glass-filled square you stare through is a <vocabulary>window</vocabulary>.
mado.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>mad doe</reading> out in the storm stares at you through the glass-filled square in the wall, rain streaming down her face but never yours, and you name that <vocabulary form="窓">window</vocabulary> 「<reading>まど</reading>」.

madoguchi.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mouth</kanji>-shaped slot cut in a counter, where a clerk leans through to take your papers, is a <vocabulary>service window</vocabulary>.

mae.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>front</kanji> kanji standing on its own is the <vocabulary>front</vocabulary> word, meaning and all.
mae.reading_mnemonic: Farmhand <reading>Mae</reading> crosses the moonlit yard and freezes right in <vocabulary form="前">front</vocabulary> of the cow guarding its dropped knife, whispering her own name, 「<reading>まえ</reading>」, to calm it.

magaru.meaning_mnemonic: The straight road suddenly hits a <kanji>bend</kanji> and swings hard to the left. Following that bend around is what it means to <vocabulary>turn</vocabulary> a corner.
magaru.reading_mnemonic: Your driving <reading>guru</reading> sits silent on the straight road until it swings hard left at the bend, then barks <reading>まがる</reading> and you follow it round to <vocabulary form="曲がる">turn</vocabulary> the corner.

mai-counter.meaning_mnemonic: The thinnest thing you can hold in your mind is one <kanji>sheet</kanji> of paper. Stamps, plates, shirts and pancakes all share that same flatness, so you tally them as <vocabulary>flat objects (counter)</vocabulary>.

maiasa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini shutter grinds open at <kanji>every</kanji> <kanji>morning</kanji>'s first light, and that daily grind is <vocabulary>every morning</vocabulary> itself.

maiban.meaning_mnemonic: The shrine bell at Grandma Kane's rings out <kanji>every</kanji> single time the sun goes down, and that relentless repeat is <vocabulary>every night</vocabulary>.

mainen.meaning_mnemonic: Notch <kanji>every</kanji> ban onto the <kanji>year</kanji> board and the tally becomes <vocabulary>every year</vocabulary>.

mainichi.meaning_mnemonic: Slap <kanji>every</kanji> ban onto the calendar and it covers <kanji>day</kanji> after day, which is just <vocabulary>every day</vocabulary>.

mairu.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the car at the gate and walk the last stretch up to the house on foot, hat held in both hands. Coming toward someone that plainly, on foot and uncovered, is to <vocabulary form="参る">come to them humbly</vocabulary>.
mairu.reading_mnemonic: An old retainer waves away every offer of a ride, saying that walking to you in person is <reading>my rule</reading>, and sets off down the full length of the road. That slow arrival on your own two feet is <vocabulary form="参る">to go and come humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>まいる</reading>.

maishuu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Every</kanji> <kanji>week</kanji> loops back to Monday like a stubborn circle, and that loop is <vocabulary>every week</vocabulary>.

maitsuki.meaning_mnemonic: Cover <kanji>every</kanji> lap the <kanji>month</kanji> moon makes and you get <vocabulary>every month</vocabulary>.

majime.meaning_mnemonic: Hold a <kanji form="真">true</kanji> <kanji form="面">face</kanji>, no act, with your <kanji form="目">eye</kanji> fixed on the work in front of you. That is what <vocabulary form="真面目">serious / diligent</vocabulary> looks like, and it takes な before the noun it describes.
majime.reading_mnemonic: Jimmy wears a true face, no act, his eye fixed on the homework in front of him. His sister yells <reading>Ma, Jimmy</reading> is all <reading>まじめ</reading> again, so <vocabulary form="真面目">diligent</vocabulary>.

man-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>ten thousand</vocabulary> word never needed to separate, so they never did.

manga.meaning_mnemonic: Draw one loose, <kanji form="漫">unrestrained</kanji> <kanji form="画">picture</kanji>, then the next, then a hundred more in a row, and bind the stack. That runaway sequence of drawings is <vocabulary form="漫画">comic / manga</vocabulary>.

mannaka.meaning_mnemonic: Find the one <kanji>true</kanji>, exact point of a shape, the spot equally far from every edge. That <kanji>middle</kanji> point is its <vocabulary>center</vocabulary>.

marui.meaning_mnemonic: A machine at Koichi's konbini is set wrong, so every onigiri on the door shelf rolls out a perfect <vocabulary>round</vocabulary> ball instead of a triangle. The い closing the word is its adjective marker, so it can describe any noun.
marui.reading_mnemonic: The broken machine at Koichi's konbini rolls out every onigiri like a giant <reading>marble</reading> bouncing along the door shelf. He sighs <reading>まるい</reading>, because each one is perfectly <vocabulary form="丸い">round</vocabulary>.

masaka.meaning_mnemonic: You kick the ball in the backyard, look up, and <reading>my soccer</reading> ball is somehow up on the roof across the street, the jolt of cannot-be that we blurt as <reading>まさか</reading>, <vocabulary form="まさか">no way! / surely not</vocabulary>.

mata.meaning_mnemonic: Your neighbour <reading>mutters</reading> the very same complaint about the bins every single morning. That daily <reading>また</reading> means here it comes <vocabulary>again</vocabulary>.

matasareru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="待">wait</kanji> kanji sits at the centre of this word unchanged. The endings stacked after it turn plain waiting into <vocabulary form="待たされる">being made to wait</vocabulary> by someone who will not hurry.
matasareru.reading_mnemonic: You learned 「ま」 back in 待つ, so the drawn-out <vocabulary form="待たされる">to be made to wait</vocabulary> is still just <reading>またされる</reading>.

matsu.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>wait</vocabulary> is to stand on the same rubber mat by the door so long that your shoes leave two pale dents in it.
matsu.reading_mnemonic: A station guard lines up spare floor <reading>mats</reading>, counts them, then lines them up again. It is the only thing to do while he <reading>まつ</reading> for the delayed train, so he has learned to <vocabulary>wait</vocabulary>.

matsuri.meaning_mnemonic: A village <kanji form="祭">ritual</kanji> for the local gods, once the whole street piles on food stalls, drums and lanterns, has grown into a <vocabulary form="祭り">festival</vocabulary>.
matsuri.reading_mnemonic: Tomo the tanuki knows the shrine <reading>mats really</reading> fill up fast once the drums start. He stakes out his spot for the 「<reading>まつり</reading>」 hours before the <vocabulary form="祭り">festival</vocabulary> begins.

mawaru.meaning_mnemonic: A wheel jolts loose from the cart and rolls off on its own, going <kanji form="回">round</kanji> and round all the way down the hill. Something spinning in circles by itself is what it is to <vocabulary form="回る">turn</vocabulary>.
mawaru.reading_mnemonic: The loose cart wheel rolls down the hill going round and round, and a <reading>marble</reading> stuck in its hub whirls along with it. Spinning in circles like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="回る">turn</vocabulary>, <reading>まわる</reading>.

mawasu.meaning_mnemonic: You grab the stiff crank on the well and force it <kanji form="回">round</kanji>, one hard shove after another, until the bucket starts to rise. Driving a thing in a circle with your own hand is what it is to <vocabulary form="回す">turn</vocabulary> it.
mawasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 回る, so the twin where your hand is the thing spinning it is <reading>まわす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="回す">turn</vocabulary> it.

mazu.meaning_mnemonic: The kid has all of Saturday mapped out and leads with <reading>まず</reading>. That is <reading>'Ma, zoo'</reading>, so the zoo comes <vocabulary>first of all</vocabulary>.

mazu-hajime.meaning_mnemonic: On any list of things to do there is a step that comes before every other step, ahead of even sitting down. That very first move, made before anything else, is <vocabulary form="まず初めに">first of all</vocabulary>.
mazu-hajime.reading_mnemonic: The 初 here is the same 「はじ」 you already learned in 初め, so <vocabulary form="まず初めに">first of all</vocabulary> is just <reading>まずはじめに</reading>.

mazui.meaning_mnemonic: A kid in the school cafeteria takes one mouthful of the grey mystery stew, freezes, and shoves the tray away with a flat '<reading>Ma, ewwy</reading>'. That verdict on the stew is 「<reading>まずい</reading>」, <vocabulary>bad-tasting</vocabulary>, and its い ending is the adjective marker every one of them carries.

me-ga-warui.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji form="目">eye</kanji> itself has gone <kanji form="悪">bad</kanji> and anything past your own arm is a blur, that is <vocabulary form="目が悪い">to have poor eyesight</vocabulary>. The final い is the ending that makes it an adjective.

me-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eye</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>eye</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, so there is nothing new to learn here.
me-v.reading_mnemonic: <reading>May</reading> the staring doll has one <vocabulary form="目">eye</vocabulary> painted on its side, a box of eyelid with two lines for a pupil, and when it stares back you shiver 「<reading>め</reading>」.

meeru.meaning_mnemonic: You post a paper letter through a slot and it thumps onto a desk across the planet before the flap has swung back. <reading>Mail</reading> that fast is <vocabulary form="メール">email</vocabulary>, and the slot clacks out <reading>メール</reading> every time one lands.

megane.meaning_mnemonic: Bend the blurry world back into focus by wearing a tiny polished <kanji>mirror</kanji> before each <kanji>eyeball</kanji>. That pair of lenses perched on your nose is your <vocabulary>glasses</vocabulary>.
megane.reading_mnemonic: The class <reading>meganerd</reading> is blind as a bat without the thick lenses she shoves up her nose every ten seconds. Those <vocabulary>glasses</vocabulary> are her <reading>めがね</reading>.

meiwaku.meaning_mnemonic: Someone leads you <kanji form="迷">astray</kanji>, then leaves you standing there in <kanji form="惑">perplexity</kanji>, and being dropped in that state by another person is what makes them <vocabulary form="迷惑">annoying / a bother</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な comes before the noun.

mendokusai.meaning_mnemonic: You put on a stiff <kanji form="面">mask</kanji> just to answer the door, and the whole prop shelf <kanji form="倒">collapses</kanji> on you as you reach for it. A small job that turns into that much bother is <vocabulary form="面倒くさい">troublesome</vocabulary>.
mendokusai.reading_mnemonic: Mendo pulls on a stiff mask to answer the door, the whole prop shelf collapses on him, and <reading>Mendo cusses</reading> 「<reading>めんどくさい</reading>」 from under the pile, a job grown <vocabulary form="面倒くさい">troublesome</vocabulary>.

menyuu.meaning_mnemonic: A waiter at a packed diner is asked for the list of dishes by <reading>many ewe</reading> at the same moment, a whole coach tour of sheep. He keeps shouting that the <vocabulary form="メニュー">menu</vocabulary> is printed on the back of the placemat, and the sheep just bleat <reading>メニュー</reading> louder.

meshiagaru.meaning_mnemonic: An honored guest never fetches their own meal: the dishes are <kanji form="召">called for</kanji> from the kitchen and carried <kanji form="上">up</kanji> to the head of the table. Eating and drinking what has been summoned and raised to you is to <vocabulary form="召し上がる">eat or drink, honorifically</vocabulary>.

michi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>road</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>road / street</vocabulary> word are the exact same character, so they mean the exact same thing.
michi-v.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Mitch</reading> cranes his long neck to stare down the <vocabulary form="道">road</vocabulary> before his feet will advance a single step, and only then mutters 「<reading>みち</reading>」 and walks it.

midori.meaning_mnemonic: Think of a forgotten conservatory where one unstoppable vine has swallowed the glass, the benches, and the watering cans, leaving nothing any colour but <vocabulary>green</vocabulary>.
midori.reading_mnemonic: In the forgotten conservatory the vine has turned the benches and watering cans into one <reading>meadow</reading>, and the gardener who steps inside can only whisper <reading>みどり</reading> at all that <vocabulary form="緑">green</vocabulary>.

mieru.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that does the <kanji>seeing</kanji> sprouts little legs, climbs a hill, and halts right out in the open. An eye that has stopped looking and turned into the thing anyone can look at is <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary>.
mieru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is read 「み」 from 見る, so this word for <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary> is simply <reading>みえる</reading>.

migi-v.meaning_mnemonic: On its own, the <kanji>right</kanji> kanji is exactly the <vocabulary>right</vocabulary> word, no more and no less.
migi-v.reading_mnemonic: With her left hand busy holding the rice bowl, <reading>Miggy</reading> the mongoose shovels every bite to her mouth with her <vocabulary form="右">right</vocabulary>, chattering 「<reading>みぎ</reading>」 between mouthfuls.

mijikai.meaning_mnemonic: A midge is about one pencil-dot wide and lives from breakfast to lunch. That covers <vocabulary>short</vocabulary> in both size and time.
mijikai.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>midge</reading> lands on the beeping till at Koichi's konbini and lifts off again before the beep has finished. A visit that <reading>みじかい</reading> is exactly what <vocabulary>short</vocabulary> describes.

mikka.meaning_mnemonic: That stubby ladder of rungs you know as <kanji>three</kanji> lines up beside the <kanji>day</kanji> mark. Three rungs stacked on one day column add up to <vocabulary>three days</vocabulary>.

mimawasu.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye travels one full <kanji form="回">round</kanji> of the room, past every wall and back to where it started. Sweeping your gaze in a circle like that is <vocabulary form="見回す">to look around</vocabulary>.

mimi-ga-tooi.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="耳">ear</kanji> still works, but every sound now has to cross a long <kanji form="遠">distant</kanji> road to reach it and arrives faint. Sound landing that far off is <vocabulary form="耳が遠い">to be hard of hearing</vocabulary>, and the closing い marks it as an adjective.

mimi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ear</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>ear</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean the very same thing.
mimi-v.reading_mnemonic: Seen from the side, the cat <reading>Mimi</reading> is all tall outer rim and folded lines, one huge <vocabulary form="耳">ear</vocabulary> that swivels whenever you whisper 「<reading>みみ</reading>」.

minami-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>south</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>south</vocabulary> word are one and the same, with nothing added and nothing changed.
minami-v.reading_mnemonic: Two horns poke out of the box lashed to the one warm, dry wall, where the goat inside basks as if in <reading>Miami</reading>, 「<reading>みなみ</reading>」, because that wall faces <vocabulary form="南">south</vocabulary>.

minna.meaning_mnemonic: When Koichi's onigiri shelf empties, 「<reading>みんな</reading>」 in line turns <reading>meaner</reading>, and <vocabulary>everyone</vocabulary> glares at the register at once.

miokuru.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye locked on your friend while the platform <kanji form="送">send</kanji>s her off down a track you may not follow. Watching a person go until she is out of sight is <vocabulary form="見送る">to see off</vocabulary>.

mirareru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="見">see</kanji> kanji does not change when it becomes a word, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> is simply the character you have already met.
mirareru.reading_mnemonic: This 「み」 is the reading you picked up in 見る, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>みられる</reading>.

miru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>see</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to see</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries over untouched. Whether it is a quick glance or settling in to watch, it stays this one character.
miru-v.reading_mnemonic: The eye on legs walks up to a hand <reading>mirror</reading> and stops dead, blinking 「<reading>みる</reading>」, because for once it gets <vocabulary form="見る">to see</vocabulary> itself.

mise.meaning_mnemonic: A single narrow room: a counter worn smooth by elbows, a bell that jingles when the door swings, shelves of goods each wearing a price tag. That is a <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>.
mise.reading_mnemonic: Every shelf in the place is a <reading>messy</reading> landslide of jars and tins, and prising one purchase out of that heap is what buying from a <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>, a <reading>みせ</reading>, feels like.

miseru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>show</vocabulary> something is to shove it straight in front of another person's eyes so that they <kanji>see</kanji> it whether they wanted to or not.
miseru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, so to <vocabulary>show</vocabulary> a thing by holding it up to the eyes is <reading>みせる</reading>.

misete-kureru.meaning_mnemonic: A friend makes you <kanji form="見">see</kanji> something by holding it up in front of your face. That small favour, done for you, is to <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">show (to me)</vocabulary>.
misete-kureru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, the verb to look, so <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">to show (to me)</vocabulary> is <reading>みせてくれる</reading>.

misoshiru.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="味">taste</kanji> this <kanji form="噌">boisterous</kanji>, all salt and funk and noise on the tongue, comes only from fermented soybean paste stirred into a hot bowl. That bowl is <vocabulary form="味噌汁">miso soup</vocabulary>.

mitsukaru.meaning_mnemonic: A missing sock drifts out into the open until a wandering eye on legs happens to <kanji form="見">see</kanji> it, and with no one searching for it that sock has come <vocabulary form="見つかる">to be found</vocabulary>.
mitsukaru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, so for a lost thing <vocabulary form="見つかる">to be found</vocabulary> at last is <reading>みつかる</reading>.

mitsukedasu.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye catches the hidden thing, and you haul it up over the box rim until it <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>s into daylight. Dragging a buried fact into the open is <vocabulary form="見つけ出す">to discover / find out</vocabulary>.

mitsukeru.meaning_mnemonic: The eye on legs that can <kanji>see</kanji> roams the world, checking everything it passes. When it stops because it has spotted the one thing it wanted, you <vocabulary>find</vocabulary> it.
mitsukeru.reading_mnemonic: You already met this 「み」 in 見る, to see, so the word for <vocabulary>to find</vocabulary> is simply <reading>みつける</reading>.

mittsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>three</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>three things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
mittsu.reading_mnemonic: A catcher taps his <reading>mitt</reading> on each level rung of the stubby ladder and calls <reading>みっつ</reading> once he has touched all <vocabulary form="三つ">three things</vocabulary>.

mizu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>water</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>water</vocabulary> word are the same, so they carry the same meaning.
mizu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Miss Sue</reading> stands under the falling stream as its two trickles splash out to each side, and she calls that cold <vocabulary form="水">water</vocabulary> 「<reading>みず</reading>」.

mizuumi.meaning_mnemonic: A puddle you step over and a river is gone before you look twice. Water that just lies there in one huge still sheet you could row across for an hour is a <vocabulary>lake</vocabulary>.
mizuumi.reading_mnemonic: A boy on the lakeshore is sure the flat water is a quiet old woman named <reading>Miz Oomi</reading>, and every morning he greets it with 「<reading>みずうみ</reading>」. The huge calm sheet he waves at is a <vocabulary>lake</vocabulary>.

mochikaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> on the warm food box never loosens the whole walk home, right up to the moment you <kanji form="帰">return</kanji> through your own door. Carrying your meal back that way is <vocabulary form="持ち帰る">to take home / take out</vocabulary>.

mochiron.meaning_mnemonic: Ask Koichi to float you a <reading>mochi loan</reading> until payday and he is nodding before you finish the sentence. Some favours are so small the answer is just <reading>もちろん</reading>, <vocabulary>of course</vocabulary>.

moeru.meaning_mnemonic: A dropped match catches the dry grass at the field's edge, and the whole slope is orange before anyone can stand up. Something going up in flame on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="燃える">burn</vocabulary>.
moeru.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>mower</reading> on Sei's school field throws a spark into the heap of dry cuttings, and the pile is alight in seconds. Stuff catching and climbing into flame is what it means to <vocabulary form="燃える">burn</vocabulary>, 「<reading>もえる</reading>」.

mokuhyou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="標">signpost</kanji> far down the road that you keep your <kanji form="目">eye</kanji> fixed on as you walk is your <vocabulary form="目標">goal / target</vocabulary>.

mokuteki.meaning_mnemonic: Fix your <kanji form="目">eye</kanji> on the <kanji form="的">target</kanji> at the far end of the range and let everything else blur. That one held point is your <vocabulary form="目的">purpose / goal</vocabulary>.

mokuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>tree</kanji> finally grows tall enough to shade a whole <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>, turning it into <vocabulary>Thursday</vocabulary>.

mondai.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>question</kanji> set as the <kanji>topic</kanji> at the top of a worksheet, waiting for you to crack it, is a <vocabulary>problem / question</vocabulary>.

mondaiten.meaning_mnemonic: Out of a whole report, the single <kanji>topic</kanji> every <kanji>question</kanji> keeps snagging on is the <vocabulary>problem point</vocabulary>.

mono.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thing</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>thing (object)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, and they point at the same idea, a plain object and nothing more.
mono.reading_mnemonic: On the farm the cow gets a sweet name, but the farmer calls every bucket and fork in one flat <reading>monotone</reading>: 「<reading>もの</reading>」, just a <vocabulary form="物">thing</vocabulary>.

morau.meaning_mnemonic: Your neighbour keeps lobbing enormous marrows over the riverbank fence for you to <vocabulary>receive</vocabulary>. Catching <reading>a marrow</reading> in both arms, day after day, is how you <reading>もらう</reading>.

mori.meaning_mnemonic: The single character <kanji>forest</kanji> is the entire word, nothing added and nothing dropped. What you met as a kanji and what you say out loud as <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> are the same thing.
mori.reading_mnemonic: Walk into the <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> and a mole named <reading>Morrie</reading> shoves his head up between two roots. He insists <reading>もり</reading> is his family name, since he dug every tunnel under these trees.

moshi.meaning_mnemonic: Rain has turned the riverbank path to <reading>mushy</reading> mud. The guide says that <reading>もし</reading> your boots sink in you should turn back, the word that sets up a plain <vocabulary form="もし">if (hypothetical)</vocabulary>.

motsu.meaning_mnemonic: Your two hands are the first pockets anyone ever had. Close your fingers around a thing and carry it off, and you <vocabulary>have</vocabulary> it.
motsu.reading_mnemonic: Moe the furniture mover carries every crate up six flights himself, both arms wrapped tight around each one. Whatever you grip the way <reading>Moe totes</reading> a crate, you <vocabulary>hold</vocabulary> — <reading>もつ</reading>.

motteiku.meaning_mnemonic: You clamp your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> around the lunchbox and <kanji form="行">go</kanji> straight out through the crossroads with it. Carrying the thing away from the house is <vocabulary form="持って行く">to take (a thing)</vocabulary>.

mottekuru.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> stays locked around the umbrella as you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> back in through the door. Arriving with the thing still in your hand is <vocabulary form="持って来る">to bring (a thing)</vocabulary>.

motto.meaning_mnemonic: The king's family <reading>motto</reading>, carved over his gate, is one greedy word. He bangs the table shouting <reading>もっと</reading> until the servants bring <vocabulary>more</vocabulary>.

mou.meaning_mnemonic: The cow at the riverbank drags out one long <reading>moo</reading> that sounds exactly like <reading>もう</reading>. She means the milking should have happened <vocabulary>already / soon</vocabulary>.

moushikomu.meaning_mnemonic: You fill in your name and push the sheet into the <kanji form="込">crowded</kanji> stack of everyone else's forms on the counter. Adding yourself to that packed pile is how you <vocabulary form="申し込む">apply</vocabulary> for a place.

mousu.meaning_mnemonic: You bend low and aim your words at the floor near an important person's feet, so they reach that person from below. Speaking from down there, kept small on purpose, is to <vocabulary form="申す">say something humbly</vocabulary>.
mousu.reading_mnemonic: Bowed so low your words land by the chairman's feet, you speak up to him like a <reading>mouse</reading> squeaking from the floor: <reading>もうす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="申す">say</vocabulary> something humbly.

moyasu.meaning_mnemonic: You rake the fallen leaves into a heap in the yard, hold a lighter to one edge, and step back as it takes. Setting a thing alight on purpose is what it is to <vocabulary form="燃やす">burn</vocabulary> it.
moyasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 燃える, so the twin where you are the one lighting the fire is <reading>もやす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="燃やす">burn</vocabulary> something.

muda.meaning_mnemonic: A mule hauls a <kanji form="駄">burdensome</kanji> load all day and brings back <kanji form="無">nothing</kanji> for it, so every step of that trip was <vocabulary form="無駄">wasteful / useless</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so な belongs before the noun it describes.

muika.meaning_mnemonic: The lid that turns eight into <kanji>six</kanji> clamps shut on one more <kanji>day</kanji>, and that trapped day makes <vocabulary>six days</vocabulary> in all.

mukaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You throw the front door open, step out onto the path, and draw your visitor inside by both hands: doing that to a guest is how you <vocabulary form="迎える">welcome / greet</vocabulary> them.
mukaeru.reading_mnemonic: A cow pulls up in a taxi with one long <reading>moo-car</reading> honk. You throw the front door open, step onto the path and draw her in by both hooves, <reading>むかえる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="迎える">welcome</vocabulary> her.

muri.meaning_mnemonic: A demand with <kanji form="無">nothing</kanji> behind it in the way of <kanji form="理">logic</kanji> cannot be argued for and cannot be met, which makes it <vocabulary form="無理">unreasonable / impossible</vocabulary>. As a な adjective, it needs な before any noun it modifies.

mushi.meaning_mnemonic: Tip up the old flowerpot by the back step and the packed soil under it comes alive with tiny legs and feelers that pour away from the daylight. Every scurrying speck down there is an <vocabulary form="虫">insect / bug</vocabulary>.
mushi.reading_mnemonic: Tip up the old flowerpot and the soil under it is wet and <reading>mushy</reading>, pouring tiny legs and feelers away from the light: each one a <vocabulary form="虫">bug</vocabulary>, a <reading>むし</reading>.

musuko.meaning_mnemonic: This household's only <kanji>child</kanji> happens to be a boy, so the family just calls him their <vocabulary>son</vocabulary>.
musuko.reading_mnemonic: The household's only child is a boy in a <reading>Moose Co.</reading> cap, so when the family calls 「<reading>むすこ</reading>」 at dinner, everyone knows they mean their <vocabulary form="息子">son</vocabulary>.

musume.meaning_mnemonic: Every family has one child who gets away with everything, and in this house that's always the <vocabulary>daughter</vocabulary>.
musume.reading_mnemonic: In this house the one child who gets away with everything is <reading>Moose May</reading>, dragging her toy moose across the clean floor while her parents only sigh 「<reading>むすめ</reading>」 at their <vocabulary form="娘">daughter</vocabulary>.

muttsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>six</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>six things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
muttsu.reading_mnemonic: A stray <reading>mutt</reading> knocks the little lid down onto the tall eight, and the pile under it shrinks to <reading>むっつ</reading>, just <vocabulary form="六つ">six things</vocabulary>.

muzukashii.meaning_mnemonic: The screw on the konbini door has a star, a slot, and a square all cut into one head. No tool Koichi owns can turn it, and a screw nothing turns is <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary>.
muzukashii.reading_mnemonic: A moose takes the cashier job at Koichi's konbini and cannot press the till buttons with hooves. Every shift the <reading>moose cashier</reading> sighs that the work is <reading>むずかしい</reading>, which just means <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary>.

nabe.meaning_mnemonic: A heavy dish sits over a flame in the middle of the table, and everyone drops in cabbage and tofu and fishes it back out. That dish, and the shared meal made in it, is a <vocabulary form="鍋">pot / hotpot</vocabulary>.
nabe.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>neighbour</reading> hauls her huge cast-iron <reading>なべ</reading> to every winter gathering, and nobody leaves the <vocabulary form="鍋">pot / hotpot</vocabulary> hungry.

nagai-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>long</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>long</vocabulary> word are the exact same character. The い tacked onto the end simply makes it an adjective.
nagai-adj.reading_mnemonic: The old wizard's beard piles so high on the floor that his old <reading>nag</reading> of a horse trips over it at the door. A beard that <reading>ながい</reading> is as <vocabulary form="長い">long</vocabulary> as they come.

nagareru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="流">current</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="流れる">flow</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana just make it a verb, water carrying itself along with nobody pushing it.
nagareru.reading_mnemonic: The river guide never stops talking, keeping up one long <reading>nagging rule</reading> about life jackets while the raft is swept on with no paddling. Water carrying things along on its own is what it means to <vocabulary form="流れる">flow</vocabulary>, 「<reading>ながれる</reading>」.

nagasu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="流">current</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="流す">let flow</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana make it the one you do to something, so you send the water on its way yourself.
nagasu.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 流れる, so the twin where you set the water moving yourself is <reading>ながす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="流す">let flow</vocabulary>.

nageku.meaning_mnemonic: After the storm the old farmer stands in the flattened field and says the same low words about the lost year, over and over, to no one. Letting that grief out loud like that is what it means <vocabulary form="嘆く">to lament</vocabulary>.
nageku.reading_mnemonic: On a fence post in the flattened field sits <reading>a gecko</reading>, and the old farmer pours his low words about the lost year out to it, over and over: <reading>なげく</reading>, to <vocabulary form="嘆く">lament</vocabulary>.

naifu.meaning_mnemonic: A doomsday preacher holds up a sign reading the end is <reading>nigh</reading> in one hand and a whittled 「<reading>ナイフ</reading>」 in the other, the <vocabulary>knife</vocabulary> he used to cut the sign loose.

naka.meaning_mnemonic: Written alone, the <kanji>inside</kanji> kanji is simply the word for <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>.
naka.reading_mnemonic: Shove the stick through the wide mouth until it stops dead in the <vocabulary form="中">middle</vocabulary>, then <reading>knock a</reading> knuckle on it, and whatever is pinned in there squeaks 「<reading>なか</reading>」.

nakama.meaning_mnemonic: Shrink the space <kanji>between</kanji> you and the people you share a <kanji>relationship</kanji> with until you all stand shoulder to shoulder, and they are your <vocabulary>companion / comrade</vocabulary>.

nakareru.meaning_mnemonic: The person beside you suddenly bursts out <kanji form="泣">crying</kanji>, and now their misery is your problem to deal with. Being left holding someone else's tears like that is being <vocabulary form="泣かれる">cried at</vocabulary>.
nakareru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「な」 from 泣く, so that same crying aimed at you, <vocabulary form="泣かれる">to be cried at (adversity)</vocabulary>, is <reading>なかれる</reading>.

naku.meaning_mnemonic: Water wells up along your lower lids until it spills over and runs down in two warm lines, and your breath keeps catching in hiccups. All of that at once is what it means to <vocabulary>cry</vocabulary>.
naku.reading_mnemonic: Each hiccup in your breath is a little <reading>knock</reading> in your chest while two warm lines run down your cheeks, <reading>なく</reading>, and that is what it is to <vocabulary form="泣く">cry</vocabulary>.

nakunaru.meaning_mnemonic: You reach for the sugar and find the jar emptied to <kanji>nothingness</kanji> on its own. When the last of a thing quietly hits zero, it has <vocabulary>run out</vocabulary>.
nakunaru.reading_mnemonic: You already learned this reading of 無 from 無くす, so a thing fading out of the world by itself, <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary>, is <reading>なくなる</reading>.

nakusu.meaning_mnemonic: Your keys should be in the front pocket, but your fingers close on <kanji>nothingness</kanji>. When a thing drops out of the world like that, you <vocabulary>lose</vocabulary> it.
nakusu.reading_mnemonic: Your keys should be in the front pocket of your <reading>knapsack</reading>, but your fingers close on nothing, <reading>なくす</reading>; they have dropped out of the world and you <vocabulary form="無くす">lose</vocabulary> them.

namae.meaning_mnemonic: The evening hides your face, so your <kanji>name</kanji> is the one word you send out in <kanji>front</kanji> of you. A word carried ahead like that, so strangers know who just spoke, is your <vocabulary>name</vocabulary>.

nami.meaning_mnemonic: Out on the open sea the water never settles; it stacks itself into a moving ridge, throws that ridge at the land, then draws back to build the next. Each moving ridge is a <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary>.
nami.reading_mnemonic: Out on the open sea, <reading>Nami</reading> the lifeguard rides each moving ridge toward the land, and when it draws back she yells <reading>なみ</reading> for the next <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary> to build.

nan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji still needs no help here. This reading just carries it forward as <vocabulary>what (before counters)</vocabulary>.
nan.reading_mnemonic: The person who swears they can do anything boasts about stacks of <reading>naan</reading>, so you ask <reading>なん</reading> before each count: <vocabulary form="何">what</vocabulary> number of loaves, really?
nan.description: なん appears only right before a counter, as in questions about quantity or time. Used alone, 何 takes a different reading instead.

nan-desu-ka.meaning_mnemonic: The word is nothing but the <kanji form="何">what</kanji> kanji asked aloud, which is why it lands on <vocabulary form="何ですか">what is it?</vocabulary>
nan-desu-ka.reading_mnemonic: The reading 「なん」 is one you already took from 何, so keep it: <reading>なんですか</reading> is simply <vocabulary form="何ですか">what is it?</vocabulary>

nana-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
nana-v.reading_mnemonic: A fan named <reading>Nana</reading> waves the big foam finger shaped like a <vocabulary form="七">seven</vocabulary>, chanting <reading>なな</reading> as its soft long end bends and curls up.

nanatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing. The trailing つ just turns the bare number into a count of objects.
nanatsu.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 七 is read なな, so <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>ななつ</reading>.

nani.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji needs no help to become a word. Alone, it already means <vocabulary>what</vocabulary>.
nani.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>nanny</reading> hears the person swear they can do absolutely anything and asks only <reading>なに</reading>, meaning <vocabulary form="何">what</vocabulary>, exactly?

nani-demo.meaning_mnemonic: Leave <kanji form="何">what</kanji> with no fixed answer in mind and it stretches to take in <vocabulary form="何でも">anything</vocabulary>.
nani-demo.reading_mnemonic: The sound 「なん」 is already yours from 何, so just carry it over: <vocabulary form="何でも">anything</vocabulary> is <reading>なんでも</reading>.

nani-mo.meaning_mnemonic: Ask <kanji form="何">what</kanji> is left in the bag, shake it, and hear <vocabulary form="何も">nothing (with negative)</vocabulary> rattle inside.
nani-mo.reading_mnemonic: The reading 「なに」 already came from 何, so keep it as is: <vocabulary form="何も">nothing (with negative)</vocabulary> is <reading>なにも</reading>.

nannji.meaning_mnemonic: Put <kanji>what</kanji> directly in front of <kanji>time</kanji> and you get the question itself, <vocabulary>what time</vocabulary>.

nanoka.meaning_mnemonic: String <kanji>seven</kanji> <kanji>suns</kanji> together and you get <vocabulary>seven days</vocabulary>, a full week gone by.

nantonaku.meaning_mnemonic: When something tugs at you but you cannot say <kanji form="何">what</kanji> it is, that faint pull is <vocabulary form="何となく">somehow / vaguely</vocabulary>.
nantonaku.reading_mnemonic: Since 何 already gave you 「なん」, this word just rides that sound: <vocabulary form="何となく">somehow / vaguely</vocabulary> is <reading>なんとなく</reading>.

naoru.meaning_mnemonic: When a fever or a sore throat <kanji form="治">calms down</kanji> and goes quiet on its own, with no one treating it, the body is starting to <vocabulary form="治る">recover</vocabulary>.
naoru.reading_mnemonic: Nao was stuck in bed a week with fever, then jogs onto the sports field and out-runs the whole class. The cheer of <reading>Nao rules</reading> again is <reading>なおる</reading>, the sound of a body that gets better on its own and <vocabulary form="治る">recovers</vocabulary>.

naosu.meaning_mnemonic: You could pretend the wobbly stool is fine, but <kanji>honesty</kanji> makes you admit the leg is loose, so you set it straight again. Owning what is broken and putting it right is what it means <vocabulary>to fix / repair</vocabulary> it.
naosu.reading_mnemonic: Honest Sue will not pretend the wobbly stool is fine: <reading>now, Sue</reading>, she tells herself, <reading>なおす</reading>, and she sets the loose leg straight to <vocabulary form="直す">fix</vocabulary> it.

naraberu.meaning_mnemonic: Take a shelf of jumbled cans and turn every label to face front, one behind the next, until they make a clean <kanji>row</kanji>. Setting objects out in a straight rank like that, by hand, is what it means <vocabulary>to line them up</vocabulary>.
naraberu.reading_mnemonic: Night clerk <reading>Nara Bell</reading> turns every jumbled can on the shelf label-out, one behind the next, humming 「<reading>ならべる</reading>」 because her whole job is <vocabulary form="並べる">to line up</vocabulary> the cans.

nareru.meaning_mnemonic: Do the same small thing every day and the odd feeling fades on its own. Once it is completely gone, you have <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it.
nareru.reading_mnemonic: A new <reading>nurse</reading> does the same small thing every day, one blood draw after another, until the odd feeling fades and she has <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it: <reading>なれる</reading>.

naru.meaning_mnemonic: You sit beside someone who can already do the thing and copy them move for move until your hands pick the skill up on their own. Taking it straight off another person that way is what it means to <vocabulary>learn (from)</vocabulary> them.
naru.reading_mnemonic: A tame deer in <reading>Nara</reading> trails a calligraphy student all afternoon, scratching a copy of every stroke he makes into the dust. He watches it ape him and mutters 「<reading>ならう</reading>」, which is what it means to <vocabulary>learn (from)</vocabulary> someone.

naru-become.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a smooth green sapling out on the mountain trail for thirty years. Nobody prunes it, yet the trunk twists and <reading>gnarls</reading> on its own, and turning into something new like that is to <vocabulary>become</vocabulary> — <reading>なる</reading>.

naru-ring.meaning_mnemonic: A phone left face-down on the konbini counter lets out its full-volume <kanji>cry</kanji> with nobody near it. A thing sounding off by itself is what it means to <vocabulary>ring</vocabulary>.
naru-ring.reading_mnemonic: A shop cat creeping along the <reading>narrow</reading> konbini counter freezes when the face-down phone goes 「<reading>なる</reading>」 at full volume, a thing left alone to <vocabulary form="鳴る">ring</vocabulary>.

naruhodo.meaning_mnemonic: Watch a barn dance long enough and the tangle of stamping feet suddenly locks into one clear pattern, like a <reading>Nara hoedown</reading> snapping into step. That click of it all making sense is <reading>なるほど</reading>, meaning <vocabulary form="なるほど">I see / indeed</vocabulary>.

nasaru.meaning_mnemonic: When the grand duchess Nessa decides a thing will happen, it happens — <reading>Nessa rules</reading> the whole estate, and whatever task she takes on, she personally <vocabulary form="なさる">does the action, honorifically</vocabulary>. The sound of that lands as <reading>なさる</reading>.

natsu.meaning_mnemonic: By breakfast your shirt is stuck to your back and the ice in your glass is gone in a minute. When the sun is still glaring at eight at night, it is <vocabulary>summer</vocabulary>.
natsu.reading_mnemonic: At eight at night the sun is still glaring, and a cloud of <reading>gnats</reading> sticks to your sweaty shirt and drowns in your melted ice. You swat and mutter <reading>なつ</reading>, because that is <vocabulary form="夏">summer</vocabulary>.

nayamu.meaning_mnemonic: You have two job offers and one week to pick, and every night you lie awake running the same lists. Turning a hard choice over and over until it wears a groove in you is <vocabulary form="悩む">to worry / agonize</vocabulary>.
nayamu.reading_mnemonic: Lying awake over the two job offers, you <reading>gnaw a yam</reading> at midnight and run the same lists again until they wear a groove: <reading>なやむ</reading>, to <vocabulary form="悩む">agonize</vocabulary>.

naze.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, one kid stops every teacher to ask なぜ about the rules. He won't take one more step until he knows <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>.

nedan.meaning_mnemonic: Every item on the shelf is standing on one <kanji>step</kanji> of a tall staircase, and how far up its step sits is the thing's <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

negau.meaning_mnemonic: Press your palms together and name aloud the one thing you want another person to grant you. That spoken hope is to <vocabulary form="願う">wish</vocabulary> or request something.
negau.reading_mnemonic: The polite お願いします already gave you this reading, so plain <vocabulary form="願う">to wish or request</vocabulary> is <reading>ねがう</reading>.

nekkuresu.meaning_mnemonic: Slip the jewelled chain off your collarbones and the bare skin leaves your <reading>neck less</reading> dressed than before. Put the chain back to fix that and you are wearing a <reading>ネックレス</reading>, a <vocabulary form="ネックレス">necklace</vocabulary>.

neko.meaning_mnemonic: It shoves a glass off the table, watches it drop, holds your eye the whole time, then strolls away. That animal is a <vocabulary>cat</vocabulary>.
neko.reading_mnemonic: After shoving your glass off the table and holding your eye as it smashes, the <vocabulary form="猫">cat</vocabulary> strolls up your arm and drapes itself over your <reading>neck, oh</reading> so smugly, purring <reading>ねこ</reading>.

nekutai.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning you loop a silk strip around your neck and tie it in a snug knot. That plain <reading>neck tie</reading> is a <reading>ネクタイ</reading>, a <vocabulary form="ネクタイ">necktie</vocabulary>.

nen-year.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>year</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>year (counter)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they mean the same thing.

neru.meaning_mnemonic: Your eyes slam shut and the book drops onto your face. The whole day switches off by itself, and you <vocabulary>sleep</vocabulary>.
neru.reading_mnemonic: With no <reading>nerve</reading> left to keep reading, a student lets the book drop onto his face and drifts off <vocabulary form="寝る">to sleep</vocabulary> with a slow 「<reading>ねる</reading>」.

nesshin.meaning_mnemonic: A steady <kanji form="熱">heat</kanji> kept burning in the <kanji form="心">heart</kanji> is what being <vocabulary form="熱心">enthusiastic</vocabulary> about something feels like. It is a な adjective, so な goes before the noun.

netsu.meaning_mnemonic: Lay the back of your hand on a sick child's forehead and it comes away warm, like a pebble left out in full sun. That trapped warmth pouring off the skin is a <vocabulary form="熱">fever / heat</vocabulary>.

ni-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>two</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.

nichi-day.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>day</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>day (counter)</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean the same thing.

nichiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> is too bright to share the sky, so the very first <kanji>weekday</kanji> takes its name straight from it, becoming <vocabulary>Sunday</vocabulary>.

nigai.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji here means <kanji form="苦">suffering</kanji>, and suffering on the tongue is exactly what <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary> is. The い on the end marks it as a describing word.
nigai.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Nigel</reading> the goat bites a dandelion stalk, and his tongue suffers so badly that he spits it out bleating <reading>にがい</reading>: suffering on the tongue is the taste of <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary>.

nigate.meaning_mnemonic: A task that brings your <kanji form="手">hand</kanji> nothing but <kanji form="苦">suffering</kanji> every time you try it is one you are <vocabulary form="苦手">bad at</vocabulary>. It is a な adjective, so it takes な before the noun it describes.

nigeru.meaning_mnemonic: The side door is propped open a crack, and by the time the guard turns back the cell is empty. Getting clear through a gap before anyone can stop you is what it means <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.
nigeru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Nigel</reading> the gerbil works a bar of his cage loose every night and is halfway down the hall before the lights come on. A small thing bolting for the gap the moment it opens is 「<reading>にげる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.

nigiyaka.meaning_mnemonic: On sports day the school field runs three races at once, a brass band, and parents yelling from every rail. All that noise and motion piled together is <vocabulary>lively / bustling</vocabulary>.
nigiyaka.reading_mnemonic: On sports day, a dad called <reading>Knee-gear-yakker</reading> yells louder than the brass band across all three races at once. That roar is <reading>にぎやか</reading>, and the whole school field is <vocabulary form="賑やか">lively</vocabulary>.

nihon.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> clears the horizon here first, at the very <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. That country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.
nihon.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the top of the mountain trail watches the sunrise and raps her <reading>knee bone</reading> twice for the beats as she names the country it rises over, 「<reading>にほん</reading>」, and that country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.

nihongo.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> rises first over the land at the <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. The <kanji>language</kanji> they speak there is <vocabulary>Japanese</vocabulary>.
nihongo.reading_mnemonic: As the sun rises first over that land, a goose on the shore greets it with a loud <reading>knee-honk-go</reading>, the day's first word of <vocabulary form="日本語">Japanese</vocabulary>: 「<reading>にほんご</reading>」.

nikki.meaning_mnemonic: A written <kanji form="記">account</kanji> that breaks the usual rule and is only ever about your own <kanji form="日">day</kanji> is a <vocabulary form="日記">diary</vocabulary>.

niku.meaning_mnemonic: Overnight, every shelf in Koichi's konbini is restocked with nothing but <vocabulary>meat</vocabulary>. Cold steaks fill the onigiri rack, sausages crowd the drinks fridge, and a slab of ribs beeps through the till.

nimotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Any <kanji>thing</kanji> you own that isn't nailed down, crammed into two bags for the trip, becomes your <vocabulary>luggage</vocabulary>.

nin-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Stand in a doorway and tap each <kanji>person</kanji> on the shoulder as they stride through on the two legs you already know. Every tap adds one more to your count of <vocabulary>people (counter)</vocabulary>.

nishi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>west</kanji> kanji is the entire <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> word by itself, so the two mean precisely the same thing.
nishi-v.reading_mnemonic: Every evening the sinking sun burns a glowing <reading>niche</reading> into the <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> wall of the shrine. The cats curl into that <reading>にし</reading>-shaped alcove for the last of the warmth.

niwa.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the strip of bare ground that a Japanese house wraps itself around, half swept dirt and half stubborn weeds. The family still points at that patch and proudly calls it the <vocabulary>garden / yard</vocabulary>.
niwa.reading_mnemonic: Nao kneels on the strip of swept dirt the house wraps around, and each stubborn weed she yanks makes her yelp <reading>nee-wah</reading>, 「<reading>にわ</reading>」, in the family's proud <vocabulary form="庭">garden</vocabulary>.

noboru.meaning_mnemonic: The only way up to the tree house is the knotted rope, hand over hand, feet slipping on bark. Hauling yourself up something steep like that, using your whole body, is what it means <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary>.
noboru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>No bull</reading> could get up the knotted rope to the tree house, but you go hand over hand, feet slipping on bark, <reading>のぼる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="登る">climb</vocabulary>.

nokoru.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone clears out of the classroom at the bell. The one bag still by the window, after the rest are gone, is what <vocabulary>remains</vocabulary>.
nokoru.reading_mnemonic: As the bell empties the classroom, a kid spots Coral's bag still by the window and yells <reading>no, Coral</reading>, 「<reading>のこる</reading>」, since that bag is all that <vocabulary form="残る">remains</vocabulary>.

nomeru.meaning_mnemonic: No story to build here: the <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> kanji is the whole word, and <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> means the very same thing.
nomeru.reading_mnemonic: You know 「の」 already from 飲む, so <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> follows straight on as <reading>のめる</reading>.

nomimono.meaning_mnemonic: Among all the nameless <kanji>things</kanji> in the barn, the one you tip up and <kanji>drink</kanji> instead of chewing is the <vocabulary>drink</vocabulary>.

nomu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>drink</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to drink</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning does not shift. The tail kana only turns it into the verb you aim at a full glass of water.
nomu-v.reading_mnemonic: A desert <reading>nomad</reading> finishes his tray of food, stretches his mouth yawn-wide and sighs 「<reading>のむ</reading>」 until someone pours water straight in for him <vocabulary form="飲む">to drink</vocabulary>.

nooto.meaning_mnemonic: You scribble one <reading>note</reading>, then a hundred more, then clamp the whole pile flat between two cardboard covers. That fat brick of paper is a 「<reading>ノート</reading>」, your <vocabulary>notebook</vocabulary>.

noreru.meaning_mnemonic: This word adds nothing to its kanji: <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> is the <kanji form="乗">ride</kanji> kanji you have already met, unchanged.
noreru.reading_mnemonic: The 「の」 in this word comes straight from 乗る, so <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>のれる</reading>.

noru.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a peaked cap hauls itself up into the night bus and grabs the rail as the bus pulls away. That scramble up onto a moving vehicle is what it means to <vocabulary>board</vocabulary>.
noru.reading_mnemonic: The badger's electric bus rolls up with <reading>no roar</reading> at all, so you almost miss it in the dark. Jump on before the doors close and you 「<reading>のる</reading>」 — you <vocabulary>ride</vocabulary>.

nouka.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>house</kanji> standing alone out in the crop fields, pig still under its roof, worked from dawn to dusk by whoever lives there, is a <vocabulary>farmhouse / farmer</vocabulary>.

noyama.meaning_mnemonic: The open <kanji form="野">plains</kanji> the village never fenced, set against the <kanji form="山">mountain</kanji> at their back, are together the <vocabulary form="野山">fields and mountains</vocabulary>.

nugu.meaning_mnemonic: The only way to <kanji>escape</kanji> a soaked raincoat is to peel it down off your arms and let it drop. Peeling a garment off your body like that is what it means to <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary>.
nugu.reading_mnemonic: A walrus flops onto the riverbank and drags its dripping wetsuit off over its head. It grunts 「<reading>ぬぐ</reading>」 as a cold <reading>nugget</reading> of riverweed plops from the sleeve, because it will <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary> anywhere.

nurasu.meaning_mnemonic: You tip a full watering can straight over the folded picnic blanket until it is soaked through and heavy. Pouring water onto a thing until it is soaked is what it is to <vocabulary form="濡らす">wet</vocabulary> it.
nurasu.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>gnu</reading> grabs the full watering can in its teeth and tips it over your folded picnic blanket until it sags heavy. Soaking it on purpose like that is to <vocabulary form="濡らす">wet</vocabulary> it, <reading>ぬらす</reading>.

nureru.meaning_mnemonic: The sky opens while you are still ten minutes from home with no umbrella, and by the corner your shirt is stuck to your back. Rain landing on you until you are soaked is what it is to <vocabulary form="濡れる">get wet</vocabulary>.
nureru.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 濡らす, so the twin where you end up <vocabulary form="濡れる">wet</vocabulary> with no say in it is <reading>ぬれる</reading>.

nurui.meaning_mnemonic: Louie pours you a coffee that has sat out so long it is neither hot nor cold. A drink stuck at room temperature like that is <vocabulary form="ぬるい">lukewarm</vocabulary>, and hearing <reading>new Louie</reading> pour another one is how you keep hold of 「<reading>ぬるい</reading>」.

nyuugaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary form="入学する">enter school</vocabulary> is simply to <kanji form="入">enter</kanji> through the gate on your first morning and join the <kanji form="学">learning</kanji> already going on inside.

nyuuin-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="入">enter</kanji> the medical <kanji form="院">institution</kanji> as a patient, the doors fall shut, and you are not sleeping at home tonight. Ending up kept inside like that is what it means <vocabulary form="入院する">to be hospitalized</vocabulary>.

nyuusu.meaning_mnemonic: The bundle on the counter holds nothing but <reading>new</reading> things — a fire last night, a price that jumped this morning, none of it old yet. A stack of only-just-happened facts is the <vocabulary form="ニュース">news</vocabulary>, and you ask for it as <reading>ニュース</reading>.

oba.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mother</kanji> figure who's still just a <kanji>youth</kanji> herself, holding kids anyway, is your <vocabulary>aunt</vocabulary>.
oba.reading_mnemonic: Still a youth herself, your <vocabulary form="叔母">aunt</vocabulary> holds the little cousins on her lap anyway and calms them with one squeaky <reading>oboe</reading> note that sounds just like <reading>おば</reading>.
oba.description: An aunt younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

obaasan.meaning_mnemonic: An old woman dozes in a sunbeam and lets out a long, satisfied <reading>おばあさん</reading> — <reading>"ohh, baa, sun"</reading> — and that sigh is exactly what you call your <vocabulary>grandmother (polite)</vocabulary>.
obaasan.description: Also used to politely address any elderly woman, not just your own grandmother.

oboeru.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>memorize</vocabulary> a list is just <kanji>remembering</kanji> forced on purpose. You drill each item into your skull, over and over, until it cannot slip back out.
oboeru.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing school hallway a kid plays the same four bars on her <reading>oboe</reading>, eyes shut, until her fingers move on their own. Drilling something in until it sticks like that is <reading>おぼえる</reading>, which is how you <vocabulary>memorize</vocabulary> anything.

ocha.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tea</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>tea</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing; meeting it again as a word changes nothing.
ocha.description: In everyday Japanese お茶 usually means green tea, not tea in general.

ochiru.meaning_mnemonic: A ripe chestnut lets go of its branch above the mountain trail. It <vocabulary>falls</vocabulary> to the path on its own, with no hand anywhere near it.
ochiru.reading_mnemonic: Under the chestnut tree on the mountain trail, a hiker hears one ripe nut let go and calls <reading>oh, cheerio</reading>, 「<reading>おちる</reading>」, as it is left to <vocabulary form="落ちる">fall</vocabulary> on its own.

odaiji-ni.meaning_mnemonic: A sick friend should treat getting better as a <kanji form="大">big</kanji> <kanji form="事">matter</kanji>, barbed to them so they cannot set it down. Telling them so is how you say <vocabulary form="お大事に">take care (get well)</vocabulary>.

odoroku.meaning_mnemonic: You lift a plant pot to move it and the whole underside is crawling with woodlice spilling out at once. The jump in your chest and the step back you take before you can think is being <vocabulary form="驚く">surprised</vocabulary>.
odoroku.reading_mnemonic: You tip up what looks like an <reading>odd rock</reading> by the step and it opens into a crab and runs across your foot. You are standing before you have decided to move, and that jolt at a thing you did not expect is 「<reading>おどろく</reading>」, <vocabulary form="驚く">to be surprised</vocabulary>.

odoru.meaning_mnemonic: Your hips swing, your feet cross and stamp, and your arms cut shapes in the air in time with a beat. All that patterned motion to music is what it means to <vocabulary>dance</vocabulary>.
odoru.reading_mnemonic: Your hips swing and your feet stamp in time with the beat until you crash into the <reading>odd door</reading> in the hall, <reading>おどる</reading>, still moving: that is to <vocabulary form="踊る">dance</vocabulary>.

ohayou.meaning_mnemonic: Say the word slowly and it comes out as <reading>Ohio</reading>, the American state. Land that sound before dawn and you have <reading>おはよう</reading>, the <vocabulary>good morning</vocabulary> you give before anyone has had coffee.

oikakeru.meaning_mnemonic: A bun rolls off the bakery shelf and a boy runs after it down three aisles, hands out, never quite closing the gap. Staying right behind a thing that will not stop, trying to catch it, is what it means <vocabulary form="追いかける">to chase</vocabulary>.
oikakeru.reading_mnemonic: The baker bellows <reading>oi, cack-a-roo</reading> at the boy hopping down three aisles after the runaway bun, never quite closing the gap: <reading>おいかける</reading>, to <vocabulary form="追いかける">chase</vocabulary>.

oishii.meaning_mnemonic: You try the free sample at Koichi's konbini, your eyebrows shoot up, and all you can say is '<reading>oh, I see</reading>' — now you finally get the queue outside. That jolt of understanding is 「<reading>おいしい</reading>」, <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>, and its final い marks it as an adjective.

oji.meaning_mnemonic: A backup <kanji>father</kanji> who shows up every holiday, spoils you rotten, and sneaks you extra sweets is your <vocabulary>uncle</vocabulary>.
oji.reading_mnemonic: Every holiday the backup dad sneaks you so many extra sweets that your parents gasp '<reading>oh, gee</reading>', the <reading>おじ</reading> sound that follows your spoiling <vocabulary form="叔父">uncle</vocabulary> everywhere.
oji.description: An uncle younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

ojiisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a <vocabulary>grandfather (polite)</vocabulary> groans 「<reading>おじいさん</reading>」, sounding just like <reading>oh, geez, Sam</reading>, every time his grandson rings the giant bell too hard.

okaasan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji is already mother, so <vocabulary>mother (polite)</vocabulary> just wraps that same meaning in politeness.
okaasan.reading_mnemonic: With a small child tucked under each arm, she cannot open the <reading>car</reading> door, so the kids politely call 「<reading>おかあさん</reading>」 until their <vocabulary form="お母さん">mother</vocabulary> nudges it open with her hip.
okaasan.description: Use お母さん to speak to or about someone else's mother. For your own mother, switch to the plainer 母 when talking to an outsider.

okaerinasai.meaning_mnemonic: You hand the sweeper to whoever just <kanji>returned</kanji> through the front door, and the greeting that goes with it is <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary>.
okaerinasai.reading_mnemonic: You already know 帰 is 「かえ」 from 帰る, so <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary> is <reading>おかえりなさい</reading>.

okane.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>money</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>money</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
okane.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her gold coins in a little roofed safe, and when she lifts the lid, visitors gasp '<reading>oh, Kane</reading>' at so much <vocabulary form="お金">money</vocabulary>: 「<reading>おかね</reading>」.

okashi.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Cakes</kanji> come in adult size, but shrink each one to <kanji>child</kanji> size and you can eat twelve without comment. A bowl of those miniatures is <vocabulary>sweets / snacks</vocabulary>.

oki-ni-mesu.meaning_mnemonic: A fine object <kanji form="召">calls</kanji> out to a person's <kanji form="気">spirit</kanji> and lifts it like steam off a mown field. Something that can do that has managed <vocabulary form="お気に召す">to be pleasing (honorific)</vocabulary>.
oki-ni-mesu.description: Honorific, and used only about what pleases someone you are raising up, such as a guest, customer, or superior. Never use it for your own likes.

okiru.meaning_mnemonic: The alarm has howled for a full hour. Your eyes crack open, your back peels off the futon, and you <vocabulary>wake up / get up</vocabulary>.
okiru.reading_mnemonic: After the alarm howls for a full hour, Roo the kangaroo peels his back off the futon, mumbling <reading>OK, Roo</reading>, 「<reading>おきる</reading>」, and finally has to <vocabulary form="起きる">get up</vocabulary>.

okonau.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="行">go</kanji> from talking about a plan to running it for real. Taking a ceremony or a survey and actually staging it is what it means to <vocabulary form="行う">carry out / conduct</vocabulary> it.
okonau.reading_mnemonic: Koichi opens every konbini restock drill by clapping once and calling 「<reading>OK, now</reading>」. That is his cue to 「<reading>おこなう</reading>」 the plan, to <vocabulary form="行う">carry out / conduct</vocabulary> it exactly as written.

okoru-angry.meaning_mnemonic: Someone slides into the parking spot you waited ten minutes for and smirks at you through the glass. Your face goes hot, your voice climbs, and that sudden flare of temper is what it means <vocabulary form="怒る">to get angry</vocabulary>.
okoru-angry.reading_mnemonic: The driver who slid into your parking spot smirks at you over a tub of <reading>okra</reading>, and your face goes hot as your voice climbs: <reading>おこる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="怒る">get angry</vocabulary>.

oku.meaning_mnemonic: You set the heavy box down on the floor exactly where you want it, then lift your hands away. Leaving a thing to rest in a chosen spot is to <vocabulary>put</vocabulary> it there.
oku.reading_mnemonic: You set the heavy <reading>oak</reading> box down on the floor exactly where you want it, 「<reading>おく</reading>」, and lift your hands away, which is to <vocabulary form="置く">put</vocabulary> it there.

okureru.meaning_mnemonic: The last train slides out of the station without you. Slipping behind the clock, with only your slow feet to blame, is to <vocabulary>be late</vocabulary>.
okureru.reading_mnemonic: Sei reaches the platform with a bag of <reading>okra</reading> just as the last train slides out, 「<reading>おくれる</reading>」. Missing it because of slow feet is to be <vocabulary form="遅れる">late</vocabulary>.

okuru.meaning_mnemonic: A parcel bound for another city and a friend boarding the last train get the very same treatment: you hand it over, then stand there watching it get smaller. That watching-it-leave is what it means to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary>.
okuru.reading_mnemonic: Every week the farmer mails a crate of <reading>okra</reading> to her sister and weeps on the platform as the train goes. The town decided that to <reading>おくる</reading> is to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary> with your whole heart.

okusan.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever rules the <kanji>interior</kanji> of the house earns the title <vocabulary>wife</vocabulary>.
okusan.reading_mnemonic: From an <reading>oak</reading> chair deep in the house's interior she rules every room, so visitors bow and greet her 「<reading>おくさん</reading>」, the <vocabulary form="奥さん">wife</vocabulary> of the house.

okutte-ageru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="送">send</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="送ってあげる">to send (for someone)</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing.
okutte-ageru.reading_mnemonic: You already know 送 is 「おく」 from 送る, the verb to send, so <vocabulary form="送ってあげる">to send (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>おくってあげる</reading>.

okyakusan.meaning_mnemonic: That same visitor, but bowed to on the way in, thanked on the way out, and spoken of only in the polite words staff keep for people they serve, is a <vocabulary>customer (polite)</vocabulary>.

omedetou.meaning_mnemonic: A baker flips a flawless omelette off a lump of fresh <reading>omelette dough</reading>. The whole cafe stands up and shouts <reading>おめでとう</reading>, which is how you say <vocabulary form="おめでとう">congratulations</vocabulary>.

omoi.meaning_mnemonic: A suitcase you pack full of bricks and then cannot drag an inch across the floor is <vocabulary>heavy</vocabulary>. The い on the end is what makes it an adjective, the same ending every describing word like it takes.
omoi.reading_mnemonic: Old Omura grabs the suitcase packed full of bricks and tugs, but it will not budge an inch across the floor. He groans <reading>oh my</reading>, <reading>おもい</reading>, because it is far too <vocabulary form="重い">heavy</vocabulary>.

omoshiroi.meaning_mnemonic: A clown's <kanji>mask</kanji>, painted flat <kanji>white</kanji>, is the thing the whole room turns to watch. Whatever pulls every eye in a room like that is <vocabulary>interesting / funny</vocabulary>.

omou.meaning_mnemonic: You never reason this kind out; you just hold it, the way you cup a warm mug or trust a quiet hunch. Carrying an opinion around like that is to <vocabulary>think, to feel</vocabulary>.
omou.reading_mnemonic: A cow cups a warm mug in her hooves, trusts a quiet hunch and lets out a soft <reading>oh, moo</reading>, 「<reading>おもう</reading>」, which is how you <vocabulary form="思う">feel</vocabulary> a thing without reasoning it out.

onaji.meaning_mnemonic: Two socks from one dryer load, worn to a matching grey heel, are for every purpose the <vocabulary>same</vocabulary>. Handle it as a な adjective, so な lands before the noun it describes.
onaji.reading_mnemonic: Pulling two grey-heeled socks from one dryer load, a boy holds them up to his gran and sighs <reading>oh, Nan, gee</reading>, 「<reading>おなじ</reading>」, since the pair really is the <vocabulary form="同じ">same</vocabulary>.

onaka.meaning_mnemonic: The soft drum you pat after a big lunch, the part that growls in a silent room, is your <vocabulary>stomach / belly</vocabulary>.
onaka.reading_mnemonic: One more dumpling drifts toward the sumo trainee and he waves it off, both palms flat on his <vocabulary>stomach / belly</vocabulary>: <reading>oh, not a</reading>nother bite. The groan lands as 「<reading>おなか</reading>」.

oneesan.meaning_mnemonic: A lost traveler at the riverbank asks a young woman for directions, calling her <vocabulary>older sister (polite)</vocabulary> before he even learns her name.
oneesan.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the lost traveler stretches his polite 「<reading>おねえさん</reading>」 into a long horse-like <reading>neigh</reading>, asking the way from a young woman he has never met but calls <vocabulary form="お姉さん">older sister</vocabulary>.
oneesan.description: Use お姉さん for any young woman addressed politely — a shop clerk, a stranger — not only an actual older sister.

onegaishimasu.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>request</kanji> held out flat in both hands, with <vocabulary>please</vocabulary> set on top like a bow on a box. That polite wrapping around the ask is the whole word.
onegaishimasu.reading_mnemonic: You hold your request out flat in both hands, a bow on top like a gift box, and murmur <reading>oh, need I ask</reading>, 「<reading>おねがいします</reading>」, the polite wrapping that means <vocabulary form="お願いします">please</vocabulary>.

ongaku.meaning_mnemonic: Take the kind of <kanji>sound</kanji> that makes you sit up in a silent room and string it along a branch like ice beads until sitting and listening is pure <kanji>comfort</kanji>. That is <vocabulary>music</vocabulary>.

ongakushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Pack every <kanji>sound</kanji> a school makes into one room where the only <kanji>music</kanji> is on the timetable, and that is the <vocabulary>music room</vocabulary>.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: A tired customer at Koichi's konbini calls the teenage clerk an <vocabulary>older brother (polite)</vocabulary> before he even rings up her onigiri, though they have never met.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the teenage clerk bangs his <reading>knee</reading> on the counter grabbing her onigiri, and the tired customer gasps 「<reading>おにいさん</reading>」, still politely calling a stranger her <vocabulary form="お兄さん">older brother</vocabulary>.
oniisan.description: Use お兄さん for any young man addressed politely — a waiter, a stranger — not only an actual older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: The door meant for any <kanji>person</kanji> gets repainted with a <kanji>woman</kanji> stick figure, so now it specifies exactly which <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary> may enter.
onnanohito.description: 女 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific woman; 女の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: A costume shop sells a miniature <kanji>woman</kanji> outfit sized only for a <kanji>child</kanji>, and whoever fits into it is simply called a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>.

ooi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>many</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>many</vocabulary> word are the same character. The い hooked on the end marks it as an adjective, a habit every い adjective keeps.
